item.title: Four Months After Rafael, Corpus Christi Is Rebuilding — and Reckoning
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: On the four-month mark of Hurricane Rafael's landfall, the Bayside Ledger surveys what has been repaired, what has been reformed, and what still remains undone — through statistics, court records, and the voices of people who stayed.
item.content:encoded:
Four months ago, Hurricane Rafael came ashore before dawn on a Tuesday with 125-mile-per-hour winds and a storm surge that turned the streets of Districts 3 and 4 into rivers. This newspaper has covered nearly every development since — the grid collapse, the water crisis, the spill in the bay, the hospitals overwhelmed beyond capacity, the federal investigations, the fraud arrests. Standing in those same districts on a gray morning, it is worth asking what the numbers say, and what they don't.

By most statistical measures, the recovery is on track. Power has been back on for every customer since Oct. 19. Eighty-nine percent of businesses that were open before Rafael have reopened. The $2.1 billion in insurance claims filed across the three-county region is moving through the pipeline, though adjusters and homeowners' attorneys say the more complex commercial claims could take another year to resolve. Part of the bay's fishing grounds reopened last week after testing; of the 340 oiled birds recovered after the tanker spill, 218 were treated and released back to the Gulf.

Not everything that changed was scheduled. The 12-hour gap in bilingual emergency alerts — which the hospitals' joint after-action report directly linked to a preventable spike in gastroenteritis among Spanish-speaking households — produced an institutional response: Nueces County commissioners voted in October to require that Spanish-language versions of emergency notices be released within 30 minutes of the English text. Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center now maintain 24/7 Spanish-speaking clinical staffing in their emergency departments. Operation Sandbar brought 14 arrests in December in the disaster-fraud case that targeted Districts 3 and 4; the case is pending in federal court.

Some threads are still loose. The federal investigation into the cyberattack on area utility infrastructure — publicly acknowledged in the weeks after the storm — remains open, and no attribution for it has been made public. The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has implemented enhanced operational-technology security protocols, but officials say they cannot discuss the investigation's specifics. Infrastructure hardening in Districts 3 and 4 is still underway under a federal mitigation grant, with targeted completion set for spring.

On Lipan Street in District 3 on Monday, a homeowner who declined to give her name was pulling the last of a storm-damaged interior wall out of her house. She said she expected to be done with repairs by spring. 'I'm getting there,' she said. 'But I'm still not there.' A few blocks over, a retired longshoreman who had ridden out Rafael in his home said he thought the city had handled the aftermath about as well as a city could.

item.title: Rafael, four months on: four neighbors, four kinds of waiting
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño, Ellie Navarro
item.description: A home health aide, a schoolteacher, a shrimper and a bait shop owner take stock as rebuilding continues and reviews of water, aid, port security and contracting go on.
item.content:encoded:
Four months after Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island, the Coastal Bend is still rebuilding, and the reviews are still running: of the water system, of who got aid, of port security, of emergency contracts. For the people the Ledger has followed since the storm, recovery looks different on every street.

Near the bay. Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, finally has a ceiling. Her landlord patched the hallway leak the first week of January, she said. Her aid application is still pending, and she is still waiting for the door-to-door teams the county and FEMA announced in December to reach her street. "Bob is retired," she said of the bucket that caught the drip for months. "Now I need FEMA to un-pend me. They're slow, but I'm stubborn."

In Calallen. Leticia Ramos, 45, the schoolteacher who organized her neighbors' water runs during the five-week boil-water notice, still keeps her spreadsheet. "I deleted the jug column. I kept the phone numbers," she said. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds; Ramos wants dates. "A plan without a deadline is a wish," she said.

In Aransas Pass. Shrimper Huy Nguyen, 51, saw part of the fishing grounds reopen last week after testing. His is one of about 4,200 spill damage claims filed so far. "Some water open. No check yet. Boat payment every month," he said.

In Port Aransas. Bill Hargrove, 64, has his bait shop near the jetties stocked again, mostly. "Two-thirds of a store and all of the jokes," he said. He is counting the weeks to spring break. "If the fish come back and the tourists come back, I'll forgive this whole year. Probably."

The analysis that showed low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like Elizondo's got aid dollars at about half their share of residents is part of what the reviews are now weighing.

Elizondo said the day she is waiting for isn't on a calendar. "When my kids stop asking if the water is coming back," she said, "that's when it's over."

item.title: Port of Corpus Christi starts 2028 with an open channel and a longer to-do list
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Exports are flowing after two closures in a single fall. The port's spokesman says resilience and security will shape the year.
item.content:encoded:
A loaded tanker slid under the Harbor Bridge on Monday morning, trailed by gulls, the kind of sight that drew no attention a year ago and drew a few phone cameras this fall, when the channel sat empty for weeks.

The Port of Corpus Christi enters 2028 with its channel open, exports flowing and a list of lessons from a fall that closed it twice: first for Hurricane Rafael in September, then for 14 days after an explosive device went off beside a tug near the Port Aransas jetties in October.

Since then, the channel reopened Nov. 11 and exports resumed. Vessel operators were told by the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. And last week, U.S. officials attributed the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems to a foreign government they did not name.

"The channel is open, the docks are working and our customers are shipping," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This fall taught us that being ready for hurricanes isn't the whole job anymore. We'll keep working with the Coast Guard and our federal partners on the rest of it."

Salinas declined to discuss specific security measures.

The stakes reach well beyond Nueces County. Before the storm, the port was handling about half of U.S. crude exports. When the channel closed, those exports stopped. The partial reopening in October also left relief cargo waiting in an anchorage backlog.

What to watch this year: whether vessel operators finish the vendor-access reviews federal agencies have urged; how the port and its tenants plan for the next storm-season closure; and whether lessons from the anchorage backlog turn into new procedures before June.

"We had a hard fall," Salinas said. "We'd like a boring summer."

item.title: Opinion: Finish the door-to-door work before the last chapter of Rafael is written
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: An opinion column. A federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted. The neighborhoods that got the least still need someone to knock.
item.content:encoded:
I've spent four months in the neighborhoods near the bay where the water came up highest and help came last. I've watched people fill out the same form three times, sit on hold through a lunch break, and wait months on a ceiling that dripped into a bucket.

In December, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher put a number on what those residents had been telling us since September: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

This week, a federal civil forfeiture filing put a number on something else: about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid that, the filing says, went to bank accounts tied to two storm contractors. Those claims have not been proven in court, and the companies are entitled to answer them. But the figure lands hard in neighborhoods that got about half their share.

In December, the county and FEMA promised door-to-door registration in those neighborhoods. That promise is the most useful thing to come out of this review season. It is also the easiest to let slide once the headlines move on.

Here is what finishing it looks like. Knock on every door, and go back to the ones that don't answer. Send people who speak Spanish. Leave paper, not just a link. Publish how many households were reached, by neighborhood, every two weeks until the job is done. And make sure every applicant whose deposit details were hijacked is repaid, as FEMA has promised.

The church halls that fed these neighborhoods before the trucks came are still open. They should not have to be the plan.

Marisol Treviño is the Ledger's city and disaster reporter. This column reflects her views.

item.title: From a sole-source award to a forfeiture filing: the paper trail on two storm contractors
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: In less than four months, two companies hired after Rafael went from emergency contracts to a federal filing naming a shared offshore owner. A timeline from the public record.
item.content:encoded:
Four months ago, few people in the Coastal Bend had heard of Vantorra Restoration or Quellmar Fuel Partners. On Thursday, a federal civil forfeiture filing said both share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick, and that about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid landed in bank accounts tied to the firms. Here is how the public record got there.

Sept. 24: Ten days after landfall, the county awards Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.

Oct. 4: Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi to Quellmar, after the station's regular supplier flooded.

Oct. 25: During a power interruption, the station's backup generator fails, the station says. Power is restored, and the cause goes under review.

Nov. 17 to Nov. 24: In a separate FEMA matter, aid applicants report deposit details changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirms unauthorized access, then says 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts. FEMA says affected applicants will be repaid.

Nov. 28: Quellmar is suspended by the Navy, pending a fuel quality review tied to the generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

Dec. 1: Records show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane denies overbilling.

Dec. 3: Payments to Vantorra are put on hold while the county audits its billing.

Dec. 7: Emergency debris and fuel contracts across the Coastal Bend come under a federal inspector general's review.

Dec. 27: FBI agents execute search warrants at both companies' offices.

Jan. 6: The forfeiture filing names the shared owner and the diverted aid. Vantorra says it will respond through its attorneys; Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr says the company will respond in court.

A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and the filing's claims have not been proven in court. No one has been criminally charged in the public record so far.

What the public record does not yet show: how the aid was diverted, whether anyone will face criminal charges, and what the county audit and the inspector general's review will find. The Ledger will keep reading the filings.

item.title: Fishing grounds partly reopen after testing as spill claims reach about 4,200
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Part of the bay waters closed since the September oil spill reopened after testing. Shrimpers say it's a start, and the claims keep coming.
item.content:encoded:
Part of the fishing grounds closed since oil spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays in September reopened after testing, and about 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed by fishers and shoreline owners, officials said Friday.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, after surge and wind carried crude spilled at an Inner Harbor terminal across about 33 square miles of water. The fishing closure was extended in October, and spill cleanup moved to monitoring at the end of that month.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Areas that are still closed stay closed until their results say otherwise. Check the current closure maps before you go out."

Since September the tanker owners' claims center has taken property damage claims, and since Nov. 16 it has also taken lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses. Whitaker urged anyone who lost income or property to the spill to file and to keep records. "If you haven't filed and you think you're owed, file. If you filed, keep your receipts and your trip logs," he said.

In Aransas Pass, shrimper Huy Nguyen said the news was welcome and not enough.

"Part of the bay is part of a living," said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose boat survived the storm but whose season did not. "I filed my claim in November. I'm still paying on the boat. Fuel is not cheaper because the oil was in the water."

Nguyen said he planned to run his boat out to look at the reopened water before deciding what to do with the rest of the winter. He has fished these bays most of his life, and he said he wanted to see the water for himself before trusting it.

"The test says it's OK. I believe the test," he said. "I still want to look."

He counted it out the way he counts most things, in numbers.

"Four thousand two hundred people waiting. I'm one," he said. "We'll see who gets paid first."

item.title: Federal filing: storm debris and fuel contractors share offshore owner; accounts got $3.9 million in diverted aid
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: A civil forfeiture filing says Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners are both owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company, and that bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
item.content:encoded:
Two companies hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, and bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing names debris hauler Vantorra Restoration LLC and fuel supplier Quellmar Fuel Partners. It lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick.

A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person, and it is not a criminal charge. The filing's claims are allegations that have not been proven in court.

"The filing speaks for itself. Its claims are allegations, and the owners of the property will have the opportunity to respond in court," said Alan Reyes, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. He declined to comment on anything not described in the filing.

Both firms have been under scrutiny for months. The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract on Sept. 24. Records reported by the Ledger in December show it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated, which the company denies; the county paused payments pending an audit. Quellmar was awarded a $2.1 million contract to supply emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review, and the company says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts Dec. 7, and FBI agents searched both companies' offices on Dec. 27.

The filing describes the $3.9 million as diverted disaster aid but does not say how it was diverted, and Reyes would not elaborate. Separately, in November, FEMA said 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts and their deposit details changed, and that affected applicants would be repaid.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said Thursday that the company "did the work we were hired to do" and would respond through its attorneys. He did not answer questions about the company's ownership.

Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, said in a statement that "all product Quellmar delivered met specifications" and that the company would respond in court.

item.title: Opinion: The storm was natural. The port's defenses have to account for what wasn't
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: An opinion column. Federal officials now say a foreign government tried to exploit Rafael. The port and its partners should plan for the next hurricane as a security event, too.
item.content:encoded:
For four months, the story of Hurricane Rafael on the water has been told in the language of weather: surge heights, wind speeds, the bad luck of two loaded tankers at the berth when the storm came in. On Tuesday, federal officials changed the vocabulary.

U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government, which they did not name, and called them attempts to exploit the hurricane. Every port authority, terminal operator and shipping line on the Gulf should read that sentence twice.

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports. For 14 days this fall, after the blast at the jetties, it handled none. A hurricane will always close the channel for a while. The lesson of Rafael is that a hurricane can also be cover.

Some of the work has started. Last week, the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to take a hard look at which vendors can reach their cargo systems remotely. In December, the Navy ordered a security review at its Texas air stations. Those are good first steps, and they are mostly federal.

What is missing is a local plan that treats the next storm as both a weather event and a security event. When the next hurricane closes the channel, who keeps watch on the water while no ships can move? Who checks which outside vendors can log into ships at the berth before the wind arrives? Who tells residents, quickly and plainly, what is known and what is not?

The port, the Coast Guard and the companies that use the channel should answer those questions together, in public, before June. They do not need to publish anything that would help an adversary. They do need to show the rest of us that someone owns the problem.

The next storm will not wait for the after-action report.

Grant Okafor covers the port and business for the Bayside Ledger. This column reflects his views.

item.title: 'Somebody did this': Coastal Bend reacts as U.S. blames a foreign government for tanker intrusion, channel devices
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro, Grant Okafor
item.description: For shrimpers who lost a season and workers along the channel, Tuesday's attribution answers one question and leaves others open.
item.content:encoded:
Huy Nguyen was mending a net on his boat in Aransas Pass on Tuesday when another shrimper shouted the news across the harbor.

U.S. officials had attributed the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government they did not name, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

"Since September, everybody says 'under investigation,'" said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose season was lost to the spill closure. "Now they say somebody did this. OK. Somebody did this. My nets are still dry."

The oil spilled from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Rafael arrived in September, an estimated 9,000 barrels. Surge and wind carried it into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department closed fishing and shellfish harvesting in both. By Sept. 20, six days after landfall, investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, the Coast Guard said.

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, said the company "has cooperated fully with every agency from the first day." He declined to discuss the investigation. "Today's announcement is the government's to explain. We'll leave it to them to say more," Lang said.

Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the attribution does not change the work on the water. Cleanup moved to monitoring in October, and testing continues. "Whoever was responsible, the oil was in our bays, and the job is the same: monitor, keep testing and get the bays ready to reopen when it's safe," Whitaker said.

The attribution also covered the explosive devices in the channel, including the one behind the Oct. 28 blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties, which injured two crew members and closed the channel for 14 days.

Nguyen filed a lost-income claim in November, after the tanker owners' claims center began accepting them. He said Tuesday's news doesn't change his math.

"Boat payment is the same. Fuel is the same. Claim is still pending," he said. "Tell me who did it, fine. I still want to know when I can fish."

item.title: City plans to harden water plant's power feeds; state reviews bridge wind-closure rules
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens plant failed when Rafael hit, setting off five weeks of boiling water. The city says it will harden them, and the state is reviewing when bridges close in high wind.
item.content:encoded:
The city of Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, after both feeds failed early in Hurricane Rafael and left residents boiling their water for five weeks, officials said Sunday.

The state, meanwhile, is reviewing its procedures for closing bridges in high wind. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed as Rafael's winds rose and stayed shut until inspections finished, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown.

"We lost both feeds, and when the power goes, the pumps go. We owe it to everyone who boiled water for five weeks to make sure it doesn't happen the same way again," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "I'm sorry it took a storm to get us here. But we're here."

When Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, the plant lost both feeds, its pumps were damaged and pressure dropped citywide. A boil-water notice followed four days later. Temporary pumps limited capacity while the utility waited for replacement parts, which were delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded and had to ship from out of state. The parts arrived Oct. 20, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.

In Calallen, near the plant, schoolteacher Leticia Ramos organized her neighbors' water runs during the notice. She said she is glad to hear about a plan and wants to see it on paper.

"We hauled water for five weeks. I had a spreadsheet of who needed jugs and who could drive," said Ramos, 45. "So I'd like a schedule. When does the work start, when does it finish, and who do I call when it doesn't?"

Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the bridge review matters to anyone who lives on the far side of the water. "When those bridges close, a big piece of this county gets cut in half," Pruitt said. "Any review that helps us plan around that is welcome."

The Ledger has asked the city for its plan documents and will report on the details as they become available.

item.title: 2027: The year Rafael came ashore, and everything that came after
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A Category 3 hurricane, an oil spill, five weeks of boiling water, a blast at the jetties and a long fight over aid. The Ledger looks back on the year.
item.content:encoded:
For most of the Coastal Bend, 2027 will be divided into before and after about 1 a.m. on Sept. 14, when Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm.

September. About 11 feet of surge pushed into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and about 43 square miles flooded across three coastal counties. Oil spilled from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived, an estimated 9,000 barrels. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds, and four days after landfall the city issued a citywide boil-water notice. In some neighborhoods, churches and neighborhood hubs were handing out food and water before official distribution arrived.

October. Pump repairs and testing cleared the way for the city to lift the boil-water notice Oct. 23. Five days later, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast.

November. The channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure. FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 to long lines, and within two weeks FEMA said 410 applicant accounts had been taken over using passwords stolen elsewhere.

December. Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher reported that low-income surge-zone neighborhoods had received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. The county paused payments to its debris contractor pending an audit, a federal inspector general opened a review of emergency contracts, and on Dec. 27 FBI agents searched the offices of two storm contractors. This week, the Coast Guard and a federal cyber agency urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.

"I've worked a few storms in this job, and this one didn't end when the wind stopped," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It kept finding new ways to test us. What I'll remember is the neighbors who showed up before we could."

Plenty is unfinished as the year turns. The reviews of contracts continue, the fishing closure in the bays holds, and many families in the surge zone are still waiting on repairs. The Ledger will keep reporting in 2028.

item.title: After Monday's searches: what a federal warrant means, and what comes next
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Monday's FBI searches at two storm contractors are a step in an investigation, not a finding. Here is how the process works and which other reviews are under way.
item.content:encoded:
FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, two companies hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael. Readers have asked what that means. Here is what the records and the process can tell us.

What a warrant is. A federal search warrant is signed by a judge, who must find probable cause that evidence of a crime will be found at the place to be searched. It allows agents to collect documents, devices and other material. It does not charge anyone with a crime, and it does not mean a judge has found anyone did anything wrong.

"A warrant is part of an investigation. Charges, if any are ever filed, are allegations until they are proven in court," said Alan Reyes, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. He declined to discuss the investigation further.

What else is under way. Three other reviews predate the searches. The county paused payments to Vantorra on Dec. 3 pending an audit of its debris billing. The Navy suspended Quellmar on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the backup generator failure at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. And a federal inspector general's review of emergency debris and fuel contracts across the Coastal Bend has been under way since Dec. 7.

What the companies say. Vantorra denies overbilling. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications.

Why these contracts. Emergency rules let governments hire quickly without full competition. Vantorra's $14.2 million debris contract was sole-source, awarded ten days after landfall. Quellmar's $2.1 million fuel contract was awarded after the air station's regular supplier flooded. Records reported by the Ledger this month show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated.

What to watch. Investigations that involve search warrants can take months, and the public often learns little until something is filed in court. Court filings are public records, and the Ledger checks federal dockets for new filings involving companies that hold storm contracts.

We will report what the records show, and we will tell you when they show nothing new.

item.title: Federal cyber advisory puts vendor access in the spotlight, three months after the Inner Harbor spill
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The Coast Guard and CISA urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. The chief of the vendor whose credentials were misused says every operator should read it.
item.content:encoded:
Three months after oil spilled from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Tuesday urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to their cargo systems.

The joint maritime cyber advisory asks operators to look hard at which outside companies can reach cargo systems from a distance, a routine arrangement that lets vendors service equipment without sending a technician aboard.

In Corpus Christi, the question is not abstract. Six days after landfall, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, which released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth. Two days later, Brightwake Marine Systems said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access.

"We shut off every remote session in September, and we've been rebuilding how access works ever since," said Owen Pryce, Brightwake's chief executive. "I support this advisory. I'd tell every operator and every vendor in this business to read it twice. We were the ones whose credentials were misused, and I'm not going to pretend that didn't happen."

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth where the tankers were moored, said the company has been "cooperating fully with every agency involved" and would review the advisory with its customers.

"Questions about the vessels' own systems are for the vessel operators and the investigators," Lang said.

The spill's costs are still being counted. The claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses since November, and Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remains in place.

The Coast Guard has said it will not discuss the details of its open investigation, and no finding on the source of the access has been released.

item.title: FBI agents search offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Agents executed search warrants Monday at the two companies, which hold emergency debris and fuel contracts after Hurricane Rafael. The FBI would not say what investigators were seeking.
item.content:encoded:
FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, two companies that won emergency contracts after Hurricane Rafael and have since come under separate county and Navy reviews.

The searches came Monday, Dec. 27, the first business day after the holiday weekend.

"We can confirm FBI agents executed court-authorized search warrants today in Corpus Christi. Because this is an ongoing investigation, we have no further comment," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.

Alan Reyes, a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas, said the investigation is ongoing. "A search warrant is an investigative step. It is not a charge, and it should not be read as one," Reyes said.

Vantorra received a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract from the county Sept. 24. Records reported by the Ledger this month show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling, and the county has paused payments pending an audit.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended the company Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications.

Separately, a federal inspector general has been reviewing the region's emergency debris and fuel contracts since Dec. 7. It is not clear whether Monday's searches are connected to that review.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said "no comment" when reached by phone Monday afternoon and hung up.

In a brief written statement, Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, said, "All product Quellmar delivered met specifications. We will respond to any questions through the proper channels."

The FBI did not say what agents were looking for, and neither company has been charged with a crime.

item.title: Winter on the bays: spill cleanup has moved to monitoring, but the fishing closure holds
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Three months after crude spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, the shoreline work has given way to testing. Fishers are still waiting.
item.content:encoded:
A north wind pushed whitecaps across Nueces Bay on Monday morning, and the marsh grass along the shoreline had gone winter-brown. In September, stretches of the same grass were stained black at the roots.

As Hurricane Rafael arrived, oil spilled at an Inner Harbor terminal, and the surge and wind carried it out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The sheen covered about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes. Crews deployed boom as the winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline opened.

On Oct. 28, spill cleanup moved to monitoring. The closures of fishing and shellfish harvesting in both bays, set by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services, remain in place.

"Monitoring doesn't mean we walked away," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "It means the big shoreline work is done and the job now is testing, and testing again, before anybody reopens anything. If you see oiled wildlife, call the hotline."

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the timing put oil in places it normally would not reach. "The oil is sitting in marsh a normal tide never reaches, so the tide can't do much to flush it back out," Brooks said.

How long those marshes take to recover is uncertain, he said. "Marshes heal on their own clock, and winter is the slow part of it. Spring growth will tell us more than anything we can measure in January."

For commercial fishers, the closure has meant a lost season. The claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken their lost-income claims since Nov. 16.

Whitaker said the agencies' reopening decisions will follow test results. "The bays open when the data says so, not before," he said.

Along the Portland shoreline Monday, a few people walked dogs on the sand, and a pair of white pelicans worked the shallows. It looked, for a moment, like any other December.

item.title: After a Christmas Eve shift in the ER, a charge nurse heads home for Christmas
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Alyssa Cortez volunteered to work Christmas Eve. She walked out Saturday morning with one granola bar left and some advice for anyone heating a storm-damaged home this winter.
item.content:encoded:
Alyssa Cortez walked out of the emergency department a little after 7 a.m. on Christmas morning, twelve hours after she walked in. One scrub pocket still held a granola bar. The other was empty.

"The one I keep for a teammate found a teammate around 3 a.m.," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department. "That's how you know it was a real shift."

Cortez volunteered weeks ago to work Christmas Eve. As always, she would not discuss individual patients. She would describe the room: a paper garland taped along the nurses' station, a plate of pan dulce a church dropped off before dark, and a waiting room that never looked like the ones she worked this fall.

The fall came at her department in waves. In the first days after Hurricane Rafael, people from neighborhoods near the oiled shorelines arrived with burning throats, watery eyes and rashes. During the boil-water notice, stomach-illness visits climbed to about 180% above normal, health officials reported at the time, and patients waited on stretchers in the hallway. By late October, officials said, visits had settled back near normal everywhere except the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they still ran about 40% above normal.

"A regular night. That's what I wanted for Christmas, and that's what we got," Cortez said. "After this year, regular is a present."

Her worry for the weeks ahead is the cold. Many families near the bay are still living with storm damage, roofs that leak and windows that won't close, and when the temperature drops, she said, people improvise.

"Creative heating is how I meet people at 2 in the morning," she said. "Don't heat the house with the oven. Don't bring the grill inside. Don't run a generator in the garage with the door cracked. Get a heater made for indoors, keep it away from the blankets, and turn it off when you sleep."

What readers should know: Carbon monoxide has no smell. Headaches, dizziness or nausea that ease when you step outside are a warning sign; get everyone out of the house and call 911. And if something is wrong over the holiday weekend, don't wait until Monday to call a doctor.

Cortez planned to sleep into the afternoon and then join her family for Christmas dinner. She did not sign up for New Year's Eve.

"Somebody else gets to find the eye wash," she said.

item.title: Christmas Eve at the fellowship hall: tamales, coats and a list of names
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hub has fed its neighborhood since before official aid arrived after Rafael. On Christmas Eve, it is still going.
item.content:encoded:
By 9 a.m. Friday, tamales were steaming in two borrowed roasters at the back of the fellowship hall, and Pastor Gloria Whitfield was already working down a list on her penciled binder.

"This one is the widow on the next block who needs her blood-pressure medicine picked up. This is the family on the corner with the new baby," she said, tapping names. "Everybody on this list needs something, and most of them need somebody to remember they need it."

Whitfield, 59, has run meals and supplies out of her church's fellowship hall since the days after Hurricane Rafael, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay.

Three months later, the hub is quieter, but it has not closed. On Christmas Eve, volunteers handed out tamales, donated coats and a table of wrapped toys sorted by age.

The neighborhood's wait has now been measured. Last week, Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher published the numbers: aid dollars reached low-income surge-zone neighborhoods at about half their share of residents. Two days after that, the county and FEMA said registration teams would go door to door there.

"I've been saying it since September, and now there's a number on it," Whitfield said. "Door to door. Good. I've got a list of doors."

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who rents nearby and whose hallway ceiling still leaks, as the Ledger reported last Saturday, came by with her three kids and left with tamales and a bag of oranges.

"Christmas is Christmas," Elizondo said, balancing the bag on one hip. "The roof can wait one more day. It's been waiting since September."

The volunteers, most of them neighbors, worked in shifts. Some had been coming since the week after the storm, when the hall had no power and the water came in cases.

Whitfield said the hub will stay open after the holidays. "Christmas doesn't end the need," she said. "It just makes it easier to see."

item.title: Relief forwarder's lesson from Rafael: the cargo was ready, the channel wasn't
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Gulf Relief Logistics booked 40 relief containers before the storm. They landed about a month late. Its regional manager says next season's plan starts at the anchorage.
item.content:encoded:
Terry Akins keeps a printout of the MV Gulf Provider's last position taped to the wall of his office near the port. He doesn't need it anymore. He keeps it anyway.

Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. In August, relief agencies had stocked warehouses ahead of peak season, and forwarders like his had signed standby relief contracts. On paper, the Coastal Bend was ready.

Then the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships ahead of the storm, with 14 vessels waiting at the offshore anchorage. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14, the anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including Gulf Provider. The ship finally berthed and unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17, about a month late.

"We had the boxes stuffed, the bookings confirmed, the drayage lined up on the other end. Everything we control, we controlled," Akins said. "What you don't control is the queue at the sea buoy. Fourteen ships ahead of you and a channel that's half open, you're just a line on somebody's lineup."

Relief also came by air. Beginning Oct. 18, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landed at NAS Corpus Christi over ten days.

Akins said the holiday lull is when forwarders rewrite their hurricane playbooks, and his rewrite starts with the lesson that a ready cargo is only as fast as the channel.

"Next season I want a plan B that doesn't depend on one channel. Some of it pre-positioned inland before the cone even points at us, some of it ready to move by truck," he said. "Ships are cheap per box. They get real expensive when they're sitting at anchor."

He said he would also push for relief cargo to get clearer priority in any post-storm reopening, though he acknowledged that decision belongs to others. "I'm not the Coast Guard. I just know what a month late looks like to a family waiting on water," he said.

"June comes fast," Akins said. "It always does."

item.title: What the hallway beds taught: an ER nurse and an epidemiologist look back on Rafael's health toll
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Stomach illness from the boil-water weeks has faded. Health officials say the lessons, and the slower recovery in low-income neighborhoods, should not.
item.content:encoded:
Alyssa Cortez remembers the moment she knew the boil-water weeks were going to be bad. "It was the hallway," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department. "When you're putting stretchers in the hallway before lunch, you know the day is already lost."

Hurricane Rafael knocked out both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant on landfall day, damaging pumps and dropping water pressure citywide. A citywide boil-water notice followed four days later. Within days, wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and by Sept. 22, ER visits for stomach illness were running about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use.

Stomach illness visits began to ease by late September. The notice was lifted Oct. 23 after pump repairs and testing.

"People ask me about the worst case. I don't talk about patients," Cortez said. "I'll tell you about the staff. We had nurses boiling water at home for their own kids and then coming in for twelve hours. Everybody complained. Everybody came."

Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District who runs its wastewater surveillance, said the testing gave the district an early warning. "The wastewater signal showed up while ER visits were still climbing. That's the value of watching it," Shah said. "It told us to get the hand-washing message out before the hallways filled."

Respiratory and skin complaints near oiled shorelines, which rose after the spill in September, were easing by early October.

Not every neighborhood recovered at the same pace. By late October, ER visits were back near normal except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

"When a neighborhood takes longer to come back, it's rarely one thing," Shah said. "Our job is to keep measuring until it does."

Her advice for the holidays was the same as it was in September. "Soap, a sick day at home and an early call to your doctor if you're not getting better. That list hasn't changed," she said.

item.title: Debris and fuel contracts: where the reviews stand
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: A debris hauler and a fuel supplier hired after Rafael face a county audit, a Navy suspension and a federal inspector general review. Both deny wrongdoing.
item.content:encoded:
Three months after Hurricane Rafael, two companies that won emergency work in its aftermath face separate reviews by the county and the Navy, and a federal inspector general is reviewing storm contracts in the region. Records reviewed by the Ledger show where each review stands.

Vantorra Restoration LLC received a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract from the county on Sept. 24, ten days after landfall. The Ledger reported Dec. 1 that, according to records it obtained, the company's bills covered about 2.3 times the debris tonnage estimated by the county's own drone and satellite surveys. On Dec. 3, the county paused payments to Vantorra pending an audit.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, has denied overbilling. "We've been out there working around the clock since the week of the storm, and we stand behind every load," Sloane said this month.

Quellmar Fuel Partners holds a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded, according to federal contract records. The station's backup generator then failed during a power interruption in October. On Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar pending a fuel quality review linked to that failure.

"All product Quellmar delivered to the station met specifications. We've said that from the start, and we expect the review to show it," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager.

On Dec. 7, a federal inspector general announced a review of the Coastal Bend's emergency debris and fuel contracts. The announcement did not name specific companies.

Sole-source contracts are legal in emergencies, when governments must hire quickly and cannot run a full competition. For the same reason, they tend to draw scrutiny once the emergency passes.

None of the reviews has announced findings, and neither company has been charged with a crime. The Ledger has records requests pending with the county and federal agencies and will report what they show.

item.title: Three months after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still waiting on repairs
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The home health aide and mother of three rents near the bay. Her ceiling still leaks into a bucket and her aid application is stuck, as officials promise to knock on doors.
item.content:encoded:
The bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway has been there so long her kids gave it a name. "Ese es Bob," she said Friday, pointing at the plastic pail under a brown stain in the ceiling. "Bob catches the rain. Bob is the only one in this house with a steady job."

Elizondo, 38, works as a home health aide and is raising three children. She rents a duplex in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that sat inside the surge zone when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. She doesn't own a car. Before the storm, she was among the residents without cars who waited on county buses to get out of the surge zone.

Three months later, the roof over her hallway still leaks, a back bedroom still smells of mildew, and her landlord has told her repairs are coming "after the holidays."

Her application for federal disaster aid, started in November when registration opened, has stalled. "Every time I call, it's 'pending,'" she said. "Pending, pending. I'm pending too. Ay, Dios."

Her neighborhood is the kind of place a recent analysis was about. Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. For weeks after the storm, residents there said they waited days for help.

On Wednesday, Nueces County and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods. Elizondo said she will believe it when someone knocks. "If they come, Bob and I will be home," she said. "If they come."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run meals and supplies out of her church fellowship hall since before official distribution reached the neighborhood, said the knock matters more than the announcement.

"Rosa is not a case number. She's a woman with three kids and a bucket under a hole in her roof," Whitfield said. "Door to door means every door, and it means coming back when nobody answers the first time."

Elizondo said she isn't asking for much for Christmas. "A ceiling," she said. "And for Bob to retire."

item.title: County, FEMA to send aid registration teams door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The announcement comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received storm aid at about half their share of residents.
item.content:encoded:
County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that aid registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, bringing federal disaster aid applications to residents who have not been able to get to them.

"If you can't get to us, we'll come to you," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We're going to knock on doors, and we're going to keep knocking."

The announcement came two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said residents should know how to recognize the teams. "Our people carry federal photo ID, and they will never ask you for money," Ostrander said. "If someone at your door asks for a fee, or for your account password, that's not us. Close the door and call the helpline."

FEMA added extra verification to applicant accounts after saying Nov. 24 that 410 accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, who rents near the bay and does not own a car, applied the week registration opened Nov. 13 after riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending. She said the teams should start with her neighbors.

"There's a lady on my street who's 80 and doesn't have a phone. Knock on her door first," Elizondo said. "Then come to mine, and I'll make coffee."

Officials did not release a schedule Wednesday. FEMA individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers.

item.title: Three months after Rafael: where the Coastal Bend stands
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño, Ellie Navarro
item.description: The water is safe, the channel is open and the bays are still closed. Aid, contracts and investigations remain unfinished business.
item.content:encoded:
Three months ago today, Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles across three counties. Here is where the recovery stands.

Water: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice. Replacement pump parts arrived Oct. 20 after delays, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.

Aid: Residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties have been able to register for FEMA individual assistance since Nov. 13. FEMA said Nov. 24 that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere; it added verification and said affected applicants will be repaid. On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

The bays: Shoreline cleanup from the roughly 9,000-barrel spill moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The tanker owners' claims center began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.

"I'm a fisherman who doesn't fish," said Huy Nguyen, 51, an Aransas Pass shrimper who filed his claim in November. "Ask me in the spring."

The port: The ship channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure that followed the Oct. 28 explosion near the jetties, and exports resumed. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment began loading the next day. The FBI is investigating the blast. Investigators are also still examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill.

Contracts: The county paused payments to debris contractor Vantorra Restoration on Dec. 3 pending an audit, after records obtained by the Ledger showed the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated; the company denies overbilling. Separately, on Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, which had supplied emergency fuel to the air station, pending a fuel quality review. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general followed on Dec. 7 with a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the region.

On the island: Bill Hargrove, 64, is still rebuilding his bait shop near the Port Aransas jetties. "Three months? Feels like three years," he said. "But the drywall's half up, and the pelicans don't care what month it is."

item.title: 14 Arrested in Hurricane Fraud Ring That Filed $23 Million in Fake FEMA and Insurance Claims
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Federal and state authorities say Landmark Pacific Holdings and affiliated operators targeted Districts 3 and 4 — the neighborhoods hardest hit by Rafael — recruiting disaster victims as unwitting fronts for a scheme that generated nearly 300 fraudulent claims.
item.content:encoded:
Federal agents and Texas Department of Public Safety officers arrested 14 people on fraud charges Monday in connection with what prosecutors are calling one of the largest disaster-fraud schemes in Texas history. The defendants, affiliated with a Corpus Christi property management company called Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, allegedly filed 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims totaling more than $23 million in false demands, according to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas.

Prosecutors allege that Landmark Pacific and its network of 'claim runners' recruited storm victims in Districts 3 and 4 — the neighborhoods most heavily affected by Rafael's surge, the extended boil-water notice, and the 57-day wait for FEMA Individual Assistance — and used those residents' identities and property information to submit fictitious damage claims. In many cases, investigators say, real victims who signed up with Landmark Pacific believing they were getting help received little or no money; the company allegedly skimmed the majority of any disbursements that came through. A second entity, FastDry Coastal LLC, was charged separately in connection with fraudulent water-damage remediation claims.

The fraud unraveled in part through digital forensics. FBI investigators using photo hash-deduplication software found that the same 23 photographs — purportedly documenting damage at multiple distinct properties — appeared across dozens of separate claim files. Separately, IP address clustering analysis traced 94 IA applications to a single office address on South Staples Street. 'They reused the same pictures of a flooded living room 11 times,' said FBI Houston Division Special Agent in Charge Carlos Medina at a press conference Monday. 'Eleven different addresses. Same buckled floorboards. We found it because we were looking, and we were looking because disaster fraud is a priority.'

The complaint alleges violations of federal mail fraud statute 18 U.S.C. 1341, wire fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1343, and false statements to federal agencies under 18 U.S.C. 1001. The 14 defendants face sentences of up to 20 years on the fraud charges if convicted. For families in Districts 3 and 4 who interacted with Landmark Pacific representatives in the weeks after Rafael, Monday's news was a complicated reckoning. 'They came to our neighborhood with pamphlets,' said a Westside resident who said he had signed paperwork with a Landmark Pacific agent in late October but never received any disbursement. 'I thought they were helping. I didn't know.' Legal aid organizations say they are tracking dozens of potential victims who may have unknowingly provided personal information used in the scheme and could face complications with their own legitimate FEMA applications as a result. Those individuals are urged to contact the National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721.

item.title: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of storm aid, analysis finds
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher also found the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "I could have told them that for free," one resident said.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo read the number off her phone Monday morning and laughed, not happily.

"Half? I could have told them that for free," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay and has no car.

In Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, low-income neighborhoods got aid dollars at about half their share of residents, an analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, found. The analysis also found that the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

"About half" is how the researchers summarized the ratio. The Ledger has not independently analyzed the underlying data.

Marquez said the result reflects who could reach help. "When getting help depends on a car, a smartphone or a day off work, the people without those things fall behind," she said. "The storm didn't treat everyone the same, and neither did the recovery."

The findings match what the Ledger has heard from residents since September. Residents without cars spent the evacuation waiting on county buses. After the storm, the 911 center took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help. Church hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Elizondo applied for FEMA individual assistance the week registration opened Nov. 13, riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending, she said, and the ceiling in her rental still bears water stains from the storm.

"Everybody keeps telling me to be patient," she said. "I am patient. I'm the most patient woman in Texas. Patience doesn't fix a roof."

Marquez said the next step is understanding the causes. "The number tells you where to look," she said. "Now somebody has to go look."

item.title: Twelve-hour shifts and a season that won't quit: an ER nurse heads into the holidays after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Charge nurse Alyssa Cortez worked through the oil-spill complaints and the stomach-illness wave. Now she's bracing for flu season, and has advice for readers.
item.content:encoded:
Alyssa Cortez can tell you which week of the fall was the worst by what her emergency department ran out of.

"First it was eye wash and inhalers for the folks near the oil. Then it was hallway beds for the stomach bug. Then it was everything, all at once," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who works twelve-hour shifts.

The fall came in waves. Within days of landfall, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines. After the boil-water notice, wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness rose to about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use, before easing in late September. By late October, visits were back near normal across most of the region, health officials said, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

Cortez said she can't discuss individual patients, but she notices patterns. "I still see the same neighborhoods more than I'd like," she said. "People who couldn't leave, couldn't get to a clinic, waited too long. They come to us because we're open."

Now she is bracing for the usual winter rush. Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, said the habits that helped during the fall's stomach-illness wave apply to flu season, too.

"Wash your hands, stay home when you're sick, and get your flu shot if you haven't," Shah said. "It's not too late."

What readers should know:

For a cough, cold or minor injury, a primary care doctor or urgent care clinic is often faster than an emergency room.

Go to the emergency room or call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke or a serious injury.

If you're caring for someone at home with a stomach bug, keep them drinking fluids and watch for signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or little urine.

Cortez is working Christmas Eve. She volunteered.

"Somebody's got to," she said. "Might as well be somebody who knows where the eye wash is."

item.title: What a federal inspector general review is, and what it isn't
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: A federal watchdog is reviewing emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend. Here is how such reviews generally work, and how this one differs from the county's audit and the Navy's fuel review.
item.content:encoded:
A federal inspector general opened a review this week of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael. Here are answers to readers' common questions.

What is an inspector general? Most federal departments and many agencies have one: an independent office that audits programs and investigates fraud, waste and abuse involving federal money. Inspectors general report to their agency's leadership and to Congress, and many of their findings are published.

What is being reviewed? Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend. The specific contracts and the timeline have not been announced.

Does a review mean someone did something wrong? No. A review is neither a charge nor a finding that anyone did wrong. Reviews can end with a report that finds no problems, with recommendations to agencies or with referrals for further action.

How is this different from the county's audit? The county paused payments to its debris contractor, Vantorra Restoration, on Friday pending its own audit, after records obtained by the Ledger showed the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. That audit is the county's. The company denies overbilling.

How is it different from the Navy's review? Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, was suspended by the Navy on Nov. 28 pending a review of fuel quality connected to the station's October generator failure. That review is the Navy's. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

Why would a federal watchdog look at these contracts? Emergency work after a federally declared disaster can be paid for or reimbursed with federal money, and federal agencies sign their own emergency contracts, as the Navy did for fuel. Either can bring a federal watchdog into the picture.

How long do these reviews take? It varies. Many take months, and some take more than a year.

Where can I see the records? Federal contract awards are posted in public databases, and county contracts can be requested under the Texas Public Information Act. The Ledger requests records on every emergency contract and reports what it finds.

item.title: Federal inspector general opens review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The review adds federal scrutiny to storm contracts this fall, after the county paused payments to its debris contractor and, in a separate matter, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier.
item.content:encoded:
A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend awarded after Hurricane Rafael, the Ledger confirmed Tuesday.

The Ledger could not immediately determine which specific contracts the review includes or how long it will take. Inspectors general are independent watchdog offices inside federal agencies that audit and investigate how federal money is spent.

Two emergency contracts in the region have drawn public scrutiny this fall.

On the debris side, the county awarded Vantorra Restoration LLC a $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract Sept. 24. Records obtained by the Ledger and reported Dec. 1 show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The county paused payments to Vantorra on Friday pending an audit. The company denies overbilling.

"We've got nothing to hide," said Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner. "Bring on the reviews. Every one of them is going to find the same trucks and the same tickets."

In a separate matter, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar held a $2.1 million emergency contract awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

"We'll cooperate fully with any review," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, who repeated that all product the company delivered met specifications.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county would cooperate with federal reviewers. "Whatever they ask for, they'll get," he said.

An inspector general's review is not a criminal charge or a finding of wrongdoing. Such reviews can end in public reports, recommendations to agencies or referrals for further action.

The Ledger has filed records requests on emergency contracts since the storm's first weeks and will continue to report on the review.

item.title: North Beach in December: quiet sand, pelicans and a neighbor who still checks the tide line
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: More than two months after oil washed ashore on North Beach, cleanup has moved to monitoring. Marcus Bell still walks the shoreline every morning, looking for black.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Bell walks North Beach at 7 a.m., hands in his jacket pockets, eyes on the tide line.

"I'm looking for black," said Bell, 67, a retired welder. "Haven't seen any in a while. Doesn't mean I quit looking."

Bell has had a front-row seat to Rafael. When the storm hit Sept. 14, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, cutting North Beach and Portland off from downtown until the bridges reopened after inspections Sept. 17. Then came the oil. Surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and it washed onto North Beach and Portland shorelines and into marshes.

"I smelled it before I saw it," Bell said. "Like somebody left a truck running in your kitchen."

In September, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from people near oiled shorelines, and health officials told residents to avoid contact with oil. Those complaints were easing by early October, health officials said.

Shoreline cleanup moved into a monitoring phase Oct. 28. Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said that means the shoreline is still being watched and crews respond if anything turns up.

"Monitoring isn't walking away," Whitaker said. "If somebody sees oil, we want to know about it."

If you see oil or an oiled animal, don't touch it. Report wildlife to the hotline that opened in September, and report oil to the spill response. Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

On a gray December morning, the beach belongs mostly to Bell, a man flying a kite and a line of brown pelicans cruising the surf.

"Pelicans came back before the people did," Bell said. "Smartest residents we've got."

He spent Thanksgiving with neighbors, he said, frying a turkey in a driveway and arguing about the bridge. "Everybody's got a bridge story now," he said. "Mine's the best one, but I'm biased."

item.title: In Calallen, the tap water is safe again. Trust is taking longer.
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Six weeks after the boil-water notice was lifted, some residents near the O.N. Stevens plant still reach for bottled water. Here is what the utility says, and what to do now.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos keeps a case of bottled water by her back door, a habit she says she can't shake.

"My head knows it's fine. My hand still goes for the bottle," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen, not far from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant. This fall, she organized her neighbors' runs to water distribution sites.

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in Hurricane Rafael, and pumps were damaged. A citywide boil-water notice followed Sept. 18. Replacement pump parts were delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded and parts had to ship from out of state. They arrived Oct. 20, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23 after repairs and testing.

The weeks in between were hard on the city's health. Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal at their peak before easing in late September.

"The notice was lifted after repairs and testing, and the water meets standards," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "We know we asked a lot of people this fall, and we're sorry for that. We also understand it takes time to trust the tap again."

What you can do:

Water you stored in jugs during the fall can go to plants or cleaning. Refill with fresh tap water.

If you have a refrigerator water filter or ice maker and haven't already done so, replace the filter and throw out old ice, as is generally recommended after a boil-water notice.

If a faucet hasn't been used in weeks, run cold water for a few minutes before drinking from it.

If you have questions about your water, call the utility.

Ramos said she made her Thanksgiving turkey brine with tap water. "That's progress," she said. "Next step is the coffee."

She still wants more from the city. "What I want is for somebody to tell us what's being done so this doesn't happen again," she said. "Not a press release. A plan."

Gallegos said the utility would share more about its plans as they develop.

item.title: County pauses payments to debris contractor Vantorra pending audit
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The pause follows a Ledger report that the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. Vantorra denies overbilling and says it welcomes the audit.
item.content:encoded:
The county has paused payments to Vantorra Restoration LLC, the company hired under a $14.2 million sole-source contract to clear Hurricane Rafael debris, pending an audit, a county spokesman said Friday.

"Until the audit is done, payments on that contract are on hold," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "That's not a finding of anything. It's us counting before we pay."

The pause comes two days after the Ledger reported that records obtained through public records requests show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company has denied overbilling.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said the company welcomed the audit. "Our tickets will speak for themselves," he said. "In the meantime, I've got crews with families to take care of at Christmas, and I'm asking the county to move quickly."

Pruitt declined to say how much the county has paid Vantorra so far, who would conduct the audit or how long it would take. He said residents with questions about debris on their streets should continue to contact the county.

The county awarded the contract Sept. 24, ten days after landfall, without competitive bidding. Emergency rules allow sole-source awards when delays would endanger the public. The Ledger requested records on the contract soon after it was awarded and has since asked for the load tickets and monitoring records that support the company's invoices.

Debris removal has been one of the most visible parts of the recovery since Rafael made landfall Sept. 14. An audit is not a criminal proceeding, and the county has not accused the company of wrongdoing.

The Ledger's reporting found that the tonnage figures diverged; it did not determine why. Sloane has said the county's surveys, not his company's invoices, are the problem. "Surveys are guesses," he told the Ledger Wednesday. "Tickets are facts."

item.title: Load tickets and flyovers: how storm debris is counted, and why Vantorra's bills are drawing questions
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The Ledger found Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage county surveys estimated. Here is how debris is generally measured, and what the company says.
item.content:encoded:
Every truckload of storm debris is supposed to leave a paper trail.

After a disaster, debris haulers are generally paid by the amount they remove, measured by volume or by weight. Trucks are measured before they start. Each load is supposed to get a ticket recording what was hauled, from where and to which disposal site. Monitors often check loads along the way.

Aerial surveys work from the other direction. Drones and satellites photograph debris on the ground, and analysts estimate how much is there before anyone picks it up. Neither method is perfect. Surveys can miss debris hidden under roofs or trees. Tickets can be wrong if a truck's capacity is overstated or a load is counted twice.

That is why the gap the Ledger reported Wednesday matters. Records obtained through public records requests show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated under the $14.2 million sole-source contract the county awarded Sept. 24. Which number better reflects what was actually hauled away, the records do not say.

In an interview Wednesday, Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, denied overbilling and said the surveys, not the invoices, are the problem.

"Surveys are guesses. Tickets are facts," Sloane said. "A picture from a few hundred feet up can't see what's under a pile of wet drywall and a fallen oak. My guys can, because they're the ones lifting it."

Sloane said the company's load records are on file with the county. "We've been working around the clock since the water went down," he said. "I'm proud of these crews, and I'll put my tickets up against a satellite any day."

Asked why the gap was so large, Sloane said he had not seen how the county's surveys were done and would not comment on them. "I'm not a satellite guy," he said. "I'm a trucks guy."

The county has not announced any change to the contract. The Ledger has asked the county for the load tickets and monitoring records that support the invoices and will report what they show.

item.title: Debris contractor billed for 2.3 times the debris county surveys estimated, records show
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda, Grant Okafor
item.description: Invoices and survey estimates obtained by the Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for far more debris than the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling.
item.content:encoded:
