Vantorra Restoration LLC, the company awarded a $14.2 million sole-source contract to clear Hurricane Rafael debris, billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated, according to records obtained by the Bayside Ledger.

The Ledger obtained the company's invoices and the county's survey estimates through public records requests filed after the contract was awarded Sept. 24. Taken together, the records show the tonnage Vantorra billed running at roughly 2.3 times the tonnage the county's surveys estimated.

Vantorra denies overbilling.

"We bill for what we haul, load by load, and every load is documented," said Derek Sloane, the company's managing partner. "Our crews have been working around the clock since this storm hit. Pictures from the sky don't pick up debris. Trucks do."

Survey estimates are not exact counts, and the records alone do not show why the figures differ. Drone and satellite surveys estimate how much debris is on the ground; invoices reflect what a contractor says it hauled. The records do not show which figure is closer to what was actually removed.

The county awarded the contract without competitive bidding in the storm's second week, as debris blocked streets across the region. Emergency rules allow sole-source awards when delays would endanger the public, and such contracts typically draw scrutiny once the emergency passes.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county had received the Ledger's questions. "We're looking at the records, and I'm not going to get ahead of that," he said.

The Ledger shared its findings with Vantorra before publication. Sloane said anyone who doubts the company's numbers is welcome to see the work for themselves. "Ride along with one of my trucks," he said. "Bring a lunch."

The Ledger has requested additional records on the contract, including payments to date. Those requests are pending.

item.title: Column: Ask hard questions about storm contracts. Don't pass along fake numbers.
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The new rumor wave about "stolen aid" borrows real questions and buries them under false claims. Coastal Bend residents deserve real answers.
item.content:encoded:
I have covered two hurricanes before Rafael, and each one brought a second storm: the one that blows through our phones.

This week's version says contractors are "stealing aid." Posts claim the county's debris contract is worth $140 million. Public records show it is $14.2 million. Posts claim FEMA stopped paying families so it could pay contractors. FEMA registration remains open. Those claims are false, and Harborline 6's fact-checkers said so Sunday.

Here is what bothers me most: the false posts make it harder to ask the true questions.

The county awarded its debris contract to Vantorra Restoration sole-source, without competitive bidding, ten days after landfall. That is allowed in an emergency. It also deserves a close look after the emergency. On Sunday, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier, Quellmar Fuel Partners, pending a fuel quality review tied to October's generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Those are fair questions, and they deserve documented answers.

My colleagues on the Ledger's investigations desk file records requests on every emergency contract. It is slow work. It does not go viral. It is how you learn whether what was billed matches what was done.

Some of the loudest posts come from accounts that spread false claims after landfall that the military was seizing homes. @CoastTruthTX, one of the most shared, is back at it. An account that was wrong about your house in September does not get the benefit of the doubt about your aid in November.

So here is my ask. Before you share, look for a document. If a post has a number, check it. If it has no number, ask why. If you have a real question about a contract, send it to the county or the Navy, or send it to us.

Families in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay waited days for help after this storm. Many are still waiting on aid applications and repairs. They deserve accountability built on records, not on somebody's all-caps guess.

Marisol Treviño covers city government and disasters for the Ledger.

item.title: Hurricane season ends today. On the Coastal Bend, Rafael's season doesn't.
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: The Atlantic season officially closes Nov. 30 after forecasters called for an active year. For the bays, the water plant and the people who live by them, recovery keeps its own calendar.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlantic hurricane season officially ends today, and nobody on the Coastal Bend is throwing a party.

In late August, forecasters expected above-normal activity for the rest of the season. Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Sept. 4, crossed the Yucatan, became a hurricane in the southern Gulf four days later and made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm.

"The calendar says the season's over, and the odds of another storm here this late are very low," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "But the end of the season isn't the end of the storm for anybody still fixing a roof."

Rafael's footprint is still visible. A surge of about 11 feet swept into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and floodwater covered about 43 square miles of the three coastal counties. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds, and a citywide boil-water notice lasted from Sept. 18 to Oct. 23. About 9,000 barrels of crude escaped two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal, and the surge spread sheen across about 33 square miles of bay and shoreline.

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the timing made the spill worse. "For a few hours, the surge moved the whole bay inland," he said. "Whatever was floating in the ship channel moved with it."

Cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, but fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Brooks cautioned against expecting a quick timeline. "Marshes recover on the scale of seasons and years, not weeks," he said. "The honest answer is that we'll know more after another season of monitoring."

Arceneaux said the off-season is the time to prepare for the next one. Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and he said that advice stands.

"Check your insurance, write down your plan, and if you don't have a ride out, tell somebody now, not when the cone is over your house," he said. "June comes faster than you think."

item.title: Navy suspends air station's emergency fuel supplier pending quality review
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The review of Quellmar Fuel Partners is linked to the October failure of a backup generator at NAS Corpus Christi, the station says. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that has supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi since Hurricane Rafael, pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October, the station said Sunday.

"We have suspended the supplier while a fuel quality review is completed," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We take the reliability of the station's power seriously, and we're not going to get ahead of the review."

Quellmar disputed the move. "All product we delivered meets specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We'll cooperate with the Navy's review, and we expect it to confirm that."

Federal contract records that became public in early October show the Navy awarded Quellmar a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the air station after the station's regular supplier flooded in the storm.

On Oct. 25, the station said its backup generator had failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the station said at the time that the cause was under review. Sunday's announcement was the first time the Navy publicly tied that review to the station's fuel.

Hale declined to say how long the review would take, what it had examined so far or how the station is being supplied while it is under way, saying the station does not discuss details that bear on security.

Kerr said the company had answered the call when the station needed fuel. "We stepped up when the regular supplier was under water, and we'd do it again," she said.

Naval Air Station Corpus Christi trains Navy pilots and hosts Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's main helicopter repair depot. The station's training aircraft flew to Fort Worth ahead of the storm and began returning six days after landfall.

item.title: Bays stay closed as the fall season slips away for Coastal Bend fishers
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: More than two months after the oil spill, fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishers are filing damage claims and waiting.
item.content:encoded:
The nets on Huy Nguyen's shrimp boat are dry, folded and stacked, and the boat is tied up at Aransas Pass the way it has been most of the fall.

"Ten weeks, and I fished zero days in the bay," said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper. "My father used to say a boat that doesn't move is just an expensive house for pelicans."

Nguyen's boat survived Hurricane Rafael. His season did not. As the storm arrived in mid-September, surge and wind carried crude oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The Unified Command estimated the release at about 9,000 barrels, and sheen spread across about 33 square miles of water, marsh and shoreline.

Fishing in both bays has been closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife since Sept. 18, when the Texas Department of State Health Services also stopped shellfish harvesting; the fishing closure was extended in early October. It remains in place as the fall bay season winds down, and the oyster season that opened Nov. 1 has brought no harvest from the closed waters.

Shoreline cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28. Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the health and wildlife agencies will keep the closures until the science supports lifting them.

"Nobody wants these bays open more than the people who fish them," Whitaker said. "And nobody wants them open too early, either."

The claims center run for the tankers' owners began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses Nov. 16. Nguyen filed his claim two days later, bringing a grocery bag of fuel receipts and the eleven spiral notebooks his father taught him to keep.

"I write everything down. Pounds, price, fuel, ice," he said. "They want numbers, I have numbers. What I don't have is a paycheck."

Whitaker said fishers should keep records of lost trips and expenses and file with the owners' claims center. Bay shrimpers had reported a fair start to the season in July, Nguyen said, though fuel costs were already squeezing margins before the storm took the rest.

Asked about Thanksgiving, Nguyen shrugged.

"We ate. Family came. Nobody asked me about the boat," he said. "That was the gift."

item.title: On Black Friday, a gutted Port Aransas bait shop sells from coolers and waits for winter
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Ten weeks after Rafael's landfall, Coastal Bend small businesses head into the holiday season with damaged storefronts, closed bays and customers stretched thin.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Hargrove's Black Friday sale is written in grease pencil on a sheet of plywood: "LIVE SHRIMP. CHEAP ADVICE. NO REFUNDS ON EITHER."

Hargrove, 64, has sold bait and tackle near the Port Aransas jetties for years. Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm made landfall on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Ten weeks later, he is selling out of coolers on the porch while a carpenter works inside.

"Black Friday on the island used to mean the Winter Texans rolling in and buying a rod they didn't need," Hargrove said. "This year it's me, two coolers and whoever's brave enough to drive out."

Rafael hit at the end of a strong summer. Port Aransas businesses reported busy bait shops and charters in August. Then the storm pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties.

For businesses that depend on the water, the fall brought one closure after another. The ship channel closed Sept. 13 ahead of the storm and only partly reopened Oct. 14. An explosion near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28 closed it again for 14 days, until Nov. 11. And because of the oil spill, fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have stayed closed since Sept. 18.

The reopened channel matters for the port, where crude exports resumed in mid-November. For a bait shop, Hargrove said, it matters less than people think.

"Big ships don't buy bait," he said. "Fishermen buy bait. And the bays are closed."

Back in Corpus Christi, shoppers lined up before dawn outside big-box stores on South Padre Island Drive. Plenty of carts held more plywood, box fans and extension cords than televisions.

Hargrove said he hopes to have the shop's walls closed in by Christmas, depending on the drywall crew.

"They're on island time, too," he said. "I can't complain. I invented island time."

item.title: 410 accounts, 220,000 tries: FEMA details how aid accounts were hijacked
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The agency says attackers used passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. A threat researcher says the method is common, cheap and aimed at reused passwords.
item.content:encoded:
Attackers made about 220,000 automated attempts to sign in to FEMA disaster-aid accounts and took over 410 of them, the agency said Wednesday, putting numbers to a problem Coastal Bend applicants first reported last week.

The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen elsewhere, according to FEMA. The agency said it has added extra verification to applicant accounts and that applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.

"Every applicant affected will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification. Check your deposit information anyway, even if you're sure nothing changed."

FEMA did not say how much money was diverted, how many of the 410 accounts belonged to Coastal Bend residents or who was behind the attempts. Ostrander declined to discuss who might be responsible.

The sequence, according to FEMA and applicants: Individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. On Nov. 19, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts and urged applicants to verify their deposit information. On Wednesday, the agency released the totals.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said the figures fit a familiar pattern known as credential stuffing, in which attackers test stolen username and password pairs against a new site until some of them work.

"Fewer than two in every thousand attempts worked, and that's typical," Feld said. "It's a numbers game. Attackers get lists of leaked passwords, run them through software and wait for the people who reused one."

Feld said she would not guess who was behind the attempts. "That's for investigators to say, not me," she said.

The defense, she said, is unglamorous: a different password for every account, and a second sign-in step wherever one is offered. "Start with your email," Feld said. "If someone controls your email, they can reset everything else."

Applicants who see deposit details they don't recognize should contact FEMA and their bank, Ostrander said.

item.title: From declaration to deposit: how federal storm aid reaches a household, and where it can stall
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Ten weeks after Rafael, many Coastal Bend households have registered for FEMA aid and are still waiting. Here is how the process works, step by step, and what officials say applicants can do now.
item.content:encoded:
Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, many households on the Coastal Bend have registered for federal disaster aid and are waiting to hear back. Others have not registered at all. Here is how the process has worked so far, and what officials say applicants can do this week.

Why registration came when it did. When the federal disaster declaration came Sept. 18, it paid for debris removal and emergency protective measures, not aid to families. Help for households had to wait on damage assessments, which dragged as teams worked around spill-zone limits and flooded streets. The state asked for Individual Assistance in October, FEMA approved it Nov. 10, and registration opened Nov. 13 to long lines at recovery centers.

After you register. FEMA reviews each application and may ask for more documents. Renters, for example, may be asked to show they lived at the damaged address. "If we ask you for something, answer as fast as you can, and call the helpline if a letter doesn't make sense," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "A pending application is usually waiting on something. Find out what it is."

Getting paid. Approved aid is paid by check or by direct deposit. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and on Nov. 19 FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. The agency has urged every applicant to log in through its official website and verify where the money is set to go. It has not said how many accounts were affected.

Not registered yet? Phone and online registration count the same as standing in line, county officials say. "If two buses to a recovery center is what's stopping you, call instead, or find a church or neighborhood hub with a laptop out," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.

Who is waiting longest. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents said help took days to arrive after the storm, and many households have no car. As the Ledger reported Monday, some applicants there now check their deposit details every morning while their applications sit.

Keep a folder. Put your registration number, every FEMA letter and a log of each call, with the date and the name of the person you spoke to, in one place. Ostrander said that record makes it faster to sort out a problem if one turns up.

item.title: Thanksgiving week near the bay: a pending application, a daily account check and a fellowship hall turkey
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Rosa Elizondo's FEMA application is still pending, and she checks her deposit details every morning. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is planning Thursday dinner for whoever shows up.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo has a new morning routine. Coffee. Kids up. Lunches. Then, on the bus at 6:10, she opens her FEMA account and checks the bank number.

"Still mine," Elizondo, 38, said Sunday, showing her phone screen to a reporter at the fellowship hall that has become her neighborhood's front door this fall. "Every morning I say, good morning, little account, you're still here."

Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay, registered for federal disaster aid on Nov. 13, the day registration opened. She said FEMA is still reviewing a school letter she submitted as proof that she lives in her rental, so her application remains pending. Her hallway ceiling still leaks into a bucket.

On Friday, FEMA said some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization, and it has asked all applicants to double-check their direct-deposit details. Earlier last week, some applicants said they had found deposit details they never entered. FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected.

At the hall, Pastor Gloria Whitfield was counting folding chairs. She is planning a Thanksgiving dinner Thursday for anyone who comes, with turkeys from church members, tamales from a neighbor and pies from a bakery that called her. The laptops will stay out on a side table, she said, with a volunteer and a sign: "Check your deposit before dessert."

"I don't want anybody worrying over their plate," Whitfield said. "But I don't want them finding out in December that their money went somewhere else either. So we'll eat, and we'll check."

Whitfield said the families on her list are more tired than angry. "They followed every instruction. They stood in the lines. They found the papers. Now they're guarding an account like it's a front porch," she said. "And they still showed up Wednesday to help me sort cans."

Elizondo said her youngest, who is 6, has asked twice whether there will be turkey. There will be. "At Pastora's, there's always turkey," Elizondo said.

Asked what she was thankful for this year, she thought about it on the walk to the bus. "My kids are okay. My clients are okay. Mine is still mine," she said. "Next year I want to be thankful for a ceiling."

item.title: Still drying out before the holidays? A health checklist for storm-damaged homes
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Rafael's emergency is over for most of the county. For families still living with leaks and damp walls, a health official and an ER nurse offer practical advice.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving is Thursday. For many Coastal Bend households, it will be the first holiday in a home that is still drying out from Hurricane Rafael.

The health picture has improved since the boil-water weeks. Stomach illness visits began easing in late September, and the boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23. But emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal in late October, after visits elsewhere had settled, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said.

"A home that took on water or has a leaking roof can keep affecting health for months," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "The good news is that a few practical steps make a real difference."

Here is what Shah and Alyssa Cortez, 34, an emergency room charge nurse at a Nueces County hospital, recommend:

Find and fix moisture. Where you see or smell mildew, dry the area and clean hard surfaces with soap and water. Throw out soaked drywall, carpet and padding that can't be dried. Wear gloves and a mask while you clean.

Protect the most vulnerable. Keep young children, older relatives and anyone with asthma or lung disease out of damp rooms while you clean. If someone's breathing gets worse at home, take it seriously.

Don't wait for an emergency. "We still see people who put off care until they couldn't anymore," Cortez said. "A cough that won't quit, a rash that's spreading, a prescription you ran out of in October. Come in before it's midnight and scary." She urged patients to bring a list or photos of their medications.

Mind the stress. Shah said sleep problems, worry and short tempers are common months after a disaster. "If you're not feeling like yourself, tell your doctor. That's a health issue too," she said.

Wash hands, especially when cooking for a crowd. "Holiday kitchens are busy," Shah said. "Hand-washing is still the cheapest medicine we have."

Cortez said her emergency room would be open through the holiday, as always. "We'll be here Thursday," she said. "I'd just rather see you Tuesday at a clinic."

item.title: Opinion: Aid that lands in the wrong account isn't aid
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A column by Bayside Ledger city and disaster reporter Marisol Treviño on what FEMA owes the applicants it asked to check their own accounts.
item.content:encoded:
Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Two months after Hurricane Rafael, federal aid registration finally opened on the Coastal Bend. Damage assessments had dragged, and FEMA did not approve individual assistance until Nov. 10. People lined up before dawn. Some took two buses. Others registered on borrowed laptops in church fellowship halls because they don't own a computer.

Six days later, FEMA confirmed that some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization. Some applicants had already found bank details on their applications that they never entered. FEMA's advice was sensible: log in, check your direct-deposit information, call the helpline if anything is wrong.

That advice puts the work on the people with the least time to do it.

I have spent this fall in the neighborhoods near the bay where residents waited days for help after the storm, where church hubs handed out water before official distribution arrived, and where emergency room visits stayed well above normal long after they settled elsewhere. The people there are not careless. They are tired. Many share a phone. Many work hourly jobs where an afternoon on hold is an afternoon unpaid.

FEMA owes them three things, and soon.

First, the facts. How many accounts were affected? How were they accessed? Did any payments go to the wrong place? "We will share more when we can" is a start, not an answer. Applicants can't judge their risk without knowing the scale.

Second, a promise in writing. If an applicant's payment went to an account they did not authorize, will FEMA make them whole, and how quickly? People are budgeting rent around this money.

Third, help where people are. FEMA staff at the church and neighborhood hubs that have carried this recovery would let residents check their accounts with someone who can actually fix a problem on the spot. Pastors and volunteers have been doing that job for free since September.

Nobody expects a federal agency to stop every bad actor on the internet. But the measure of a disaster program is whether help reaches the people it was meant for. Until FEMA can say plainly that it has, the people standing in line deserve more than a reminder to check their own accounts.

item.title: FEMA confirms some aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The agency urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit details but did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether payments went astray.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA confirmed Friday that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, two days after applicants in Nueces County reported finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

In a statement, Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said the agency had confirmed that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. "Please log in and look at where your payment is set to go," she said. "If it isn't your account, call our helpline right away."

The statement did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, when the access occurred, or whether any aid payments had been sent to changed accounts. Asked those questions Friday, Ostrander said FEMA would release more information when it could.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13 for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Long lines formed at recovery centers, and church and neighborhood hubs helped many residents register by phone and online.

In September, days after the storm, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. FEMA did not say whether the unauthorized access was related to any earlier scam, and the Ledger is not suggesting that it was.

At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall near the bay, where volunteers have helped neighbors check their accounts all week, the confirmation was not a surprise. "My neighbors told me Wednesday. FEMA told us Friday," Whitfield said. "I'm glad they said it. Now tell people how they get their money if it went to the wrong place."

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who registered at a recovery center on the first day, said she had checked her deposit information again Friday morning. It was still correct. "I'm checking it like my kids check the fridge," she said. "Every hour, for no reason, just in case."

The Ledger has requested records from FEMA on the number of accounts affected and the agency's response. Applicants who believe their information was changed can call FEMA's helpline.

item.title: An Aransas Pass shrimper files his spill claim with a stack of spiral notebooks
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael, and the pass is open again. The bays are not. On Thursday he put his lost season on paper.
item.content:encoded:
ARANSAS PASS — Huy Nguyen brought his evidence in a grocery bag: eleven spiral notebooks, a rubber-banded stack of fuel receipts from his truck visor, and his boat papers in a plastic sleeve.

"My whole life is in here," said Nguyen, 51, setting the bag on his kitchen table Thursday before he filed his spill damage claim. "Every trip. How many pounds. How much diesel. How much ice. My father taught me to write it down. He said someday somebody will ask. Somebody is asking."

Nguyen, a second-generation shrimper, filed two days after the claims center run for the tankers' owners began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael in September. Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in the bays on Sept. 18, the same day the state health department closed shellfish harvesting, and extended its closure in early October. It remains in place.

His boat came through the storm with little more than scraped paint. Then the bays closed. Then, for two weeks, the entrance channel to the Gulf closed too, after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. It reopened Nov. 11.

"Now the pass is open and I still can't fish the bay," he said. "One door opens, the other stays shut."

His season had started out fair, he said, though fuel prices ate into it. Since mid-September, his notebook pages read "no trip." He still owes on the boat and the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two children who has been picking up day work.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said Tuesday that claimants should start with what they have and add documents as they go. "The more you can show, the better," he said. No date has been set for reopening the bays.

Nguyen said he does not know how long a claim will take, and he is not counting on it to save the season. "Paper doesn't fish," he said again, sliding the notebooks back into the bag. "But I'm good at paper. My father made sure."

Asked what he wanted most, he did not mention money. "Tell me when I can fish," he said.

item.title: At a church relief hub, aid applicants check their accounts and some find bank details they don't recognize
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's volunteers spent Wednesday helping neighbors log in. Rosa Elizondo's information was unchanged. Others' was not, they said.
item.content:encoded:
The line at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall on Wednesday afternoon was not for water or canned beans. It was for the two borrowed laptops.

Word had spread through the neighborhood near the bay that some people who applied for federal disaster aid were finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered. Whitfield's volunteers spent the afternoon helping neighbors log in and look.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who registered for aid Saturday, checked hers three times. Her bank information was still her own.

"Mine is fine. Mine is still my little account," Elizondo said. "But I'm going to check every day now, like the weather. Before, I worried the money wouldn't come. Now I worry it comes and goes somewhere else."

Whitfield said a couple of people who came to the hall on Wednesday found account numbers they did not recognize. The Ledger could not independently verify their accounts. Harborline 6 reported earlier Wednesday that several applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge.

"These are people who registered with a phone borrowed from my table, because they don't have a computer," Whitfield said. "They did everything they were told. If somebody is getting into these accounts, the people with the least are going to lose the most, because they're the ones who can't take a day off to sit on hold."

FEMA did not respond to the Ledger's questions about the reports by Wednesday evening. It is not known how the changes were made or how many applicants are affected.

Volunteers at the hall were telling people to call FEMA's helpline if their information had changed, to tell their bank, and to use a new password that they do not use anywhere else. Whitfield wrote the helpline on the whiteboard where she used to list needs for diapers and batteries.

Elizondo said her application is still waiting on FEMA to accept the school letter she uploaded Monday to prove she lives at her rental. "So first they need proof that I live in my house," she said. "Now I need proof that my money lives in my account."

item.title: Spill claims center starts taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Two months after oil from two moored tankers spread across the bays, people who lost income can begin filing claims with the tanker owners' claims center. Officials say documentation is everything.
item.content:encoded:
Commercial fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the oil spill that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael can now file claims with the claims center run for the tankers' owners, which began taking lost-income claims Tuesday as federal oil spill law requires. Claims that go unpaid for 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income or damaged your property, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Don't wait until you have every piece of paper. Start the claim, then keep adding to it. Receipts, trip logs, tax records, photos. The more you can show, the better."

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Land Office estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived in September. Rafael's surge and wind pushed the oil out of the ship channel, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in the two bays on Sept. 18, and the fishing closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but the closures remain in place, and no reopening date has been set.

For shrimpers like Huy Nguyen of Aransas Pass, the claims process is the first concrete step since the closure. Nguyen, 51, keeps a spiral notebook for every trip, with catch, fuel and ice, and fuel receipts clipped to his truck visor.

"Finally, somebody wants to see my notebook," Nguyen said. "Years of notebooks. Good years, bad years. Now they can see what a lost year looks like."

He said he planned to file within days. "Paper doesn't fish," he said. "But paper is what I have."

On North Beach, retired welder Marcus Bell, who saw oil on the sand two days after the storm, said Sunday he wanted agencies to "tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check." Whitaker said shoreline property owners have been able to file cleanup and property damage claims with the same center since September.

Whitaker urged people to be wary of anyone who charges a fee to file a claim on their behalf. "You don't need to pay anybody to start a claim," he said.

item.title: Port works through its backlog as brigade's sealift heads out
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Four days after the channel reopened, the Port of Corpus Christi says it is catching up. A relief freight forwarder's delayed shipments are landing.
item.content:encoded:
The cranes at the Port of Corpus Christi did not stop much over the weekend.

Four days after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure, the port said Monday it was working through the line of vessels that waited offshore, and that crude loadings had resumed at every terminal ready to receive ships.

"We said we'd work around the clock, and we have," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The line is getting shorter every day. I won't give you a date it's gone, because I've learned not to promise the water anything. But we're close to a normal week."

The port's other big job is also moving. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading Friday onto a sealift ship, and the Army said the equipment would sail over a five-day period for an overseas rotation. Salinas declined to discuss the military movement beyond the Army's statement.

The reopening has also eased pressure on freight forwarders who juggled delays twice this fall. Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, said shipments held during the closure began arriving over the weekend. His firm's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider were about a month late after Rafael.

"I had a customer who's been waiting on building supplies since October. They came off a ship Saturday," Akins said. "He sent me a picture of the pallets. I don't think I've ever been sent a picture of pallets before. I saved it."

Akins said the fall wore on his customers as much as on him. "Twice this fall the cargo was ready and the water wasn't," he said. "You can only tell somebody 'it's at anchor' so many times."

At a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports, the closure stopped crude loadings cold. The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties that caused it.

item.title: Two months after the oil, North Beach still asks who pays
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Cleanup crews have moved on to monitoring. A retired welder who smelled the oil before he saw it says the beach looks better than his neighbors' finances.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Bell can tell you exactly where the black line was.

"Right there, from that post to past the lifeguard stand," said Bell, 67, pointing down the sand from the end of his street on North Beach on a gray Sunday morning. "Smelled it before I ever saw it. Then the whole edge of the sand went black."

That was two days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall in September. Surge and wind carried oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes. Responders working under the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office have put the release at about 9,000 barrels.

Now, cleanup has moved to monitoring. The sand in front of Bell's street is pale again, and on Sunday a few people were walking it with coffee.

"Looks fine. That's the thing about a beach. It forgets faster than people do," said Bell, a retired welder who spent more than 30 years on refinery and fabrication jobs along the ship channel. "My throat was raw for a week. My neighbor's grandson broke out in a rash. Who paid for those doctor visits? Them."

Health officials advised residents in September to avoid contact with oil after emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from people near oiled shorelines. Those complaints eased by early October. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in the bays remains in place.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said moving to monitoring "doesn't mean anybody walks away." Crews continue to check shorelines and marshes, he said, and a claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken cleanup and property damage claims since September. "If people see oil, we want to hear about it. Call the hotline."

Bell said he wants something simple from the agencies. "Tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check," he said. "Don't make a 67-year-old man with a bad throat figure it out from a rumor at the bait stand."

He said he would be watching the news for that. "I've welded around fuel my whole life," he said. "I know what it costs when somebody gets it wrong. Somebody ought to pay for it."

item.title: Hours-long lines as FEMA aid registration opens across the Coastal Bend
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Rosa Elizondo took two buses and waited most of the morning. A Calallen teacher brought a clipboard and a cooler.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo was at the bus stop at 6:10 a.m. Saturday, the same time she leaves for work on weekdays. This time she was going to stand in line.

By the time Elizondo, 38, reached a disaster recovery center after two buses, the line was already wrapped around the building. She registered for federal disaster aid a little after noon.

"I brought everything. My ID, my kids' papers, my lease, my bank card, a picture of my ceiling," said Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "The lady was nice. She said I'll get a call. I said, okay, I'll get a call. I've been getting a call since September."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, two months after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. FEMA had approved the aid Wednesday, Nov. 10, after delays in damage assessments. Long lines formed at recovery centers across the three counties.

"We know the lines are long, and we know people have waited a long time to get here," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Nobody loses their place by registering online or by phone instead. If you can't stand in a line, you don't have to."

Not everyone has that choice. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and many have no car and spotty internet.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a Calallen schoolteacher who ran water runs for her street during the boil-water notice, was in line with a clipboard and a cooler of water bottles. She drove three neighbors who do not have cars and kept a list of who still needed to register.

"Same list, new column," Ramos said, tapping the clipboard. "During the water notice, it was who needs jugs. Now it's who needs help with the website. I'd love to retire this clipboard someday."

Elizondo said her neighbor watched her children so she could come. She planned to ride the two buses home and make dinner. "Today I did my part," she said. "Now it's their part."

item.title: Channel reopens after 14 days; port says exports are moving again
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The Port of Corpus Christi began working through a backlog of waiting ships Thursday. A relief freight forwarder says this is the first good morning he's had since October.
item.content:encoded:
Two weeks to the day after an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, ships were moving again Thursday.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, and crude exports resumed. Navy teams had found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last Friday.

"This is a good day for the Port of Corpus Christi and for everyone who depends on it," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is open from the jetties to the Inner Harbor. Our terminals are working, and we will be at it around the clock until every ship that waited for us is served."

Salinas would not estimate how long it would take to clear the backlog of vessels that held offshore during the closure. "We'll go as fast as safety allows," he said. "Faster than that, we don't go."

The closure halted crude loadings at a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was the second shutdown this fall; the channel was also closed from the day before Hurricane Rafael's landfall in September until a partial reopening in mid-October.

For Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, Thursday was a relief in more ways than one. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider came ashore about a month late after the storm. This time he had customers' cargo waiting again.

"First good morning I've had since October," Akins said. "I called three customers before 8 o'clock and told them the word I've been waiting to say, which is 'moving.' I didn't say when it lands. I've learned."

The reopening also clears the way for a Fort Hood aviation brigade whose movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation was delayed twice, by the hurricane and by the blast. Fort Hood had not announced a new date as of Thursday morning.

The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion, which injured two crew members on the harbor tug Corrin Bay.

item.title: FEMA Grants Individual Assistance to Storm-Battered Counties; Registration Opens Saturday
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Federal aid authorization unlocks rental assistance, home repair grants, and personal property replacement for residents of Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties — 57 days after Rafael made landfall.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA has approved Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties, the agency announced Wednesday, authorizing direct financial aid for eligible Hurricane Rafael survivors eight weeks after the storm struck. The approval, long awaited by tens of thousands of displaced and damaged households, does not open the application line at once: registration begins Saturday, Nov. 13, through FEMA's disaster hotline, its online portal and local recovery centers.

Beginning Saturday, eligible residents can apply by calling 1-800-621-FEMA or visiting DisasterAssistance.gov. The approved programs include rental assistance for displaced households, grants for essential home repairs, and personal property replacement funds for lost or destroyed belongings. FEMA said it will open three Disaster Recovery Centers in Corpus Christi the same morning: at the Oveal Williams Senior Center at 1414 Martin Luther King Drive, a facility at 5301 Ayers Street, and Memorial Coliseum Annex at 902 N. Shoreline Blvd. All three sites will operate Monday through Saturday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Residents will not need an appointment.

The 57-day interval between landfall and approval is longer than is typical for major hurricane declarations. FEMA officials attributed the delay partly to the pace of household damage assessments: access limits around the oil spill zone, flooded roads and the extended power outage — parts of Corpus Christi's grid remained impaired into mid-October — hampered field teams' ability to reach and assess damaged properties, particularly in Districts 3 and 4. The state formally asked for Individual Assistance on Oct. 9. 'The prolonged outage created verification challenges we do not normally encounter to this degree,' said FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander. 'Our teams could not safely or accurately assess many properties without stable utilities in those neighborhoods.'

Local advocates said the delay compounded hardship for families already stretched thin. At St. John's Episcopal Church on Staples Street, a volunteer coordinator who has been running informal aid distribution since the second day after the storm said the announcement drew spontaneous applause from the two dozen residents waiting for donated food Wednesday morning. 'People have been holding on,' she said. 'Bills piled up. Landlords got impatient. This comes late, but it comes.' FEMA urges all eligible survivors to apply as soon as registration opens Saturday. Applicants should bring identification, proof of residency, and documentation of losses — but Ostrander said FEMA can work with incomplete documentation. 'Bring what you have,' she said. 'Don't wait once the line opens.'

item.title: Explainer: Who decides the ship channel is safe again, and what happens next
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Oct. 28. Here is how a reopening decision gets made, and what to expect when it comes.
item.content:encoded:
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for nearly two weeks, and the question on every dock and in every bait shop is the same: when? The honest answer is that nobody has said. Here is what is known about how that decision will be made.

Who closed it? The Coast Guard closed the channel after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured. According to the Navy, an explosive device caused the blast. The FBI is investigating.

Who is searching? Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard. On Friday, they found a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. No one was hurt.

Who decides it is safe? The Coast Guard's Captain of the Port for Corpus Christi controls whether vessels may move through the channel. "The search has to be complete, and the Captain of the Port has to be satisfied the channel is safe. Then it reopens," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That decision rests on what the teams in the water tell us."

Why won't anyone give a date? Because the search sets the schedule. "The search is finished when the teams say it is finished, not when the calendar says so," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. The Navy has declined to describe the devices or its methods, citing safety and the investigation.

What happens when it reopens? Expect a staged restart, not a flood. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, a backlog at the offshore anchorage delayed relief cargo for days. This time, inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted Oct. 28, so the entrance is the only bottleneck. Crude loadings, halted since the blast, would resume as tankers come in.

What about the Army brigade? A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment are waiting to move through the port for an overseas rotation. Fort Hood has said it will move when the port is ready and has not announced a date.

What about fishing? The closures of fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, set by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services because of the oil spill, are separate and remain in place. The channel reopening does not change them.

item.title: Opinion: The port is a national asset. The people who work it need to be treated like one
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: A column by Bayside Ledger business and port reporter Grant Okafor on the second shutdown of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.
item.content:encoded:
Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Twice this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi has been open for business with no way for ships to reach it. The first time, the cause was a hurricane we watched coming for days. The second time, it was an explosion beside a tugboat at the jetties in the middle of the night, followed Friday by the discovery of a second explosive device near the entrance channel.

The Navy and Coast Guard are right not to put a date on reopening. Nobody on the Coastal Bend wants a tanker captain or a tug crew to be the test of whether a sweep was finished. Patience with that work is not optional.

But patience is easier for some of us than others.

This port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It is a strategic military seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment have now been delayed twice on their way to an overseas rotation. When the channel closes, the country notices. Traders notice. Washington notices.

What the country does not see is the deckhand who has not worked since Oct. 28, the line handler paid by the job, the trucker whose loads stopped, or the freight forwarder who waited a month for 40 relief containers to berth after Rafael and is now explaining a second delay to his customers. It does not see the shrimpers at Aransas Pass, whose bays have been closed to fishing since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill and whose route to the Gulf runs through the closed entrance.

Those workers absorbed the storm, then the spill, and now this. Most of them do not have a market desk to price in the risk.

Three things would help. First, regular, scheduled updates from the Coast Guard and the port, even when the update is "no change," so businesses can plan around something other than rumor. Second, a plain-language guide from local and state agencies to what help exists for workers idled by a closure that was nobody's fault on the waterfront. Third, when investigators are able to speak, a full public accounting of what happened at the jetties.

The channel will reopen. When it does, the ships will move again quickly. The people who keep them moving should not have to wait longer than the cargo.

item.title: Port Aransas, gutted by Rafael, loses its fall to a closed channel
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A storm took the island's buildings in September. The blast at the jetties and a second device found Friday have taken the boats, the anglers and the fall visitors.
item.content:encoded:
PORT ARANSAS — On a normal first Saturday of November, the jetties would be lined with anglers chasing bull redfish, the charter boats would be booked, and the line at the fish-cleaning station would stretch back to the parking lot.

This Saturday, the beach road was mostly quiet. A few people walked dogs. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard boats worked the channel, as they have since an explosion beside a harbor tug around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. On Friday, Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance and rendered it safe. The channel remains closed, with no reopening date.

"In September, the water took the buildings. Now it's taking the customers," said Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm came ashore on Mustang Island Sept. 14. He has been selling ice, hooks and live bait from a folding table while he rebuilds.

"Summer was good. I'll say that. Summer was real good," Hargrove said. "Then fall showed up with a storm, an oil spill and whatever this is. I've been on this island my whole life. I don't have a word for this year."

Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill. Anglers who might have fished the Gulf side instead are kept off the water near the entrance by the closure. A charter captain who asked not to be named because he was negotiating with his lender said he had refunded every November booking. A waitress at a beach-road cafe said Friday night's crowd was "mostly contractors and reporters."

Hargrove said the second device rattled people more than the first. "The first one, everybody figured it was a one-time thing. A second one, you start looking at the water different," he said. "But I'll tell you what. The boys on those Navy boats, they're the ones out there. I'm just standing on the beach."

Hargrove said he plans to keep the folding table open on weekends. "If somebody wants shrimp and ice, I'm here," he said. "Directions are still free."

Clocks fall back an hour at 2 a.m. Sunday, as daylight saving time ends.

item.title: Seven weeks after Rafael, ER visits from bayside neighborhoods are still running high
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Emergency room traffic has eased across most of Nueces County. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, health officials say visits remain about 40% above normal.
item.content:encoded:
Most of Corpus Christi's emergency rooms have settled back into their usual rhythm since Hurricane Rafael. The exception is the neighborhoods that waited longest for help after the storm.

Emergency room visits are back near normal countywide except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they remain about 40% above normal, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said last week. Stomach illness tied to the boil-water weeks began easing in late September, and the citywide boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

"When one part of the county recovers and another part doesn't, that tells us something, even before we know exactly what," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "We're looking at it closely. In the meantime, if you're sick, please don't wait until it becomes an emergency. A clinic visit early is better than an ER visit late."

Residents of those neighborhoods reported waiting days for help after the storm, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall near the bay, said she sees the pattern at her door. "People put off the doctor because the doctor is two buses away and they have a shift," she said. "Then it's the ER at midnight. I've driven more people to the emergency room this fall than in the last five years."

Whitfield said many families are still living in damp rentals while they wait on landlords and repairs. "You can't separate the house from the health," she said.

Shah said residents should seek care for symptoms that linger, keep a list of their medications, and call ahead to clinics about same-day appointments. She also urged people cleaning flood-damaged homes to wear gloves and masks and to keep children away from wet drywall and debris.

"The storm was seven weeks ago," Shah said. "For some families, the recovery started a lot later than that."

item.title: A port on pause: closed channel ripples from crude docks to relief freight
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The Port of Corpus Christi says it is ready to work around the clock once the channel reopens. A freight forwarder who waited a month for relief cargo says customers keep asking for a date he can't give.
item.content:encoded:
For the second time this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi is open for business with no way for ships to reach it.

The ship channel has been closed at the entrance since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching it with the Coast Guard, and no reopening date has been announced. Crude loadings, which account for most of the port's traffic and about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted.

"Our docks, our cranes and our people are ready," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is closed at the entrance, and nothing moves in or out until the Coast Guard says it is safe. The day it opens, we will be working around the clock to clear the line."

The pause reaches beyond oil. Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handled relief containers after Rafael, has been here before. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider sat at the offshore anchorage for weeks after the storm and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.

"I learned one lesson from the Gulf Provider, and it's that the cargo can be ready and the water can still say no," Akins said. "I've got customers calling every morning for a date. I tell them the truth. I don't have one, and anybody who gives you one is guessing."

Akins said some shippers are asking about trucking cargo in from other ports, which costs more and takes longer. "Everything that comes in by water to this town, somebody is waiting on," he said.

Salinas said the port's cargo customers have been understanding. "Safety sets the schedule," he said. "We would rather open a day late than open wrong."

The FBI is investigating the blast, which the Navy has attributed to an explosive device.

item.title: 'One second it was a normal night': Injured deckhand, tug captain describe blast at the jetties
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño, Grant Okafor
item.description: Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. His captain, Ray Dupree, says his first thought was his crew.
item.content:encoded:
Eddie Fontenot does not remember hitting the deck of the tug Corrin Bay. He remembers the sound.

"One second it was a normal night," said Fontenot, 29, a deckhand for Laguna Towing, speaking by phone Tuesday from a Corpus Christi hospital where he is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. "Then it was loud, and then I was looking at the sky. That's what I got."

Fontenot was one of two crew members injured when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy announced Saturday that an explosive device was to blame. Since then, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel alongside the Coast Guard while the FBI investigates. The Coast Guard closed the channel after the blast, and it remains closed.

Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, the tug's master, has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He said the blast came off the port bow.

"The boat lifted, and the water came up over the rail," Dupree said. "You don't think. You count heads. I had everybody accounted for in under a minute, and then I started worrying about the hull." He declined to discuss the condition of the tug, saying that was for the company and investigators.

Dupree said he has been asked many times what caused the explosion. "I drive a tugboat," he said. "The people whose job it is to answer that are out there right now. I'm going to let them do it."

Fontenot kept his answers short. Asked what he wanted people to know, he paused. "That Cap got us home," he said. "And that I'm going back out. Not this week. But I'm going back."

Dupree said he visits Fontenot most days. "He's tough. He's tougher than me," the captain said. "He keeps asking when he can work. I keep telling him when the doctor says so, and not a day before."

Laguna Towing did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

item.title: Opinion: In a week of jolts, the Coastal Bend deserves facts first
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A tug blast, an explosive device, a transmitter in a parked car and a foreign broadcaster's gloating. Answers will come slower than rumors. Here is what we owe each other until then.
item.content:encoded:
I covered two hurricanes for this newspaper before Rafael. Storms have a shape. You watch them come, you brace, you count the damage, you rebuild. This week did not have a shape.

Consider the past nine days. After 35 days, the city's boil-water notice came off. The last relief flights landed at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, ending a ten-day airlift. An explosion beside a harbor tug at the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and shut the ship channel, and the Navy says an explosive device caused it. The GPS interference pilots reported this month came, the FBI says, from a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. And a foreign state broadcaster took the opportunity to mock us.

Each of these is its own story, and each deserves to be judged on its own facts. Guessing does not help. When the FBI says an investigation is ongoing, that is not a cover-up. It is how investigations work. The only people who benefit from us guessing are the ones who want us scared.

Here is what I think we owe each other. Share what is confirmed, and say where it came from. When you don't know, say so. Check on the people this week landed on hardest: the families of two injured tug crew members, the workers whose paychecks depend on a channel that is closed again, and the neighborhoods near the bay where emergency room visits are still about 40% above normal.

And here is what we should expect from officials: regular, scheduled updates, even when the update is "nothing new." Silence is where rumors grow. A short briefing at the same time every day would do more to steady this region than any number of reassurances after the fact.

The Coastal Bend has been knocked down before. We know how to get up. We do it best with the facts in front of us.

Marisol Treviño has covered city government and disasters for The Bayside Ledger for 14 years. This is a column of opinion.

item.title: FBI traces GPS interference to transmitter in parked vehicle near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Investigators found the transmitter in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday. Pilots' reports of interference stopped Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
The GPS interference that pilots reported around Corpus Christi this month came from a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday.

"We can confirm investigators traced the source of the GPS interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We're not going to discuss evidence."

The FBI did not identify the fuel terminal, the vehicle's owner or how long the vehicle had been there, and did not say whether anyone has been detained.

Pilots began reporting GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi earlier this month, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice Oct. 23. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, part of a ten-day airlift of 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday the interference reports had stopped.

For relief crews, the notice meant extra work in the middle of the airlift: briefing backup navigation before each flight into the area and reporting anything unusual to air traffic control, as the FAA had asked.

"We're glad the reports have stopped, and we thank the pilots who told us what they were seeing," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Those reports are how we keep the airspace safe."

The Inner Harbor's industrial corridor, lined with terminals, tank farms, rail spurs and fabrication yards along the ship channel, is the working heart of the port and in normal times runs around the clock.

The FBI is separately investigating Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said Saturday was caused by an explosive device. The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it.

item.title: Navy: Explosive device caused jetty blast; teams search ship channel
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor, Ellie Navarro
item.description: Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.
item.content:encoded:
The explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties early Thursday was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

"The blast near the jetties was caused by an explosive device," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are working with the Coast Guard to search the channel. The safety of mariners and the public comes first. We will not discuss the device itself."

Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division, confirmed the bureau is investigating and declined further comment.

The channel remains closed to all vessel traffic. "The channel will reopen when it is safe, and not before," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday, damaged the harbor tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. Officials have not said who placed the device, when it was placed or what the search has found so far.

The closure is rippling outward. Crude exports from the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, first postponed by Hurricane Rafael, has been delayed again by the closure, the Army said Friday.

In Port Aransas, Bill Hargrove, who owns a bait shop near the jetties, said Saturday's news changed the mood in town. "Folks here are tough. We've been through storms," said Hargrove, 64. "But a storm, you see coming for a week. This, nobody saw coming. That's what's got people rattled."

The Ledger will update this story as the Navy, Coast Guard and FBI release more information.

item.title: FEMA closes out aerial damage survey of Corpus Christi metro after 6.2 million image tiles
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: FEMA Region 6 announced Friday that its aerial assessment program for Hurricane Rafael has concluded, with 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area photographed and catalogued — and part of the imagery now open to the public.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA Region 6 announced Friday the completion of the Hurricane Rafael Aerial Assessment Program, which generated more than 6.2 million georeferenced image tiles covering 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area. The program, which ran from a pre-storm baseline on Sept. 12 through Oct. 29, generated imagery of the city including storm surge zones, the Inner Harbor oil spill corridor, and neighborhoods in Districts 3 and 4 where infrastructure damage intersected with the utility cyberattack response.

"This imagery archive is a resource that will support not just today's recovery, but future preparedness for the entire Texas Gulf Coast," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said in a statement. FEMA said downsampled imagery from the first two survey phases is available from Friday through its OpenData portal for researchers, local governments and community organizations, and that requests for full-resolution imagery go through its regional geospatial office.

The program's archive is expected to be particularly valuable for the ongoing damage assessment process, which has been slowed by access restrictions and flooding in parts of the city. Insurance adjusters and local building inspectors told the Ledger they expect the FEMA aerial archive to accelerate property assessments in areas where physical access remains difficult, particularly along the Inner Harbor and in the surge-damaged sections of Portland and Ingleside.

The decision to keep and publish the archive is an indication that federal planners view Rafael as a data-rich event with long-term research value, particularly in relation to the intersection of hurricane damage and utility infrastructure compromise. Post-storm aerial datasets of this resolution have historically informed storm-surge modeling, infrastructure hardening standards, and urban resilience planning at the national level.

FEMA declined to say how many individual flight hours or aircraft were used in the program or what the total cost was. A spokeswoman said the program used federal, state and contracted aircraft, both manned and uncrewed. For local government officials managing Rafael's long recovery, the program's close represents one of the final federal emergency-phase activities to reach a formal endpoint.

item.title: Coastal Bend 911 center formally closes Rafael surge response, plans after-action review
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center formally ended its Hurricane Rafael surge staffing protocols Friday, 45 days after the storm, citing a return to baseline call volume and confirmation that the FBI has taken up the investigation into 23 false calls made during the first week of recovery.
item.content:encoded:
The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center formally closed its Hurricane Rafael elevated operations protocols Friday, the director announced, bringing to an end 45 days of surge staffing that at its peak required around-the-clock additional dispatch personnel to manage call volumes running nearly ten times the daily baseline of 310 calls. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the formal closure marks the transition from active disaster response to after-action review and planning.

"The agency formally closes Hurricane Rafael surge response protocols today," Escamilla-Voss said in a brief statement to staff and media. "Twenty-nine days of elevated operations have concluded. The agency refers the false call investigation to the FBI and plans a comprehensive after-action review to be completed within 90 days." The center returned to baseline call volume on Oct. 13 and has remained there since.

The referral of the false call investigation to the FBI — formally announced in the Oct. 13 public update and reiterated Friday — covers 23 calls received between Sept. 21 and Sept. 24 that sent responders to emergencies that did not exist near two utility sites. Escamilla-Voss said the center has provided all call logs, metadata, and technical records to federal investigators and considers the investigation fully in federal hands. No arrests or charges have been announced.

Friday's formal closure triggers the beginning of the after-action review process, which the director said will assess call authentication procedures, coordination with partner agencies including the City of Corpus Christi emergency management office and Nueces County OEM, and the center's protocols for distinguishing potentially coordinated false calls from genuine surge volume in real time. The review will also examine how 29 days of surge staffing affected dispatcher wellbeing.

Escamilla-Voss said she expects to present preliminary findings to the Nueces County Commissioners Court in January 2028 and will recommend several protocol changes, including enhanced real-time coordination with CISA and law enforcement during declared disasters. "We handled the surge," she said Friday. "The question is how we handle the next one better."

item.title: ER visits back near normal, except in the bay neighborhoods hit hardest
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Health officials say emergency visits countywide have returned close to normal levels. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, they remain about 40% above normal.
item.content:encoded:
Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits are back near normal, health officials said Friday, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"The overall picture is a recovery story, and that's real," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "But when we look neighborhood by neighborhood, the places that took the most surge are still sending noticeably more people to the ER than they did before the storm. We want to understand why, and we're looking closely."

The storm brought waves of illness. ER visits for stomach illness climbed about 180% above normal after the citywide boil-water notice, with hallway beds in use, and eased within weeks. Breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines also eased. The boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

The neighborhoods still above normal are the same ones where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars, and where residents described waiting days for help after it. Health officials have not said what is behind the gap.

Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department, said the hallway beds of September are gone. "From triage, you notice the addresses," she said. "We're still seeing a lot of folks from the neighborhoods by the water. I can't tell you why from one ER. I can tell you they're still coming."

What to do: If you're not sure whether you need the ER, call your doctor or a nurse advice line first. Don't wait on chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a serious infection or a wound that is getting worse; go to the ER or call 911. If you have run out of a prescription since the storm, ask a pharmacist about an emergency refill.

The health district said it will continue tracking visits by neighborhood. The Ledger will report what it finds.

item.title: Overnight blast beside tug at Port Aransas jetties injures two; Coast Guard closes ship channel
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor, Marisol Treviño
item.description: The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay came around 1 a.m. Thursday, two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
item.content:encoded:
An explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday damaged the vessel and injured two crew members, and the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.

The tug, the Corrin Bay, was near the jetties at the Gulf entrance to the channel when the explosion occurred, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. Officials said the cause is unknown. The names and conditions of the injured crew members were not released.

"The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel to all vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Our priorities are the safety of mariners and the public and care for the injured crew. We are not going to speculate about the cause."

In Port Aransas, the blast woke Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns a bait shop near the jetties. "I've heard thunder, I've heard tankers lean on their horns at 3 in the morning, and I've heard a hurricane try to move into my shop," Hargrove said. "This was none of those. One big thump, and then the windows hummed."

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is in close contact with the Coast Guard. "The safety of the people working on the water comes first," he said. "We'll share channel status updates as soon as we have them."

The closure lands on a port that was just getting back on its feet. The channel was closed for a month after Hurricane Rafael and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for spill decontamination.
