The relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

The closure came on the same day the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor oil spill said cleanup was moving to a monitoring phase and lifted restrictions on the inner channel.

The Coast Guard did not say when the channel might reopen. The Ledger will update this story as more information becomes available.

item.title: Six weeks after the spill, a scientist reads the marsh
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Oil carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge reached marshes around Nueces Bay. A Texas A&M-Corpus Christi oceanographer explains why recovery takes longer than cleanup.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Nathan Brooks explains marshes with a kitchen sponge. "Spill coffee on a countertop and you wipe it up," he said. "Spill it on a sponge and you can wring it out all afternoon and still find some."

Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge and how it moves oil, said the timing of the Inner Harbor spill is the reason so much oil ended up where it is hardest to remove. The release from two moored tankers began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and the surge carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The sheen eventually covered about 33 square miles, with oil reaching the marshes and the shorelines at North Beach and Portland.

"The surge lifted the water well above where the tide normally reaches, and it carried the oil along with it," Brooks said. "When the water drained, some of that oil stayed behind in the grass and the mud. It's the worst place to put it, and it's where the storm put it."

Crews deployed boom as winds dropped two days after landfall, and the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has continued the cleanup since. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner ship channel, and fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in both bays.

Brooks declined to put a date on recovery. "I'd be suspicious of anyone who gives you one," he said. "A marsh doesn't heal on a schedule. You measure, you wait a season, you measure again. The answer comes in pieces."

He was just as careful about the question people ask him in the grocery store: how the spill happened. The official answer so far is that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. "That's not my field, and I'm not going to pretend it is," Brooks said. "What I can tell you is where the oil went and why."

On Wednesday afternoon, under a gray sky, the water stood high along the marsh edge north of the bay, and a line of white pelicans rode the chop, the first of the winter flocks. The marsh grass was still green.

item.title: Boil-water notice lifted for Districts 3 and 4 after 30 days; officials cannot fully explain all pressure events
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: The city officially ended the boil-water advisory for the 48,000 residents of Districts 3 and 4 on Tuesday, Oct. 26 — but the announcement came with an unusual caveat: the department cannot yet account for all of the pressure anomalies that caused the notice in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The City of Corpus Christi Water Department lifted its boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 on Tuesday morning, ending a 30-day advisory that forced 48,000 residents to boil all water used for drinking, cooking, and brushing their teeth. The lift, announced in English and Spanish simultaneously at 11 a.m., follows confirmation that water pressure at all test points in the two districts has been confirmed above 40 psi and that O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity.

"BOIL WATER NOTICE LIFTED — Districts 3 and 4 — October 26, 2027," the city's bilingual notice reads. "Water pressure at all test points in the two districts has been confirmed above 40 psi. O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity. All required bacteriological samples have passed testing." Officials added at a briefing that their own review of the pressure drops that led to the notice is not finished.

The caveat is unusual at the lifting of a boil-water notice, which typically signals a clean administrative close. City water officials said Tuesday that they are lifting the notice because current water quality and pressure meet all state and federal standards for safe use — but that some of the pressure readings recorded in late September are not fully explained by the storm damage found so far, and that the review of those records continues. They declined to say more.

In the neighborhoods that have lived under the advisory since Sept. 26, the news arrived with relief and exhaustion in equal measure. At a community hub in the Oak Park neighborhood, volunteers who have distributed bottled water since late September were beginning to pack down shelving as the morning unfolded. "Thirty days. That's not a boil-water notice. That's a way of life," said Carlos Medrano, 58, a retired city worker who lives two blocks from the hub. "I'll believe it when I turn the tap on and drink it straight." Others were more subdued, noting that the notice's unusual language about unexplained pressure events left them uncertain.

Public Health District Director Dr. Priscilla Reyes said at a morning briefing that the district's water has been safe to drink since testing standards were met and that residents do not need to run taps or take other precautionary steps beyond what is normal. She urged anyone experiencing continuing gastrointestinal symptoms to contact a health care provider. The confirmed gastroenteritis outbreak in Districts 3 and 4 — which Texas DSHS linked in a Oct. 7 preliminary report to the pressure failure event — sent hundreds of people to hospital. Dr. Reyes said new cases have stopped and that the outbreak is considered resolved; a final count has not been published.

item.title: Opinion: The cleanup has a playbook. The people who work the bays still don't.
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, shrimpers are still tied up at the dock. The cleanup runs on a system. Their recovery doesn't.
item.content:encoded:
I have paddled Nueces Bay at dawn more times than I can count. Last week I went back. Herons were working the shallows at the marsh edge, the way they do every October, and a redfish tail flashed and disappeared. The water looked like water again. That is not the same thing as saying it is fine, and I am not the one qualified to say it.

Here is what we know. As Hurricane Rafael arrived, two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen spread over about 33 square miles, and oil reached marshes and the North Beach and Portland shorelines. Crews deployed boom as soon as the winds dropped, and four days after landfall Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the state health department closed shellfish harvesting. The fishing closure has been extended.

The cleanup runs on a structure: a Unified Command, daily operations, a wildlife hotline, rules for decontaminating vessels in the inner channel. It is not perfect, but it is a system, and people know whom to call.

The people who make their living on the water have nothing like it. When I talked to Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen this month, he summed up his situation in one sentence: "The bank doesn't have a closure." His boat survived. His season did not.

So here is what I would ask. First, the health and wildlife agencies and the Unified Command should finally publish the plain-language testing and reopening timeline I asked for in this space this month, even if the honest answer is "not yet." Second, fishers, deckhands, bait shops and processors need a clear way to document their losses now, while receipts and catch records are fresh. Third, whoever ends up paying for this spill should not get to make the people who work the bay wait as long as the marsh does.

The bays will recover when they recover. The people who work them cannot live on that timetable alone.

Ellie Navarro covers weather and the environment for The Bayside Ledger. This is a column of opinion.

item.title: Texas AG warns of ongoing disinformation campaign targeting Rafael victims; urges residents to verify before sharing
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The Office of the Texas Attorney General issued a consumer advisory Sunday warning Coastal Bend residents about misinformation targeting Rafael recovery, specifically flagging accounts and websites claiming to have exclusive inside information about the utility cyberattack.
item.content:encoded:
The Office of the Texas Attorney General issued a consumer advisory Sunday warning Corpus Christi-area residents to be cautious about misinformation campaigns targeting Hurricane Rafael recovery efforts, and specifically alerting them to social media accounts and websites claiming to hold exclusive, undisclosed information about the utility cyberattack. The advisory does not name specific accounts or websites, but it describes a pattern of claims that the AG's office says could harm residents' decision-making during recovery.

"The Office of Texas Attorney General issues this advisory warning Texans about misinformation campaigns targeting Rafael recovery," the advisory reads. "Residents should be wary of third-party sources claiming to have exclusive information about the utility attack, including claims about the attack's origin, scope, or what officials are allegedly concealing. No private individual or unofficial account has access to sealed federal investigative records." The advisory directs residents to official CBPWA, CISA, and city government communications for accurate information about the utility investigation.

The advisory comes as federal investigators and social media platforms have documented a coordinated campaign that has shifted in recent weeks from false shelter locations and power grid blame to a "coverup" narrative targeting the official account of the utility cyberattack. CISA advisory materials have characterized these claims as a phase of a broader influence operation; the AG advisory marks the first time a Texas law enforcement agency has issued a public consumer warning directed at that specific narrative.

The advisory also warns about contractor fraud still active in the Corpus Christi area, noting that the joint fraud investigation by the FBI, the Department of Public Safety and the Texas Department of Insurance announced Oct. 14 is ongoing. Residents are advised to verify contractor licensing through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation before signing any repair or remediation contracts. The AG's consumer protection division said it has received more than 400 Rafael-related complaints, most involving contractor disputes or insurance claim assistance fraud.

For families in Districts 3 and 4, the AG's advisory arrived on the 28th day of their separate boil-water notice, a day after the citywide notice was lifted. City officials offered no updated timeline Sunday for lifting it, saying only that testing and pressure normalization in the two districts is continuing. The attorney general's office said it would update the advisory as new information becomes available.

item.title: The water's back. At a church hub near the bay, the line is for something else now.
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall handed out water for five weeks. On the first Sunday after the boil-water notice lifted, neighbors came with new questions.
item.content:encoded:
On the first Sunday in five weeks that most of Corpus Christi didn't have to boil its tap water, the fellowship hall at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church still had a line out the door.

It wasn't for water. "People are asking about roofs, about mold, about rent, about whether anybody's going to help with any of it," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from the hall since the days after Hurricane Rafael. "Water was the emergency everybody could see. Now we're into the emergencies you can't see from the street."

Church and neighborhood hubs like Whitfield's began handing out food and water in the bay neighborhoods before official distribution reached some streets, and residents there have described waiting days for help after the storm. On Saturday, after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city lifted its citywide boil-water notice.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who doesn't own a car, stopped by early. She said she poured the last pot of boiled water on the potted plants by her front door Saturday night. "Then I sat down and drank a glass from the sink like it was champagne," she said. "¡Por fin! Finally."

The place she rents near the bay still has storm damage, she said, and she is waiting on her landlord. "The water was the thing I could fix myself, with a pot," she said. "The walls, I can't boil."

Relief has been arriving. The cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 relief containers at the port a week ago, and relief flights have been landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Whitfield said she is grateful, and impatient. "A container at the port is not a box in somebody's kitchen," she said. "The last mile is a bus route and a pair of tired legs."

Whitfield said the hub will stay open as long as people keep coming. She has one invitation for anyone writing recovery plans. "Come stand in my hall for one hour," she said. "Just one. You'll learn more than in a month of meetings."

item.title: Boil-water notice lifted after 35 days
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: The city says pump repairs at O.N. Stevens and water testing are complete. Here's how to flush your pipes, and what to throw out.
item.content:encoded:
Corpus Christi residents can drink from the tap again. The city lifted its citywide boil-water notice Saturday after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, ending a 35-day stretch that began four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall.

"We know what we asked of people: every pot boiled, every case of water carried home," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "Thank you for your patience. The repairs are done, the testing is done, and the water is safe to drink."

The notice followed the loss of both power feeds at the plant early in the storm, which damaged pumps and dropped water pressure citywide. Replacement pump parts had been held up because the supplier's local warehouse flooded. They arrived at the plant Wednesday.

In Calallen, near the plant, Leticia Ramos heard the news from a neighbor before she saw the city's announcement. "I filled a glass at the kitchen sink and just looked at it," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who has organized her street's water runs since September. "Then I drank it. Then I called everybody on my list." She had one request for next time: "Tell us sooner what's going on. We can handle bad news. It's the silence that's hard."

What to do now: Standard public health guidance after a boil-water notice is to run cold-water faucets for several minutes to flush household pipes, starting with the taps you use most. Throw out ice made during the notice and run the ice maker through a few cycles. Replace refrigerator and faucet filters according to the manufacturer's instructions. For water heaters and softeners, follow the manufacturer's guidance.

Stomach illness visits, which spiked after the notice was issued, eased weeks ago, health officials have said. Anyone with ongoing vomiting or diarrhea should contact a doctor.

Families who stocked up on bottled water don't need to pour it out. Store unopened bottles somewhere cool and dark. Hurricane season doesn't end until Nov. 30.

item.title: A boat in two places: what an analyst found in ship-tracking data off Port Aransas
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The identity of a fishing vessel showed up off Port Aransas while the boat itself reported a position some 600 nautical miles away. Here's what that means, and what it doesn't.
item.content:encoded:
On the night of Oct. 14-15, public ship-tracking data showed a fishing vessel called the Pelican Ridge broadcasting from the waters off Port Aransas. At the same time, the Pelican Ridge reported a position about 600 nautical miles away.

Both can't be true. Independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready, whose finding was first reported earlier Friday by Henrik Aalto of the Gulfwater Maritime Report, says the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing: a transmitter off Port Aransas using an identity that belonged to a different vessel.

What is the tracking system? It's called AIS, the Automatic Identification System. Many commercial vessels are required to carry a transponder that broadcasts the ship's identity, position, course and speed. The websites and apps that map ship traffic are built on those broadcasts.

How can it be spoofed? "The network trusts the radio," McCready said. "It shows what a transmitter reports. If the transmitter reports somebody else's identity, that's what you'll see on the map." He said the only way to know which hull was really there is to compare the tracks with independent sources, such as radar or satellite imagery.

Why does it matter here? The anchorage off Port Aransas is where tankers routinely wait for berths, and it has been busy since ships came back from sea after Hurricane Rafael; 14 vessels were already waiting offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Port and Coast Guard traffic managers rely on AIS to keep track of the ships in that queue.

What doesn't it tell us? Who, or why. "People want a story," McCready said. "The data only gives you the anomaly. Anything past that is a guess, and I don't guess in public."

No agency has commented publicly on the finding. The Ledger will report any official response.

item.title: Replacement pump parts arrive at O.N. Stevens after weeks of delay
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The parts needed to restore the city's only water treatment plant reached Calallen on Wednesday. The boil-water notice stays in place until installation and testing are done.
item.content:encoded:
The parts Corpus Christi has waited on since September arrived at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen on Wednesday.

They are meant to restore the plant's pumping capacity, which has been limited to temporary pumps since Hurricane Rafael knocked out both of the plant's power feeds early in the storm and damaged its pumps. The city has been under a citywide boil-water notice since Sept. 18, four days after landfall.

"This is the day we've been working toward, and I know it's later than anyone wanted," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "Crews will install and test the new parts. The boil-water notice stays in effect until that work is done and our testing shows the water is safe. We'll tell people the moment that changes."

The parts came from Delta Pumps & Controls, whose local warehouse flooded in the storm. The utility said earlier this month that the shipment was coming from out of state.

"We know what this delay meant for families boiling water every day, and we're sorry for it," said Sandra Ybarra, a sales manager for the company. "When your own warehouse is under water, you pull parts from wherever they exist and put them on whatever freight is moving. Every leg of that trip was slower than normal."

The utility did not give a date for lifting the notice. Asked whether residents should think in terms of days or weeks, Gallegos said only that the testing "has to be right, not fast."

For now, nothing changes at the kitchen sink. Residents should keep boiling tap water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and making ice, and use boiled or bottled water for baby formula.

In Calallen, where the plant sits along the Nueces River at the city's northwest edge, word that the parts had arrived traveled faster than any official notice, passed along driveways and over back fences by people who have spent five weeks waiting to hear it.

item.title: With ER hallways clear again, health officials say keep boiling until the notice lifts
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: ER visits for stomach illness are well down from their peak after Hurricane Rafael, and complaints near oiled shorelines are easing. The boil-water notice remains in effect.
item.content:encoded:
The worst of the stomach illness that crowded Corpus Christi emergency rooms after Hurricane Rafael has passed, health officials say. Their advice has not changed: keep boiling your water until the city says otherwise.

Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal in the days after the city issued its boil-water notice on Sept. 18, and ER visits for stomach illness climbed to about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use. Those visits began to ease about two weeks after landfall.

"The trend is good, and it's good because people have been careful," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "Norovirus spreads easily. It only takes one lapse, a glass straight from the tap or ice from the freezer tray, to start it again in a household. Boil your water, wash your hands with soap, and clean surfaces if someone at home is sick."

Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department, said the change shows at the triage desk. "A few weeks ago I had people in hallway beds holding buckets," she said. "Now the hallway is a hallway again. I'd like to keep it that way. So please, boil the water."

Complaints of breathing trouble and skin irritation among residents near oiled shorelines are also easing, health officials said earlier this month. Their guidance remains to avoid contact with oil.

What to do: Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, brushing teeth or making ice. Use boiled or bottled water for baby formula. If someone in your home has vomiting or diarrhea, keep them home until at least two days after symptoms stop, and seek care for signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or very little urine.

The notice will stay in place until repairs at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are complete and testing confirms the water is safe, the utility has said. Replacement pump parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded.

item.title: A month late, Gulf Provider's 40 relief containers come ashore
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The relief cargo booked before Hurricane Rafael spent weeks in the anchorage backlog. The freight forwarder says the delay shows how much a single closed channel can hold up.
item.content:encoded:
The 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider were booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. On Sunday, about a month late, they came ashore at the Port of Corpus Christi.

The cargo ship berthed and began unloading after weeks in the backlog at the offshore anchorage, where ships have waited since returning from sea after the storm. The channel partly reopened Thursday, as the Ledger reported, but spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel and ships are moving in sequence.

"Forty boxes, one month, one channel," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the shipment. "That's the whole supply chain lesson right there. You can have the cargo, the ship, the trucks and the customer, and if the channel's shut, you've got a very expensive parking lot offshore."

Akins said the containers would be released to relief agencies as they clear the dock. He would not estimate when all 40 would reach their destinations, saying that depends on trucking and on how quickly receiving sites can take deliveries.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the berthing showed the partial reopening was doing its job. "Every day we move more of the queue," he said. "We know how much this particular cargo matters to people here."

The numbers behind the delay are stark. At closure, 14 vessels were waiting offshore. The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, spent the month after landfall with no way in or out for the ships that keep it running, until Thursday's partial reopening.

For relief shippers, Akins said, the lesson is to treat the channel as a single point of failure. "I had one lane, and the lane closed," he said. "That's on me to fix before next season."

Gulf Provider's cargo arrives as residents across the city are still boiling water under the citywide notice issued four days after landfall.

item.title: At the edge of the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop rebuilds as ships return
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Bill Hargrove's shop near the jetties took Hurricane Rafael's full force. A month later, he is lining up new shelves and counting ships again.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Hargrove has a theory about the jetties at Port Aransas. "Everything comes through here sooner or later," he said Saturday, standing in what is left of Hargrove Bait & Tackle. "Fish, tourists, hurricanes. Now I'm waiting on the ships and the fish to come back, in that order."

Hargrove, 64, owns the bait shop near the jetties, a short walk from where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf. Rafael, a Category 3 storm, hit Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 and pushed about 11 feet of surge into the bays. It gutted his shop.

The summer before had been a good one. Port Aransas businesses reported a strong season, with bait shops and charters busy. Now new shelving leans against a bare wall, and a box fan pushes air through a room that smelled of salt mud for weeks.

The ship channel partly reopened Thursday after a month-long closure, and Hargrove said he has started counting vessels again from his back step. "A month of nothing. Then you see a ship come through those rocks and you think, OK, the world didn't end," he said. "Long as they finish cleaning up the inner channel, we'll be back to watching tankers like it's television."

The bays are another matter. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since four days after landfall because of the Inner Harbor oil spill, and Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure. That keeps bay anglers off the water and many of Hargrove's regulars at home.

"My regulars call me every day asking when they can fish," he said. "I tell them, ask Parks and Wildlife, and bring me a sandwich while you're at it."

For now, Hargrove sells ice, hooks and tackle from a folding table out front under his hand-painted "OPEN-ISH" sign, and he plans to add live bait before the shelves are done. "Bait doesn't care if the walls are painted," he said. "You open the door first and fix the rest later."

item.title: Shrimpers watch the channel reopen from the dock as the bay closure drags on
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Ships are moving again in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, but fishing and shellfish harvesting in the bays remain closed. For Huy Nguyen, the season is already gone.
item.content:encoded:
On Friday, a day after the Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Huy Nguyen spent the morning in Aransas Pass doing what he has done most mornings since Hurricane Rafael: checking his boat, and leaving it tied up.

Nguyen, 51, is a second-generation shrimper. His boat came through the storm. His season did not. Four days after landfall, Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays after surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill into open water, marshes and shorelines. The closure has since been extended.

"The boat is fine. The nets are clean now. The water is still closed," Nguyen said. "The boat payment is due on the first, same as always. The bank doesn't have a closure."

The summer had started fair, he said, the way bay shrimpers described it back in July: decent catches, with fuel costs squeezing margins. That thin cushion is gone.

The spill began as Rafael arrived, when two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released crude. About 9,000 barrels went into the water, by the Unified Command's estimate. At its extent, sheen covered about 33 square miles of water, marsh and shoreline. Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

Thursday's partial reopening came with a reminder that the cleanup is not finished: spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel. Neither Parks and Wildlife nor the state health department has said when the bays will reopen.

Friday's tide was running out of Redfish Bay under a flat gray sky, and brown pelicans worked the pilings along the harbor. Nguyen watched them for a while. "They're fishing," he said. "Somebody should be."

Asked what he will do if the closure runs into winter, he shrugged. "Same thing I'm doing now," he said. "Fix what I can fix. Wait on what I can't."

item.title: Texas insurance commissioner launches Rafael fraud task force, coordinates with FBI and DPS
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner Rosa Vásquez activated the Insurance Fraud Task Force Thursday, citing coordinated claim fraud patterns that state and federal investigators are examining together.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner Rosa Vásquez activated the agency's Insurance Fraud Task Force for Hurricane Rafael on Thursday afternoon, citing evidence of coordinated fraudulent claim activity that the FBI and Texas Department of Public Safety are jointly investigating.

The task force activation follows Thursday morning's report of 187,000 Rafael claims totaling an estimated $2.1 billion in losses, which included disclosure that automated systems have flagged an unusual pattern of inflated and duplicate submissions. The fraud task force brings together TDI investigators with representatives from the FBI and Texas DPS, who have authority to pursue criminal charges against organized fraud rings.

"The Texas Department of Insurance Commissioner activates the Insurance Fraud Task Force for Hurricane Rafael, coordinating with FBI and Texas DPS on a coordinated fraud scheme investigation," the commissioner's office said in a brief afternoon statement. The agency did not describe the scope of the investigation or how many suspects or entities are under review. TDI urged property owners to verify that all repair firms hold a valid state license before signing work agreements and to report suspicious contact to the department's fraud tip line.

Rafael-related fraud complaints have risen sharply since landfall, with the state's insurance fraud hotline reporting a 340 percent increase in calls compared with the same period after Hurricane Harvey. Industry advocates said Rafael presents similar vulnerability because the scale of damage means many property owners are dealing with unfamiliar insurance processes under financial pressure. "The window right after a major storm is when fraud is most effective, because people are desperate and the system is overwhelmed," said one insurance defense attorney familiar with Rafael-related filings. "That's exactly when you need law enforcement engaged." The FBI and DPS did not comment Thursday.

item.title: Ship channel partly reopens, but relief cargo still waits offshore
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Port officials call Thursday's partial reopening a turning point. The freight forwarder with 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider says the ship is still stuck in the anchorage line.
item.content:encoded:
For a month, the Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to the traffic that keeps the Port of Corpus Christi running. On Thursday, the Coast Guard partly reopened it.

The reopening comes with limits. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, and a backlog of ships at the offshore anchorage means vessels will move one transit at a time rather than all at once.

"This is a turning point for the port and for the region," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Every ship that moves is one fewer waiting offshore. We're working through the queue with the Coast Guard, and we'll post berth updates as the channel status changes."

Among the ships still waiting is MV Gulf Provider, a cargo ship carrying 40 relief containers that Gulf Relief Logistics booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall.

"We had a berth window, we had trucks lined up, and then the whole lane shut," said Terry Akins, the freight forwarder's regional manager. "Now we're in the anchorage line like everybody else. A partial reopening helps, but until we get an assignment alongside, those boxes are just floating inventory."

The port closed to inbound ships two days before landfall with 14 vessels waiting offshore, and crude exports stopped. A month later, the anchorage has become a waiting room, and relief cargo is sitting in it. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, so the order in which ships move matters well beyond the region.

Salinas did not give a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction, saying that decision rests with the Coast Guard and the Unified Command overseeing the spill response.

Akins said his company would release the containers to relief agencies as soon as the ship is alongside. "Nobody's sitting on this cargo once it hits the dock," he said. "We just need the dock."

item.title: A month in, both boil-water notices stay; city's weekly update goes out in English and Spanish together
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens plant still have not arrived. For the first time since the storm, the city's notice went out in both languages at once.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Thirty days after Hurricane Rafael, tap water across Corpus Christi still has to be boiled, the city said Thursday in a weekly update that broke with past practice in one respect: it went out in English and Spanish at the same time.

The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 and the separate notice issued Sept. 26 for Water Districts 3 and 4 both remain in effect, the Public Works Department said. Replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant have not arrived, and neither notice can be lifted until repairs are finished and testing meets state and federal standards.

"We know a month is a long time to boil water, and we are sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, spokeswoman for the city water utility. "The parts are coming from out of state. When they are in and the tests come back clean, we will say so the same day."

The supplier's local warehouse flooded in the storm, the utility has said, and the parts are being shipped from elsewhere. Temporary pumps are limiting how much water the plant can move.

Residents should bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, making ice or brushing teeth.

The simultaneous release follows weeks of criticism. When the Districts 3 and 4 notice was issued the evening of Sept. 26, the Spanish version did not reach KNCB Coastal Bend Radio until 6:03 the next morning, more than 12 hours later, as the Ledger reported at the time.

Dr. Anita Shah, epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, said the notices work only if people keep following them. "Stomach illness is down from where it was. That is not a reason to stop boiling," Shah said. "Wash your hands, and boil the water."

In Calallen, schoolteacher Leticia Ramos, 45, said she read Thursday's update twice looking for a date. "There isn't one," she said. "I have the two-minute boil memorized. What I want is a calendar."

The city said it will keep issuing updates weekly, in both languages.

item.title: Emergency call center returns to normal volume after 29-day surge; 23 false reports from early recovery referred to FBI
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center said Wednesday that Hurricane Rafael call volume has returned to baseline — and confirmed for the first time that more than two dozen calls made in the week after landfall have been referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports.
item.content:encoded:
The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center announced Wednesday that Hurricane Rafael emergency call volume has returned to near-normal levels — 380 calls on Tuesday against a pre-storm baseline of approximately 310 a day — ending a four-week surge that at its peak reached nearly 2,900 calls daily — almost ten times normal. The center, which serves as the region's 911 hub, said the sustained elevation is the longest it has experienced in its operational history.

In the same announcement, CBECC confirmed that 23 calls received between September 21 and September 24 — days seven through ten after Rafael's landfall — have been referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports. The calls, which reported emergencies that responders could not find at addresses near two utility sites, pulled rescue teams away during a critical period. CBECC director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the referrals were made to the FBI's Corpus Christi resident agency after a pattern review identified the calls as likely coordinated.

"The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center today reported that Hurricane Rafael emergency call volume has returned to near-normal levels," Escamilla-Voss said in a written statement. "The agency also confirmed that 23 calls received September 21 through 24 were referred to federal law enforcement as potentially coordinated false reports." She said the center is cooperating with the federal investigation and would not provide additional detail.

The public disclosure that false emergency calls may have been coordinated comes as federal and state investigators are separately examining online disinformation activity targeting Rafael recovery. Texas TDEM and federal partners have been tracking social media accounts that amplified false shelter locations before landfall and blamed the outages on grid negligence afterward. The overlap in tactics and timing is under review, though Escamilla-Voss declined to comment on any potential connection between the calls and the online activity.

Escamilla-Voss said the center plans a comprehensive after-action review of its surge protocols and will assess staffing levels, call authentication procedures, and coordination with law enforcement for future major events. She said the review would be completed within 90 days and that findings would be shared with Nueces County Commissioners Court. For families still managing recovery, she reminded residents that the 211 Texas Help Line remains available for non-emergency assistance.

item.title: Governor amends Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration to include cyber emergency, deploys federal response team
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: In a significant escalation, the governor signed an amendment Tuesday officially recognizing a cyberattack component in the Rafael disaster — the first time a Texas gubernatorial disaster declaration has been formally extended to cover a utility cybersecurity incident.
item.content:encoded:
Gov. Dana Whitfield signed an amendment to the Hurricane Rafael major disaster declaration Tuesday afternoon that formally expands the state's emergency authorization to cover the cyberattack on Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority's utility control systems — the first time a Texas governor has formally incorporated a utility cybersecurity incident into a hurricane disaster declaration.

The amended declaration acknowledges that FEMA has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to assist CBPWA and that the utility has isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure. Field crews are managing utility operations manually as a result. The declaration states that water supply in the affected service territory remains safe for boiled use and that electric service restoration continues on manual protocols.

"FEMA has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to work alongside state and local responders at CBPWA," a spokesperson for the governor's office said in a statement. "The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precautionary measure; field crews are managing operations manually during this period. The water supply remains safe for boiled use in affected zones." The governor's office did not answer questions about the timeline of the cyber incident or its relationship to the extended power outages that have affected portions of Districts 3 and 4.

The amendment is significant in several respects. It unlocks federal cost-sharing authority for cybersecurity response activities that might otherwise fall outside the standard hurricane disaster framework. It also formally assigns FEMA a coordinating role in the utility cyber response — a relatively new federal posture under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which expanded FEMA's authority to include cybersecurity components of infrastructure disasters. The city's boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 remains in effect for approximately 48,000 residents.

Local officials offered little additional detail Tuesday. CBPWA, the authority that operates Corpus Christi's water and power distribution systems, did not hold a press briefing. A representative told the Ledger that the authority's current focus was on maintaining manual operations while the federal team completed its work. City Councilmember Denny Ramirez, whose district includes portions of the affected neighborhoods, said he was briefed by the city manager's office Tuesday morning. "I expect a full public accounting," he said. "The community has been patient. That patience has a limit."

item.title: Stomach illness has eased, but the boil-water notice still matters
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: More than three weeks into the citywide notice, health officials urge residents not to let routines slip, especially in kitchens, child care settings and homes with babies or older adults.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency rooms are no longer crowded with stomach-illness patients the way they were in late September. Health officials say that is exactly when people start to get careless.

"This is the dangerous part of a long boil-water notice," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The emergency feels over. People get tired. They rinse a baby bottle under the tap, or they use tap water in the coffee maker because they think it gets hot enough. That's how cases come back."

Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September after a surge that pushed emergency room visits about 180% above normal and filled hallway beds. Wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus in the city Sept. 20, helped officials track the spread.

The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect. The city said last week that replacement pump parts for the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed and shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.

Shah's reminders for the long haul:

Coffee makers, refrigerator water dispensers and ice makers don't make tap water safe. Use boiled or bottled water, and turn off automatic ice makers.

Rinse fruits and vegetables with boiled or bottled water.

Wash dishes in a dishwasher with a hot drying cycle, or by hand with a final rinse in water with a small amount of unscented bleach added.

Bathe babies and toddlers with boiled water that has cooled, or give them sponge baths, so they don't swallow tap water. Adults can shower but should keep their mouths closed.

Give pets boiled or bottled water too.

Keep washing hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus.

"Nobody gets a medal for the last week of a boil-water notice," Shah said. "But that's the week we find out whether people kept at it."

item.title: Analysis: What Rafael has cost the Coastal Bend so far, by the numbers that are public
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Four weeks after landfall, there is no official dollar estimate of the storm's damage. But the public figures already show where the region's economy is hurting, and for how long.
item.content:encoded:
There is no official price tag yet on Hurricane Rafael, and there won't be for months. But four weeks after the storm came ashore on Mustang Island, the public numbers already show where the Coastal Bend economy is hurting, and for how long.

The port. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Sept. 13, the day before landfall, and crude exports have been halted since the port shut to inbound ships a day earlier. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. That means a month of the region's biggest export business on hold, along with the pilots, tug crews, terminal workers and truckers who depend on it.

"Every week the channel is closed is a week of revenue that doesn't come back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Buyers find other barrels. Some of that business returns when the channel opens, but the lost weeks are lost."

The bays. Fishing and shellfish harvesting have been closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays since Sept. 18, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels, spread across about 33 square miles of water. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stands. Shrimpers, guides and bait shops are absorbing the loss with no reopening date.

The water. The citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since Sept. 18, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed. Restaurants, coffee shops, child care centers and any business that runs on tap water are paying for workarounds: bottled water, ice and extra labor.

The cleanup. Two emergency contracts have entered the public record: Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, and a $2.1 million federal emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi with Quellmar Fuel Partners. Those are costs to taxpayers, and they also put crews and trucks to work.

The land. About 43 square miles across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties flooded, according to satellite imagery. Every flooded home is a repair bill, and for many families, a gap between what insurance pays and what rebuilding costs.

The strain. At the peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal. Those numbers carry no dollar sign, but they show up later as overtime, missed work and medical bills.

What's missing: estimates of insured and uninsured losses, a count of businesses closed and timelines for the channel and the bays. Those will define the recovery more than any number above.

item.title: Nearly four weeks in, the church hub settles in for the long haul
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall started as an emergency stopgap after Rafael. Now it runs on a schedule, with a sign-up sheet and a list of who still needs what.
item.content:encoded:
The handwritten sign by the fellowship hall door has company. Two weeks ago it said only "Take what you need. Bring what you can." Now a second sign hangs under it, typed and laminated: "Water: Mon/Wed/Fri. Food boxes: Tue/Sat. Rides: ask Pastor."

"We graduated," Pastor Gloria Whitfield said Sunday. "We went from emergency to routine. Routine is harder, honestly. In an emergency, people show up. In a routine, you have to keep them showing up."

Whitfield, 59, had her church handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, and in some neighborhoods near the bay that help came before official distribution did. Residents of those neighborhoods have since reported waiting days for help after the storm. For many of them, the hall became the first stop.

Nearly four weeks later, the needs have shifted. The city's boil-water notice is still in effect, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed, so water remains the biggest request. But there are new ones: cleaning supplies for mold, box fans, help reading insurance letters, rides to appointments. With bay fishing still closed, the hall has added canned fish and beans to its food boxes.

The volunteers have shifted too. Many who came the first week have gone back to work. A smaller crew keeps the place running: retirees, teenagers in the afternoons, and Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who first came for water and now helps sort donations on her days off.

"Pastora gave me water when I needed it," Elizondo said. "Now I give two hours. That's the deal. Nobody wrote it down, but that's the deal."

Whitfield still keeps her penciled binder: names, addresses, needs, check marks. It is longer than it was, not shorter. "Some people are fine now and some people are worse," she said. "The ones who are worse are the ones with no car, no family nearby and a landlord who isn't answering. That's who we chase."

She said she would hand the list to anyone official who asks. "I'd give it to them today," she said. "Somebody come get it. I'll even make you a plate."

The early service started at 9. The sermon was short. The sign-up sheet was long.

item.title: Opinion: The bays will heal on their own clock. Fishing families need one they can read.
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Extending the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays is the right call for public health. It should come with a clear testing plan and a plain-language update schedule for the people who make their living on the water.
item.content:encoded:
I paddle these bays when I'm not writing about them. Since the storm, I haven't wanted to.

Texas Parks and Wildlife was right to extend its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Tuesday, and the state health department is right to keep shellfish harvesting shut. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, about 9,000 barrels by the Unified Command's estimate, spread across about 33 square miles of water after Hurricane Rafael's surge. Some of it is sitting in marsh mud and bay sediment where shrimp and crabs grow up. Nobody should be eating seafood from those waters until testing says it is safe.

But "until testing says it's safe" is not a plan a shrimper can take to the bank.

Huy Nguyen, the Aransas Pass shrimper I interviewed for Tuesday's story, put it as plainly as anyone could: tell me a number, and I can plan around a number. He is not asking those agencies to rush. He is asking them to show their work.

Here is what that could look like. The agencies responsible should publish what they are testing, where and how often. They should say what results would allow a partial reopening, and which parts of the bays are likely to come back first. They should update that information on a regular schedule, even when the update is "nothing has changed." And they should say it in plain English, Spanish and Vietnamese, at the docks and boat ramps, not only online.

None of that requires knowing exactly when the bays will reopen. It requires treating the people who fish them as partners rather than spectators.

The cause of the spill is still under investigation, and the claims center run for the tankers' owners is so far taking only cleanup and property claims. Fishing families shouldn't have to wait for their turn there to get the most basic thing a closure owes them: information.

Bay shrimpers started this season with a fair catch and thin margins. Now many are watching the fall slip away from a dock. The bays will heal on their own schedule, and science can't hurry it. But the people who depend on them shouldn't be left guessing.

The marsh keeps its own time. The agencies should keep a clock the rest of us can read.

item.title: With access roads still flooded and spill zones closed, damage assessments fall weeks behind
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Insurance adjusters and FEMA inspectors say the scale of Hurricane Rafael damage and ongoing environmental restrictions are creating a backlog that will take months to resolve — and the claims numbers are only beginning to come in.
item.content:encoded:
Three and a half weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, the people who must calculate the storm's cost cannot reach some of the places where it did the most damage. Access restrictions around the Inner Harbor oil spill zone, roads still flooded in low-lying sections of Portland and Ingleside, and the sheer number of damaged properties across Nueces and San Patricio counties are combining to slow damage assessments to a pace that insurance industry officials say is without precedent in recent Texas storm recovery.

FEMA and state teams are carrying out joint damage assessments in Corpus Christi, but officials acknowledged this week that the work has fallen behind the scale of the damage. Households cannot yet apply for federal aid: the disaster declaration so far covers debris removal and emergency work, and the state has now formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance. Texas Department of Insurance data shows that claims filings from the Coastal Bend are arriving at a rate consistent with what actuaries are projecting as the second-largest coastal storm insurance event in Texas history since Hurricane Harvey in 2017.

"We've had adjuster teams trying to access properties in the Hillcrest and Oak Park neighborhoods for two weeks," said one independent adjuster working claims in Nueces County, who asked not to be named because she was not authorized to speak for her firm. "Some blocks you can reach on foot but not in a vehicle. Some you just cannot reach at all yet because of the environmental closure. It slows everything down." The Inner Harbor spill zone remains under access restrictions coordinated by the Unified Command.

The delay creates compounding problems for homeowners navigating insurance claims while they wait to learn whether federal household aid will be approved. Residents say they are receiving conflicting guidance about which paperwork to gather first, and advocates at the city's recovery assistance hubs say the documentation requirements have overwhelmed elderly residents and those without reliable internet access.

The Texas Department of Insurance said it has activated its Disaster Response Team and deployed staff to the Corpus Christi area to assist policyholders. The department is also monitoring for claims fraud, which historically spikes after major disasters. Insurance industry estimates for total Rafael losses are still preliminary, but several large carriers have flagged the event in regulatory filings as a potentially significant catastrophe-year event. Full assessments, insurers say, could take until early 2028.

item.title: 'Tell us when': Calallen waits on pump parts that are coming the long way
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Neighbors of the O.N. Stevens plant are nearing three weeks of boiling water. Leticia Ramos, who runs her street's water runs, says the delay is easier to take than the silence was.
item.content:encoded:
The clipboard by Leticia Ramos' front door has a new column.

Next to the house numbers and the columns for "has car" and "needs help lifting," the Calallen schoolteacher has added one more: "Heard anything?"

"Everybody asks me if I've heard anything," said Ramos, 45. "Like I've got a direct line to the plant. I don't. I've got a clipboard."

Ramos lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. Since Sept. 18, when the citywide boil-water notice was issued, she has organized her street's water runs. This week the city said replacement parts for the plant's damaged pumps are delayed: the supplier, Delta Pumps & Controls, had its local warehouse flood in the same storm, and the parts are shipping from out of state.

Ramos said the news did not surprise her street. What stood out was that someone finally explained why.

"I'll be honest. I liked that they said it," she said. "A warehouse flooded. Okay. That's a reason. That's something I can tell the lady next door. 'Soon' is not a reason."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city knows the wait is long. "We hear Calallen, and we hear everyone," Gallegos said. "We will keep telling people what we know, as soon as we know it. And we won't lift the notice until the water is tested and safe."

Ramos is practical about what comes next. The notice will be lifted, she said, and then people will forget what it was like. She wants the city to remember. "Write down what broke and how long it took," she said. "Then fix it so the next teacher doesn't have to do this with a clipboard."

In the meantime, the routine continues. At dusk the garden wagon rolls out again: two jugs for the older couple, a case for the corner house with the baby.

"That baby is going to grow up thinking water comes from a pot," Ramos said.

item.title: Hallway beds and twelve-hour shifts: an ER charge nurse's three weeks after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Alyssa Cortez worked through the storm, the oil and the stomach-illness surge. She says the hardest part is not the patients, but how tired everyone is.
item.content:encoded:
Alyssa Cortez keeps a granola bar in each pocket of her scrubs. One for her, she says, and one for whoever on her team looks like they need it more.

"Usually it's not me," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department. "Usually it's the new grad who hasn't sat down in six hours."

Cortez has worked twelve-hour shifts since Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. As charge nurse, she runs the floor: which patient goes to which bed, which nurse takes which room, who needs help now. She will not talk about individual patients, ever. She will talk about what the past three weeks felt like from the middle of the department.

First came the storm itself, when 911 calls across the county peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal. Then came residents from near oiled shorelines with coughs and rashes. Then, after the citywide boil-water notice, came the stomach illness: emergency room visits for it ran about 180% above normal, and departments, including hers, put patients in hallway beds.

"You learn to triage the hallway," she said. "Who's the sickest. Who's the scariest. Who's the one nobody's checked on in an hour. Then you go check on them."

Stomach illness visits began to ease in late September, and the hallway has mostly emptied. The tiredness has not.

"People think the hard part is the sick people. It's not. Sick people, we know how to do," she said. "The hard part is that everybody back there has something going on at home, too: a wet house, water to boil, family to look after. And they still come in and do twelve hours."

She said the things that helped most were small. A church sent trays of food. Neighbors covered errands. A family left a card at the front desk thanking "the nurses in the hallway."

Her advice to readers hasn't changed. "If you're sick and you can be cared for at home, stay home and call your doctor. If you need us, come. Don't wait until it's an emergency on top of an emergency," she said. "And wash your hands. I'll keep saying it until I'm fifty."

At 6:50 a.m. she was in the parking lot, finishing a coffee and already checking the bed board on her phone. "Here we go," she said.

item.title: CISA and FBI Confirm Cyberattack Targeted Corpus Christi Utility Systems During Hurricane Rafael
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Federal cybersecurity and law enforcement authorities have announced a joint investigation into anomalous activity in industrial control systems at a Coastal Bend utility during the hurricane response, in what analysts are calling the most significant known utility control-system incident in the continental United States since 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Federal cybersecurity and law enforcement authorities announced Tuesday morning that unauthorized actors gained access to industrial control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during the period surrounding Hurricane Rafael, and that the agencies have opened a joint investigation into its scope, origin and impact. The statement does not say what, if anything, the activity changed, and it does not link the activity to the extended power outages that have affected tens of thousands of residents over the past three weeks. The announcement was issued jointly by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

"CISA and the FBI have confirmed unauthorized access to control systems at a Coastal Bend utility in connection with Hurricane Rafael," said CISA Director of Communications Brett Halvorsen in a written statement released at noon Tuesday. "Texas Cyber Command has been activated in support of federal and state response. No attribution is being made at this time. We are asking the public and affected utilities to follow CISA guidance on operational technology security as this investigation continues." No country or non-state actor has been publicly identified as responsible.

The announcement does not name the utility, though CBPWA's Monday statement about "anomalous access to operational technology systems" leaves little ambiguity about which Corpus Christi utility is involved. The FBI's Cyber Division and CISA's Industrial Control Systems Security team are co-leading the investigation. Officials declined to describe the specific systems that were accessed, the nature of the manipulation that occurred, or how long the unauthorized access persisted.

For Corpus Christi residents, the announcement recontextualizes three weeks of hardship. The boil water notice affecting 48,000 residents in Districts 3 and 4 — which city officials have attributed throughout to "storm damage to pumping infrastructure" — has coincided with an illness cluster that has sent more than 600 people to hospital. Power customers in northwest and central Corpus Christi who were told their outages resulted from "cascading substation failures" may now have different questions about those explanations. City spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said Tuesday that the city is "awaiting further guidance from federal authorities" before commenting on how the CISA-FBI announcement relates to previously issued statements.

Corpus Christi Mayor David Reyes said he was briefed on the investigation before the public announcement and expressed both alarm and resolve. "What was done to our city's infrastructure — if the evidence bears out — is an act of cowardice that targeted families who were already trying to survive a natural disaster," Reyes said. "We are committed to full transparency with our residents as the federal investigation proceeds." Texas Cyber Command confirmed its activation Tuesday morning.

item.title: Why the water plant's pump parts are late: a supplier explains
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Delta Pumps & Controls says its local warehouse flooded in the same storm that damaged the O.N. Stevens plant, so parts are coming from out of state. Here's how one storm can break a supply chain twice.
item.content:encoded:
When the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant's pumps were damaged in Hurricane Rafael, the city turned to its supplier. The problem was that the supplier's own building had taken water too.

"Our local warehouse flooded in the same storm," said Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls. "Parts that would normally go out our back door are now coming from out of state. I'm sorry. I live here. I'm boiling my water too."

The city's water utility said Monday that the replacement parts are delayed because Delta's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. The citywide boil-water notice, issued Sept. 18, remains in effect, and temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

How a storm breaks a supply chain twice: Utilities keep some spare parts on hand, but large pump components are expensive, heavy and often specific to one plant's equipment. Many are stocked by distributors rather than by the utility. That arrangement works most of the time, because a local warehouse can get a part to the plant fast. It fails when the same disaster hits the plant and the warehouse at once.

Then the part has to travel. Shipping from out of state means more miles and more handoffs, and after a major storm, demand for repair parts of every kind rises across the region.

"I can tell you where the parts are coming from. I can't promise you a day until they're on the truck and I see a tracking number," Ybarra said. "I'd rather tell the city the truth late than a lie early."

Teresa Gallegos, the utility's spokeswoman, said the city is in contact with the supplier. "Once the parts arrive, they still have to be installed and the system tested before we can lift the notice," Gallegos said.

The lesson may be bigger than one order. When a single treatment plant serves a whole city, and the parts for it sit in a warehouse in the same flood zone, one storm can knock out both. Whether to change that is a question for after the water is safe to drink.

item.title: Parks and Wildlife extends fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Shrimpers and anglers will wait longer to work the bays after the oil spill. Health officials say breathing complaints near oiled shorelines are easing.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting stays closed under the Texas Department of State Health Services, keeping shrimp boats and anglers off the water three weeks after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across the bays.

The closure began Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel and spread sheen across about 33 square miles of water.

"Extending the closure is about protecting the public," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which does not set the closures but helps run the cleanup that testing depends on. "Fish and shellfish can take up oil from the water and sediment. These bays shouldn't reopen until testing shows the seafood is safe to eat." No new reopening date was given.

There was better news on land. Health officials say respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing. "Fewer people are coming in with coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "That's welcome. Keep avoiding contact with any oil you see."

For bay shrimpers, the extension lands hard. Huy Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper in Aransas Pass, has kept his boat tied up since the closure.

"I understand. Nobody wants sick shrimp," Nguyen said. "But every week is a payment I don't make. Every week my deckhand looks for other work. Tell me a number. I can plan around a number."

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs squeezing margins even before the storm. Now the closure has stretched into October.

Recreational anglers are affected too. The closure covers fishing in both bays, and bait shops and guides along the coast have fielded weeks of calls from regulars asking what's open.

The bays will recover at their own pace. Oil that settled into marsh mud and bay sediment can linger, as Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi oceanographer Nathan Brooks told the Ledger last month, and testing will determine when seafood is safe.

For Nguyen, the wait is the hardest part. "The bay is right there," he said, nodding toward the water from the dock. "I can see it. I just can't touch it."

item.title: Water plant pump parts delayed after supplier's local warehouse floods
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Replacement parts for damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are shipping from out of state. The city's boil-water notice stays in effect, and the utility has not set a date to lift it.
item.content:encoded:
Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded in Hurricane Rafael, and the parts are now shipping from out of state, the city's water utility said Monday.

The supplier is Delta Pumps & Controls. The city's boil-water notice, in effect since Sept. 18, remains in place.

"We know this isn't the news anyone wanted," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the water utility. "The parts are coming, but they're coming from farther away than we planned, because our supplier's local warehouse took on water in the same storm we did. We're sorry. Please keep boiling your water."

Gallegos did not give an arrival date for the parts or a date for lifting the notice. "When the parts are in, they have to be installed and tested, and the water has to be tested," she said. "We won't lift the notice until the tests say it's safe."

The plant in Calallen, the city's only treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, damaging pumps. The utility said Sept. 24 that the damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

What it means for you: Keep boiling. Any tap water used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or baby formula needs two minutes at a rolling boil first. Bottled water is safe.

Keep washing. Stomach illness visits have begun to ease, but health officials say hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water still matters.

Conserve. With temporary pumps limiting capacity, use water sparingly. Run full loads, take shorter showers and skip lawn watering.

Check on neighbors. Older residents and families without cars may be running low on bottled water or on the energy to keep boiling it.

item.title: Records show $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Federal contract records show the award followed the flooding of the air station's regular fuel supplier. Quellmar says it is glad to support the station.
item.content:encoded:
Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael.

The records, reviewed by the Ledger on Monday, describe the award as an emergency contract and identify Quellmar as the contractor and the air station as the location served.

Quellmar is a Corpus Christi fuel supplier. Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said the company was ready when the station needed it.

"Quellmar is proud to support the air station and the people who work there," Kerr said. "When their regular supplier went down in the storm, we were in a position to help. We're committed to keeping the station supplied for as long as we're needed."

Kerr did not say when deliveries to the air station began, how much fuel the contract covers or how long it runs.

Emergency contracts like this one are common after disasters, when regular suppliers are knocked offline and agencies need goods quickly. Federal rules allow agencies to speed up purchasing in urgent situations, though they must document the reasons. An emergency award is not, by itself, a sign of a problem.

The Ledger is tracking emergency contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend since the storm. They include Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, awarded Sept. 24. The Ledger has requested records related to that contract from the county.

NAS Corpus Christi, which shares its grounds with Corpus Christi Army Depot, has been working back toward normal operations since training aircraft began returning Sept. 20. A station's fuel needs do not stop during a recovery: aircraft, vehicles and equipment all depend on a steady supply, which is why the loss of a regular supplier can force a fast replacement.

item.title: Rosa Elizondo's long September
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A home health aide with three children and no car, she spent the days after Rafael waiting for help that came first from a church hall. Now she's back with her clients, boiling every drop.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo starts her day the same way she has every day since Sept. 18: she fills the big pot, sets it on the stove and waits for the boil.

"Ten minutes to heat it, two minutes boiling, then it has to cool," said Elizondo, 38. "Three kids, one pot. I do math all day now. My middle school teacher would be proud."

Elizondo is a home health aide. She spends her days in other people's homes, helping older and disabled clients bathe, eat, take their medicine and get through the afternoon. She rents a duplex in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, and she does not have a car. She gets to her clients the way she always has: on the bus when it runs, and with rides from neighbors when it doesn't.

Rafael tested that system. After the storm came ashore Sept. 14, Elizondo said, she waited days for help, as residents of other low-income neighborhoods near the bay have also described. The first water and food on her block came from Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church fellowship hall, a few blocks from her home, before official distribution reached the area.

"I called, I waited, I called," Elizondo said. "Then the pastora opened the hall, and later she sent a boy on a bicycle with a case of water on the handlebars. Ay, Dios. I almost cried."

Whitfield, 59, laughed when she heard the story retold. "That's one of our youth group kids," she said. "He's been on that bike for two weeks. He's earned a medal."

Elizondo's clients are among the people most at risk from the stomach illness that spread through the city last month, and she has become strict. "Soap and boiled water, every time. I don't care if you're 90. You wash," she said. "Sanitizer is not enough for this bug. The health lady said so."

Health officials say stomach illness visits have begun to ease. Elizondo is not taking chances. "Easing is not over," she said.

What she wants now is simple. "Remember us next time before the storm, not after," she said. "Send the bus early. Knock on the door. We'll be ready. We're always ready. We just don't have a car."

As the interview ended, her phone buzzed: a client needing a ride to the pharmacy. Elizondo grabbed a water bottle and laughed. "See? Everybody needs a ride," she said.

item.title: More Than 600 Sickened in Four Days as Illness Cluster Hits Districts 3 and 4; Clinics Overwhelmed
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is tracking a waterborne disease cluster in Districts 3 and 4: the two main hospitals have treated more than 600 patients with acute gastrointestinal illness since Sept. 29, and community clinics on the Westside and Northside are seeing two to three times normal patient volumes.
item.content:encoded:
The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is tracking a waterborne disease cluster in Districts 3 and 4 that health officials say has sent more than 600 patients with acute gastrointestinal illness to Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center since Sept. 29 — with the count continuing to climb as residents seek care at overwhelmed community clinics. Officials are urging all residents in the two districts to strictly observe the boil-water notice and to seek medical care if symptoms develop.

Public Health District Director Dr. Priscilla Reyes said most of the patients live in Districts 3 and 4, suggesting a common source in the drinking water system. "The case pattern is consistent with exposure through the drinking water system," Dr. Reyes said at a Saturday afternoon press briefing. "We are treating this as a waterborne illness outbreak and are working with the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority and the Texas Department of State Health Services on the investigation." She said laboratory tests have confirmed Cryptosporidium and Giardia, both waterborne parasites, in multiple patient samples.

Community health clinics on the Westside and Northside reported patient volumes two to three times their normal daily caseloads this week. Administrators at the South Texas Community Health Center extended hours and called in additional clinical staff to handle the surge. The most common presentations are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramping. Dr. Reyes said the findings are consistent with people drinking tap water that had not been boiled.

Children under five and elderly residents face the greatest risk of serious complications from waterborne gastrointestinal illness, public health officials said. Residents who cannot afford to purchase bottled water are encouraged to use the city's free water distribution points, which remain open at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park. Dr. Reyes emphasized that keeping water at a rolling boil for the full time the notice specifies — not simply until hot or steaming — is necessary to kill relevant pathogens. The boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4 has been in place for six days, and city spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said the notice remains in effect while engineers continue assessing the distribution and pumping infrastructure serving the two districts.

item.title: Teaching through a boil-water notice: jugs, soap and a lot of reminders
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Leticia Ramos has spent more than two weeks hauling water for her Calallen street. The schoolteacher says children are the hardest part of a boil-water notice, because they forget.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos has a rule for every sink in her house: a strip of blue painter's tape across the faucet, and a jug of boiled water beside it.

"Kids forget," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher in Calallen. "Adults forget too, but kids forget at seven in the morning with a toothbrush in their mouth. Tape on the faucet is a reminder you can see."

Ramos has organized water runs for her street since Hurricane Rafael knocked out power to the nearby O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant.
