The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 is still in effect, and the city says damaged pumps at the plant need replacement parts, with temporary pumps limiting capacity.

Now she is thinking like a teacher. School districts across Nueces County reviewed their storm plans before the season, but no plan makes a boil-water notice easy for a room full of children.

"You can't put tape on a water fountain and expect it to work," she said. "You need a person. You need a jug with a spigot by the door, a pump bottle of soap, paper towels, and a teacher who says 'wash' forty times a day."

The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after a surge last week, when norovirus showed up in wastewater testing and visits ran about 180% above normal. Ramos said that is exactly why she isn't relaxing.

"When it gets better, that's when people stop doing the thing that made it better," she said. "I've seen it with lice. I've seen it with flu. I'll see it with this."

She has turned her own kitchen into a pilot program. A big pot boils on the back burner most of the day. A dish tub by the sink holds soapy water for hand-washing, and a second holds boiled rinse water. A sign on the refrigerator, in neat teacher's print, reads: "Tap = NO. Jug = YES. Soap = ALWAYS."

On Thursday evening, the lights were on at a high school practice field down the road, and a parent was handing out bottled water from the bed of a pickup. Ramos waved on her way past with the garden wagon.

"Normal-ish," she said. "We'll take normal-ish."

item.title: Texas DPS, AG's Office Warn of Storm Contractor Fraud After More Than 300 Complaints
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Unlicensed restoration contractors are charging Rafael survivors three to five times standard market rates for water extraction and mold remediation, according to Texas law enforcement, which is pursuing arrest warrants and civil investigative demands.
item.content:encoded:
Texas law enforcement and consumer protection officials issued an urgent statewide warning Wednesday after receiving more than 300 complaints from Hurricane Rafael survivors who say water damage contractors charged between three and five times standard market rates for water extraction, debris removal, and mold remediation work in the Corpus Christi area. Many of the operators hold no license with the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners or the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, officials said. The warning does not name any company.

"We have received more than 300 consumer complaints since the storm," said Sgt. Ramona Fierro, spokeswoman for Texas Department of Public Safety Region 2. "Complainants describe representatives arriving uninvited at storm-damaged properties, using high-pressure tactics to get homeowners to sign contracts, and then charging amounts that are three hundred to five hundred percent above what licensed contractors are charging for the same work in this area." Fierro said arrest warrants are being sought in connection with the most egregious cases and that additional charges related to fraudulent business practice are under review.

The Texas Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division has issued a civil investigative demand to several entities named in the complaints. Division Director Chandra Mitchell said the AG's office has obtained evidence that sales representatives have been approaching hurricane survivors at water distribution sites and outside shelter facilities in Corpus Christi. "Disaster fraud is a serious crime and an assault on people who are already suffering," Mitchell said. "We will pursue every available legal remedy." Investigators report that one operation has used multiple telephone numbers, at least two websites with similar domain names, and has accepted payment through cash, check, and mobile payment apps — making it difficult for victims to dispute charges.

Texas DPS advises all storm survivors to verify contractor licensing before signing any contract, insist on written estimates that itemize costs, and never pay more than ten percent as an upfront deposit. Licensed contractor lookup is available at the Texas MyLicense Office website. Residents who have been approached by unlicensed or predatory contractors are urged to call the AG's Consumer Protection Hotline at 1-800-621-0508. Officials expect the complaint count to rise as more residents return to their homes and discover the terms of contracts they signed under pressure in the storm's immediate aftermath.

item.title: Aerial survey of utility sites finds storm damage at 14 of 23; two substations flagged for inspection
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: FEMA's second survey phase covered substations, the water plant, pump stations and telecom sites. Engineers are being sent back to the Harbor View and Crosstown substations.
item.content:encoded:
A federal aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area's utility sites found visible storm damage at 14 of the 23 locations it examined and singled out two electrical substations for a closer look by engineers, according to a summary released Wednesday by FEMA's Mitigation Assessment Team.

The survey, the second phase of FEMA's aerial assessment of Hurricane Rafael, was flown from Thursday, Sept. 23, through Sunday, Sept. 26. It covered five Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority electrical substations, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, four pumping stations and nine telecommunications relay facilities, along with other utility sites.

At O.N. Stevens, the plant that supplies the city's drinking water, the summary reports moderate roof damage to the C-pump station. The plant lost both of its power feeds during the storm, and the city has been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 18.

The summary identifies two of the authority's substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, "as requiring follow-up engineering inspection due to equipment configurations observed in the imagery." It does not say what the configurations were or whether they are related to storm damage. The authority said Tuesday that crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within seven to 10 days; it did not name the facilities.

Rafael Montoya-Chen, chief of the Texas Division of Emergency Management's infrastructure division, said the value of the flights is in what they let repair crews do next. "The aerial survey has given engineers a roadmap so that when crews reach those sites, they know what to look for and can prioritize the most critical restoration steps," he said.

The first phase of the survey, released Sept. 18, estimated that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County had major or severe damage. This phase counts no homes. It looks only at the equipment that keeps power, water and communications running.

The full set of Phase 2 images is not public. FEMA said it is available to credentialed government users through the agency's GeoPlatform. The Ledger has asked the authority when the inspections at Harbor View and Crosstown will take place and whether the results will be released.

item.title: By the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop owner starts over with a sense of humor
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Bill Hargrove's shop was gutted when Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas. Two weeks later, he's tearing out walls, telling stories and waiting for anglers to come back.
item.content:encoded:
PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove has a new sign on the front of his bait shop, hand-painted on a scrap of plywood: "OPEN-ISH."

"It's honest advertising," said Hargrove, 64, owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. "I've got ice, I've got hooks, I've got opinions. Bait, we're working on."

Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm, and the surge gutted Hargrove's shop. The bait tanks, the freezers, the wall of rods and the photo board of customers' biggest catches all went.

Two weeks later he is tearing out drywall with a crowbar and a radio tuned to a country station, and selling what he can from a folding table out front.

"I rode out two storms in this shop. This one I left for, and it still rode me," he said.

Port Aransas had a strong summer before the storm, Hargrove said, with charters booked and bait selling as fast as he could keep it in the tanks. Now the island is quiet. Fishing is closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and Hargrove fields calls from regulars asking what's open.

"I tell them what the state says, not what they want to hear," he said. "Some of them want to hear I've got a secret spot. I've got a secret spot. It's closed."

He talks about the jetties the way some people talk about relatives. He has fished them since he was a boy, he said, and can tell you which rocks hold sheepshead in winter and where the tarpon used to roll in August. "The jetties don't care about a hurricane," he said. "They were here before me, and they'll be here after. The shop's the part that needs help."

He has not decided how much to rebuild. Insurance adjusters are scheduling, and contractors are booked. "I asked one guy for a quote, and he laughed and said, 'Bill, I'll put you on the list, right after my mother,'" Hargrove said.

For now, the plan is drywall out, fans on, door open. "Somebody's going to want ice," he said. "And somebody's going to want to hear a story. I can do both."

item.title: Opinion: The neighborhoods that waited longest should be counted first
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Residents near the bay say help took days to reach them after Rafael. The county should measure how long every neighborhood waited and publish the results.
item.content:encoded:
I have covered three hurricanes for this newspaper. After every one, I have heard some version of the same sentence from people who live near the bay: "We waited."

This week, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters, including Coastline Public Radio, that they waited days for help after Rafael. I believe them, because the record points the same way.

Before the storm, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation help, and advocates warned that transit gaps left many households in those neighborhoods stranded. When the evacuation order came, people without cars had to wait for a county bus. At the storm's peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. In the days after, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some of those same streets.

None of that is a secret. It is just not counted in one place.

Here is a modest proposal. Nueces County and the city should measure, by neighborhood, how long people waited: for 911 response, for water, for debris pickup, for anything government delivers after a disaster. Then they should publish the numbers, good and bad, and update them through the recovery.

Measuring is not blaming. The people who answered 911 calls and loaded water trucks this month did hard work in impossible conditions. But good intentions are not a distribution plan. If help reaches the people with cars and phone chargers first, the system is working as designed, and the design needs to change.

The fix starts with the boring stuff: bus routes that keep running, distribution sites within walking distance, door-knocking for people who can't call. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, whose fellowship hall has fed her neighborhood since the storm, keeps a handwritten list of who needs what. A county with computers can do at least that well.

Recovery from Rafael will run for months. The county has already signed an emergency debris contract, and more decisions about where help goes are coming. Before they are made, the county should know which neighborhoods waited longest, and promise they won't be last again.

item.title: Stomach illness visits begin to ease, health district says
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: After a surge that filled hallway beds, emergency rooms are seeing fewer patients with stomach illness. Officials say the boil-water notice and hand-washing still matter.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County have begun to ease, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said Tuesday, after a surge last week that pushed visits to about 180% above normal and put patients in hallway beds.

"We're seeing the curve bend down, and that's good news," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist. "It is not the all-clear. Norovirus is still out there, and the conditions that helped it spread haven't gone away."

Shah did not release new visit counts Tuesday. She said the district will keep tracking ER visits and wastewater testing, which first signaled norovirus spreading in the city on Sept. 20.

The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 remains in effect. The city's water utility said Friday that damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting the plant's capacity.

At one Nueces County emergency department, charge nurse Alyssa Cortez said the change is noticeable. "Last week, every hallway stretcher had somebody on it. Monday night, for a few hours, the hallway was empty," Cortez said. "I actually ate lunch sitting down. Don't tell anybody."

Cortez, 34, said staff are still busy and tired. She would not discuss individual patients.

Shah said people should keep doing what has worked: bottled water, or tap water held at a rolling boil for two minutes before it is used for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice or formula.

Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water after using the bathroom or changing diapers and before eating or cooking. Hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.

Stay home for two days after symptoms end, and don't prepare food for others during that time. Disinfect bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution, especially after someone in the house has been sick.

"Every family that kept washing hands and kept a sick kid home helped bend this down," Shah said. "Keep going."

item.title: County Opens NuecesInfoLine as Water Safety Calls Flood 911
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A mounting wave of water-safety inquiries after Sunday's boil-water notice has prompted the 911 center to open the NuecesInfoLine and urge residents to reserve 911 for genuine emergencies.
item.content:encoded:
The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center opened a new non-emergency information line, the NuecesInfoLine, Sunday evening to handle a mounting wave of calls about water safety, as the center reported a sharp increase in 911 contacts from residents seeking guidance rather than emergency assistance after the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4. The surge placed measurable stress on the 911 center's available lines during peak hours.

Dispatch data reviewed by The Bayside Ledger shows that boil water notice-related calls to CBECC climbed sharply after the alert went out at 5:30 p.m., with callers asking about water quality, the locations of water distribution points, and the safety of local beaches and bay areas. Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor said the volume, while not at the levels seen during Rafael's immediate landfall period, was high enough to prompt the activation. "We want people to know that the NuecesInfoLine is there for information questions," Vasquez-Okafor said. "Save 911 for emergencies."

The NuecesInfoLine, reached at 361-826-INFO, is staffed 24 hours a day with operators briefed on the boil-water notices, water distribution sites and when service is expected to be restored; callers can press 2 for Spanish. "911 is for life-threatening emergencies only," CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said. "Please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger." City spokeswoman Delia Sandoval said water distribution sites are open at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

CBECC staffing levels, which were stretched thin during Rafael's initial days when call volume hit record highs, are still supported by mutual-aid dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties, who have been in place since landfall. Vasquez-Okafor said the center's own capacity has stabilized even as the informational demand from the public remains high.

item.title: City Issues Boil Water Notice for Districts 3 and 4; Storm Damage to Pumping Infrastructure Cited
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Approximately 48,000 Corpus Christi residents in Districts 3 and 4 are under a new boil water notice, effective immediately, after the utility reported low pressure in the two districts; the citywide notice issued Sept. 18 also remains in force.
item.content:encoded:
The Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority and the City of Corpus Christi issued an emergency boil water notice for water Districts 3 and 4 effective immediately at 5:30 p.m. Sunday, instructing approximately 48,000 residents and all businesses in the two districts to boil tap water before using it for drinking, cooking, making ice, or brushing teeth. The notice comes on top of the citywide boil-water notice in force since Sept. 18.

Water Services Director James Thornton said the notice was issued as a precautionary measure after low system pressure was recorded in the two districts, which he attributed to hurricane damage to distribution and pumping infrastructure. "We identified storm-related damage to treatment and pumping infrastructure that may have caused pressure fluctuations in these districts," Thornton said. "Until we can verify that distribution integrity has been maintained throughout, the boil water notice protects public health." He said engineers are on-site conducting assessments and that the department is working as quickly and safely as possible.

Districts 3 and 4 take in downtown, Hillcrest and the Northside, and the Westside neighborhoods including Molina, in ZIP codes 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 and 78417. The rest of the city remains under the citywide notice issued Sept. 18; the new notice adds a separate low-pressure warning for the two districts and will be lifted on its own schedule. Restaurants and food service businesses within the two districts must comply immediately: they must use pre-boiled water or obtain bottled water from approved suppliers, and many are expected to close temporarily.

Under state rules, the boil water notice triggers required testing protocols. The utility must collect water samples from multiple points in the affected distribution system and receive laboratory results confirming that bacteria counts are within safe limits before the notice can be lifted. Thornton declined to estimate how long that process might take, citing the ongoing complexity of post-storm infrastructure assessments. Residents in Districts 3 and 4 who cannot boil water due to lack of power or other circumstances may obtain bottled water at distribution sites at the Tuloso-Midway High School gym, the Woodlawn Community Center and Cefe Valenzuela Park.

item.title: A fellowship hall becomes a neighborhood's front door
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church started handing out food and water before official distribution reached her bayside neighborhood. Twelve days after Rafael, the line still forms every morning.
item.content:encoded:
By 8 a.m. Sunday, the folding tables in the fellowship hall were already set: cases of water stacked by the door, a pot of rice on a borrowed burner, a cardboard box of diapers sorted by size, and a sign in English and Spanish that read "Take what you need. Bring what you can."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, stood at the end of the line with her penciled binder, greeting people by name.

"This is the front door of this neighborhood right now," she said. "People don't come here because it's a church. They come because it's close, and because we were here first."

Whitfield's church began handing out food and water within days of Hurricane Rafael, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. Many households here don't have a car, and the bus routes that serve the area had gaps long before the storm.

"You can open a distribution site across town, and that's a blessing for people who can drive to it," Whitfield said. "But the grandmother on the third floor with no car and a bad hip, she's not getting to it. So we bring it to her, or we bring her here."

Since the city issued its boil-water notice Sept. 18, water has been the hall's biggest need. Volunteers haul cases in their own trucks, and a deacon keeps a camp stove going in the parking lot to boil water for hand-washing.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who lives a few blocks away, came for water and stayed to sort donations. "Here nobody asks you for paperwork," Elizondo said. "They just ask how many kids. Tres. Okay, here."

The early service was short. Whitfield preached from a podium wedged between pallets of water. She asked the congregation to pray for neighbors who still had wet walls and for those sleeping on someone else's couch. Then she asked who could drive Tuesday.

"Faith is a verb this month," she said afterward. "It's a truck and a case of water and somebody knocking on a door."

She said she is grateful for every agency now working in the city, and she wants them in her neighborhood. "Come sit at my table," she said. "I'll tell you who needs what. I know every one of them."

item.title: Explainer: How sole-source emergency contracts work after a disaster
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: Nueces County's $14.2 million debris contract with Vantorra Restoration was awarded without competitive bidding. Here's what that means, why it's allowed and which records show how the money is spent.
item.content:encoded:
Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC on Sept. 24 without competitive bidding. That kind of award, called sole-source, is common after disasters. It also means the public record matters more than usual. Here's how it works.

What is a sole-source contract? In normal times, governments buy large services through competitive bidding: they publish what they need, companies submit prices, and the contract goes to the best qualified offer. A sole-source contract skips that step. The government picks one company and negotiates directly.

Why is it allowed? Texas law lets counties and cities skip competitive bidding when a purchase is necessary to preserve or protect public health or safety, including after a disaster. Federal rules for disaster reimbursement also allow noncompetitive contracts in an emergency, generally only for as long as the emergency lasts.

"Emergency doesn't mean no rules," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It means you can move faster on the front end. You still document everything on the back end."

Is a sole-source award a red flag? Not by itself. After a hurricane, debris blocks roads and drainage, and waiting weeks for bids can put people at risk. Many communities award emergency debris work this way.

What records show how the money is spent? The contract sets the scope of work, prices and how long the emergency terms last. Debris contracts are typically paid by volume or weight, so the key records are the load tickets and monitoring logs that show what each truck hauled and where it went. Invoices, payment records and any amendments or extensions are generally public records too, with limited exceptions.

What has the Ledger requested? The Ledger has asked the county for the Vantorra contract and related documents under the Texas Public Information Act. We file the same requests for every major emergency contract, and we will report what the records show.

What can residents do? Keep your own record: dated photos of your curbside pile and notes on when it was picked up. If you have questions about pickups, contact the county through its official channels.

item.title: Debris contractor promises fast pickup as curbside piles grow
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Vantorra Restoration's managing partner says crews will work 'around the clock' under the county's $14.2 million emergency contract. County officials ask residents to sort debris and keep it out of the street.
item.content:encoded:
On streets across Corpus Christi, the piles are getting taller: soaked carpet, cut drywall, mattresses, fence boards, the swollen remains of kitchen cabinets. Eleven days after Hurricane Rafael, they line curbs from the bayfront to the west side.

Moving those piles is now the job of Vantorra Restoration LLC, which Nueces County hired Friday under a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.

Derek Sloane, the company's managing partner, sounded like a man at a ribbon cutting. "This is what we do. We're going to be working around the clock, and folks are going to see trucks on their streets," Sloane said Saturday. "Nobody should have to look at their ruined living room on the curb for a month. We're going to get it gone."

Sloane did not give a start date for pickups, a truck count or a breakdown of how the work will be divided among crews. He said the company will follow the county's schedule.

The county has not released a neighborhood-by-neighborhood schedule. Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set.

Sorting matters, he said. Debris crews generally handle different kinds of debris separately because each goes to a different place: tree limbs and brush to be ground into mulch, building debris to a landfill, appliances to metal recyclers and household chemicals to special handling.

"If it's all mixed together, it slows everybody down," Pruitt said. "Separate piles, at the curb, out of the street, away from drains and power lines. That's the fastest way to get it picked up."

For the region's economy, debris removal is one of the first big checks to flow after a storm. It puts trucks, drivers and equipment operators to work, and it clears the way for the slower business of rebuilding. Contractors, roofers and drywall crews say they can't start until the old material is gone.

What residents should know: Keep piles off sidewalks and out of the street, and don't block storm drains, fire hydrants or mailboxes. Don't stack debris under power lines or against trees. Bag small items. Keep paint, cleaners, fuel and batteries separate from everything else.

item.title: Dispatch center confirms 23 unfounded emergency calls from prepaid phones; matter referred to law enforcement
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The calls, first reported by Coastline Public Radio, sent responders to addresses near two utility sites where no one needed help. The center will not say who it thinks made them.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-three times since Sept. 21, someone called for help in Corpus Christi and there was no one to help when responders arrived. The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center confirmed the pattern Friday and said it has passed what it knows to law enforcement.

The calls were first reported Friday by Coastline Public Radio, which obtained dispatch records through a public records request. According to those records, 23 calls from unregistered prepaid phones reported emergencies at addresses in northwest and central Corpus Christi near two utility sites. At least eleven described trapped residents. Responders found no one and no emergency at any of the locations.

Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor confirmed the unfounded calls. She said the center had flagged the cluster internally and referred the information to its law enforcement partners. No suspects have been identified.

Vasquez-Okafor declined to say whether the center believes the calls were connected to one another or why they were concentrated near utility sites. "What I can describe is the pattern: prepaid phones, addresses that did not check out, and no one there when our units arrived," she said. "What it means is a question for investigators, and I am not going to get ahead of them."

The center did not name the utility sites, and the records described by Coastline do not say which agencies are reviewing them. The Ledger has filed its own request for the call records, including the times of the calls and the units sent.

The cost of a false call is measured in crews. Each report of a trapped resident draws a response that cannot be somewhere else at the same time, and it comes while the center is still running far above its normal load. County officials said a week ago that the center had handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days after Hurricane Rafael, and that they expected volume to stay elevated for weeks.

Making a false report to 911 is a crime under Texas law. Anyone with information about the calls can contact the Corpus Christi Police Department or the Nueces County Sheriff's Office. Residents who do need help should not hesitate to call; dispatchers are sending units to every report.

item.title: County awards $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The emergency contract for storm debris removal was awarded without competitive bidding. County officials say the scale of Rafael's damage required moving fast.
item.content:encoded:
Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency contract for storm debris removal to Vantorra Restoration LLC, county officials said Friday.

A sole-source contract is awarded to a single company without competitive bidding. The county described the award as an emergency contract tied to Hurricane Rafael, which flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties after it came ashore Sept. 14.

"We have debris blocking streets, ditches and drains, and we're still in hurricane season," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You can't run a months-long bid process while that sits at the curb. We needed crews moving now."

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said the company is ready. "We're going to be working around the clock," Sloane said. "Folks around here have been through enough. Our job is to get this mess off their curbs and out of their way, and that's what we're going to do."

Sloane did not provide details about the company's crews or equipment. The Ledger has requested the contract and related records from the county under the Texas Public Information Act.

Emergency contracts without competitive bidding are common after major disasters. State and federal rules allow them when delay would threaten public health or safety, with conditions that include documenting the emergency and the costs. The Ledger will explain how those rules work in Sunday's edition.

For residents, Pruitt said the immediate message is practical. "Put debris at the curb, not in the street," he said. "Keep it away from storm drains, fire hydrants, mailboxes and power lines, and separate it as best you can: tree limbs in one pile, building materials in another, appliances in another."

The county has not announced a pickup schedule by neighborhood. Pruitt said residents should watch official county channels for routes as they are set.

item.title: In the bays' marshes, oil cleanup is slow and careful work
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: More than a week after Rafael's surge carried oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, crews are working shorelines with boom. Scientists say marshes hold oil differently than sand beaches do.
item.content:encoded:
From the shoreline at the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh, the damage is easy to miss at first. The cordgrass stands green above the waterline. Look lower, at the stems where the tide rises and falls, and they are stained dark brown, as if someone had painted a line around the marsh with a brush.

That line is oil. More than a week ago, Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried crude out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and spread it across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. At its widest, the sheen covered about 33 square miles of water; oil reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels were released from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal.

Crews began deploying boom as winds dropped after the storm, and cleanup has continued since. On sand, oil can be scraped, raked and hauled away. Marshes are another matter.

"A beach is a parking lot. A marsh is a sponge," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Oil on sand sits on top where you can get at it. In a marsh it coats the stems, settles into the mud and gets worked in by every tide. If you go in with heavy equipment, you can do more harm than the oil."

Brooks said how long oil lingers depends on the plants, the mud and how much the tides flush each marsh. "Some places will look better in weeks," he said. "Some will take longer, and honestly, we'll be learning as we go."

Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said crews are using boom to keep oil from spreading farther into sensitive areas and are working shorelines carefully. "Marsh cleanup is slow on purpose," Whitaker said. "We'd rather take an extra week than trample the habitat we're trying to save."

He asked the public to stay out of oiled areas and to report oiled wildlife to the state's hotline rather than trying to help animals themselves. "Your instinct is to pick up that bird. Please don't. Call it in," he said.

Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays under closures issued Sept. 18 by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services.

The tide was coming in as the afternoon wore on, and the dark band on the cordgrass slipped under the water, out of sight but not gone.

item.title: Cargo-systems vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating with investigators. The statement came two days after the Coast Guard said it was examining possible unauthorized remote access to the spill tankers' cargo systems.
item.content:encoded:
A company that maintains cargo-control systems for tankers said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials were misused, and that it has revoked all remote access to the systems it supports.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused. That should not have been possible, and we own that," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access, for every customer, and we are cooperating fully with investigators. No connection will be restored until we can show our customers it is safe."

The statement came two days after Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The two laden tankers were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, and the Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled there. Federal cyber teams are assisting the investigation.

Brightwake's statement did not name any vessel or say when the credentials were misused.

Asked about the statement, the Coast Guard said its investigation continues. "We are aware of the company's statement," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Sector Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "We will not characterize any party's role while the investigation is ongoing."

How remote maintenance works: Cargo-control systems are the software and hardware crews use to monitor and manage oil in a tanker's cargo tanks. Like many shipboard systems, they need updates, troubleshooting and repairs. Instead of flying a technician to a ship for every fix, vendors often connect from shore over an approved link using login credentials.

That saves time and money, but it also means the credentials work like keys. Whoever holds them can reach the system.

Pryce said the company's first job is helping customers and investigators. "We're a small company. Our customers trust us with critical systems," he said. "Right now the fix is simple and blunt: nobody gets in remotely. We'll earn the rest back."

The port's ship channel remains closed, and crude exports have been halted since Sept. 12.

item.title: ER visits for stomach illness up about 180%; hallway beds in use
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Emergency departments across Nueces County are treating far more patients with vomiting and diarrhea than normal. Health officials and nurses urge hand-washing, boiled water and home care for mild cases.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency room visits for stomach illness in Nueces County are running about 180% above normal, health officials said Wednesday, and some emergency departments have put patients in hallway beds to keep up.

"Every stretcher in the hallway is somebody who can't keep water down," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who has worked twelve-hour shifts since the storm. "We're hanging IV fluids as fast as we can. We're tired, but we're here, and nobody gets turned away."

Cortez declined to discuss individual patients.

The surge follows Monday's announcement by the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District that wastewater testing shows a norovirus signal. The city has been under a boil-water notice since Saturday; the storm cut both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant and damaged its pumps.

Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist, issued new guidance Wednesday. "Most people with a stomach bug will feel better in a day or two at home," Shah said. "The emergency room is for people who are getting dehydrated or very sick. If you can manage at home, you leave room for someone who can't."

Shah's advice: Sip small amounts of water or oral rehydration drinks often, even if you are vomiting. Go to an emergency room or call 911 for signs of serious dehydration: little or no urine for many hours, dizziness when standing, confusion, a very dry mouth, or a baby with no wet diapers. Also seek care for blood in vomit or stool or a high fever.

Use only boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing formula. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water; alcohol-based sanitizer does not work well against norovirus.

Stay home for two days after symptoms stop. Don't cook for others while sick, and clean bathrooms and surfaces with a bleach solution.

Cortez had one more request. "If you're bringing someone in, bring a water bottle and a phone charger, and be patient with the person at the front desk," she said. "Everybody back there is doing two jobs."

item.title: In Calallen, a schoolteacher runs the water line for her street
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A week after Rafael, Leticia Ramos keeps a clipboard of which neighbors need water and who has a car. Her street sits a few minutes from the plant whose failure led to the citywide boil-water notice.
item.content:encoded:
By Leticia Ramos' front door hangs a clipboard, and on it is her whole street: house numbers, household sizes, who drives, who has a newborn, who needs help lifting.

Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher, lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen. Since Hurricane Rafael knocked out the plant's power a week ago, she has organized her street's water runs, matching neighbors who have cars with neighbors who don't and keeping track of who needs what.

"I teach, so I make lists," she said Tuesday, loading jugs into a garden wagon. "The older couple two doors down can't stand in a line in this heat. The family on the corner has a newborn. Somebody has to keep track, and I'm home."

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14. Pumps were damaged, and water pressure dropped across the city. On Saturday the city issued a citywide boil-water notice and opened water distribution sites.

Ramos said what wears on her street is not the boiling but the waiting. "We hear 'soon' and 'working on it,'" she said. "Tell us what's broken and when it'll be fixed. People can handle the truth. They can't plan around 'soon.'"

The frustration is understandable, said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city's water utility. "We know how hard this is, and we're sorry," Gallegos said. "Crews are working on the plant around the clock. Until we tell you otherwise, boil your water. We will give people a timeline when we have one we can stand behind."

The stakes went up Monday, when the city-county health district said wastewater testing shows a norovirus signal and stomach illness visits are rising. Ramos has added a new item to her runs: a jug of boiled water and a bar of soap by every front door that needs one.

"Hand-washing, that's the lesson this week," she said. "I'd rather teach fractions."

By late afternoon the wagon was empty again. She checked off two more houses and went inside to boil another pot.

item.title: Norovirus signal turns up in city wastewater as stomach illness visits rise
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Health officials say sewage testing points to norovirus spreading under the citywide boil-water notice. They urge hand-washing with boiled or bottled water and staying home when sick.
item.content:encoded:
Wastewater samples from Corpus Christi's treatment plants are showing a norovirus signal, and emergency rooms are seeing a rising number of patients with vomiting and diarrhea, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said Monday.

"The sewer tells us what is circulating in the community before most people ever see a doctor," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist who runs its wastewater testing. "Right now it is telling us norovirus is spreading, and the visits we're seeing in the emergency rooms are starting to agree."

Shah did not give a case count. Norovirus, the most common cause of stomach bugs, typically brings on vomiting, diarrhea and cramps a day or two after exposure, and most people recover within a few days.

The signal comes two days after the city issued a citywide boil-water notice. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen, the city's only treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, and damaged pumps left water pressure low across the system.

Shah said it is too early to say how any single person got sick. Norovirus spreads from person to person, on hands and surfaces, through food and through water. "Families are crowded together, people are standing in lines for water, and a lot of households don't have enough clean water to wash with," she said. "All of that helps it move."

What to do: Boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, brushing teeth, making ice or mixing baby formula. Bottled water is safe.

Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, especially after using the bathroom and before eating or cooking. Shah said alcohol-based hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus and should not replace soap and water.

Clean counters, doorknobs and bathrooms with a bleach solution. Stay home while sick and for two days after symptoms stop, and don't prepare food for others during that time.

Sip water or oral rehydration drinks. Seek care for signs of dehydration, such as very little urine, dizziness or a dry mouth, especially in babies, older adults and people with chronic illness.

item.title: Mass rescue ends after five days and 1,427 people; welfare checks begin
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: County and Coast Guard officials say every known call for rescue has been answered. Residents who have not been contacted by a welfare team should call 211.
item.content:encoded:
The boats and helicopters that have worked the flooded neighborhoods of Corpus Christi since Hurricane Rafael made landfall are standing down. Officials said Sunday that mass rescue operations have concluded after five days, with 1,427 confirmed rescues.

The announcement came from Elena Vasquez-Okafor, dispatch chief of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, and Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han, commander of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. They said the operation involved 34 coordinated teams at its peak, drawn from the Coast Guard, Texas Task Force 1, the Corpus Christi Fire Department and the Nueces County Sheriff's search and rescue unit.

It also involved 87 civilian boat operators, people with their own boats who were credentialed by the county to work alongside the official teams.

Ostrowski-Han called it the largest helicopter hoist rescue operation in Corpus Christi history. By Wednesday afternoon, the second day of the response, Coast Guard and partner aircraft had already rescued 341 people by air.

Vasquez-Okafor credited the contracted drone operators whose thermal cameras found people in the dark and in debris. "That capability let us put a boat on a specific roof instead of searching a whole block," she said. "It is the difference between minutes and hours."

The end of the rescue phase is not the end of the search. Officials said the remaining teams will shift to welfare checks, going to homes where no one has yet been contacted. Residents who have not been reached by a welfare check team, or who are worried about a neighbor or relative, should call 211.

Search teams recovered two bodies during the operation, both from a submerged vehicle on Violet Road. The county's confirmed storm death toll stands at 23.

The count rose quickly through the week: 486 by Wednesday afternoon, 702 by Thursday evening, 1,427 by Sunday. The steepest climb came after teams moved inland from the bayfront into neighborhoods where the water stayed for days.

The city remains under a boil-water notice issued Saturday, and officials asked residents returning to flooded homes to photograph damage before cleaning up and to stay out of standing water.

item.title: Opinion: In Rafael's first week, the neighbors got there first
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A column. The church halls and street-corner hubs that fed people before official help arrived deserve our thanks, and a hard look at why they had to.
item.content:encoded:
The first relief many of my neighbors saw after Hurricane Rafael didn't arrive in a truck with a government seal on the door. It arrived in a borrowed wagon, pulled down a muddy street by a church volunteer.

I've spent this week in the low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where so many households don't have cars, where people waited for county buses before the storm, and where some stayed home because they had no way to leave. I've watched Pastor Gloria Whitfield turn a fellowship hall into a pantry and a message board. I've watched Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide raising three kids, count water bottles and worry more about her elderly clients than about herself.

Church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water this week before official distribution reached some of these neighborhoods. That is not a knock on the people working the official response. Many of them haven't slept. Rafael made landfall at 1 a.m. Tuesday with about 11 feet of surge. The 911 center took calls at nearly ten times its normal pace. The city's only water plant lost power, and by Saturday the whole city was under a boil-water notice.

But we should be honest about what it means when help on foot arrives before help on wheels. Advocates warned all summer that transit gaps left households near the bay without a way out. The storm proved them right, and then it proved them right again: The people who couldn't leave were also the people who couldn't drive to help.

So here is what I'd ask. Of the city and county: Find the hubs that opened their doors this week, and send official supplies to them, where people can walk. Of the rest of us: Drop off a case of water at the hall on your way home. Of everyone: Remember this week the next time a hurricane season planning meeting asks who needs a ride, and show up to answer.

Whitfield said this week that nobody asked her church to do this, and nobody needed to. She is right about that. But somebody should have planned so she wouldn't have to.

Marisol Treviño covers city government and disasters for The Bayside Ledger. The views in this column are her own.

item.title: Breathing and skin complaints continue near oiled shorelines; health district urges caution
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Health officials say people who live near oiled beaches and marshes should limit time near the water and seek care if symptoms worsen.
item.content:encoded:
Residents who live near shorelines oiled by the Inner Harbor spill are still seeking emergency care for breathing problems and skin irritation, health officials and front-line nurses said Sunday, and the health district is urging people to stay away from the oil and limit time near fouled water.

"Crude oil gives off vapors that can irritate the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, and it can irritate skin on contact," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "For most people, symptoms ease once they get away from the exposure. People with asthma, COPD or heart disease, older adults, pregnant people and small children should be the most careful."

The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays and onto North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes. The cause remains under investigation.

In one Nueces County emergency department, charge nurse Alyssa Cortez, 34, said the complaints have been a steady thread all week. "It's not the biggest thing we're seeing, but it's every shift," Cortez said. "People come in coughing, eyes red, and the first thing they tell me is where they live."

Shah said the boil-water notice the city issued Saturday adds a second layer of caution. "We're asking people near the shoreline to stay away from the oil and everyone in the city to boil their water," she said. "Both come down to the same thing: Don't put something in your body that doesn't belong there."

What to do: Keep windows closed and stay inside if fumes are strong. Don't walk, wade or fish in oiled areas; Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing, and the Texas Department of State Health Services has closed shellfish harvesting, in both bays. Wash skin that touches oil with soap and water. Seek care for trouble breathing, chest pain, dizziness or a rash that spreads, and call 911 for severe symptoms.

The health district has not released counts of spill-related visits.

item.title: FEMA aerial survey: 4,200 to 5,800 structures in Nueces County with major or severe damage
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: FEMA's first systematic aerial damage assessment of the Corpus Christi area estimates that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures sustained major or severe damage from Hurricane Rafael, a preliminary figure the agency says will be updated as the survey expands.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Federal Emergency Management Agency released the results of its first systematic aerial damage assessment of the Corpus Christi area Saturday, estimating that between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County sustained major or severe damage from Hurricane Rafael. The figures come from survey flights by eight unmanned aircraft over the past two days and will be refined as the survey expands and ground inspections proceed in areas still accessible only by boat or helicopter. The agency did not put a dollar figure on the damage.

FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander said the survey covered about 180 square kilometers of residential and coastal zones, from the barrier islands to the bayside neighborhoods. "What we can see from the air tells us the scale of this event is consistent with a major Category 3 impact on a densely developed coastal zone," Ostrander said. "The number of structures with major or severe damage — somewhere between 4,200 and 5,800 — reflects the surge depth over the barrier islands and the density of construction in the bayside communities."

The heaviest damage is concentrated on Mustang Island, in the North Beach neighborhood of Corpus Christi, and in the lowest-elevation sections of Flour Bluff that experienced the greatest surge depth. The aircraft, operated by Argus Aerial Systems under a FEMA contract, collected roughly 847,000 image tiles that were classified by automated structure analysis. Structures in surge zones that received more than four feet of inundation are classified at minimum as major damage under the FEMA assessment matrix. Further survey phases will cover the utility corridor, commercial districts and the port.

Nueces County Judge Lorena Espinoza-Watts said the figures, while staggering, are not surprising given the storm's track and the surge depth. "This is the number we feared when Rafael was a Cat 3 with its eyewall over the barrier islands," Espinoza-Watts said. "Now we begin the work of rebuilding, and we need the state and federal partners to stay at the table for the years this will take." The county has requested a preliminary damage declaration supplement to extend public assistance eligibility and has applied for a Hazard Mitigation Grant Program designation to fund future resilience investments in the most severely damaged zones.

item.title: Health and wildlife agencies close fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; a shrimper finds oil on his nets
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: The closure shuts down fishing in both bays as crude from the Inner Harbor spill spreads. For an Aransas Pass shrimper, the news only confirmed what his nets showed him.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Parks and Wildlife on Saturday closed fishing, and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting, in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays days after Hurricane Rafael carried crude from the Inner Harbor spill across about 33 square miles of water.

Huy Nguyen didn't need the announcement. The second-generation shrimper from Aransas Pass took his boat out Friday to check the grounds he works in Corpus Christi Bay, dropped a short test drag and pulled up a net streaked with oil. He wrote it down in the spiral notebook where he logs every trip: no catch, oil.

"Black," Nguyen, 51, said Saturday, holding up a fold of net at the dock. "You can't sell shrimp out of that. You can't even wash it out."

His boat came through the storm fine, he said. His season may not. "I've got a boat note, a fuel bill and a deckhand who wants to work," he said. "The note comes due on the first like always. Oil doesn't care about any of that."

"Those closures are the health and wildlife agencies' call, and nobody at the Land Office is going to argue with keeping oiled seafood off anybody's table," said Cole Whitaker, spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Our job is to get the oil out of the water so the testing can come back clean."

The spill, which the Unified Command puts at about 9,000 barrels, came from the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil into both bays, onto North Beach and the Portland shoreline and into the marshes of Nueces Bay, which serve as nurseries for shrimp, crabs and fish. The cause of the release remains under investigation.

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season this summer, though fuel costs were squeezing margins. Nguyen said that cushion is gone. "A fair season was going to get me through the winter," he said. "Now I'm hoping for any season."

He said he would clean what gear he could and wait. "My father fished these bays. I fish these bays," Nguyen said. "I'll fish them again. I just don't know when."

item.title: What Corpus Christi's citywide boil-water notice means, and how to stay healthy under it
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: The notice covers every tap in the city. Health officials explain what's safe, what isn't and who should take extra care.
item.content:encoded:
Corpus Christi residents should boil tap water before drinking it or cooking with it under a citywide boil-water notice issued Saturday, the city's water utility said, as the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant struggles to recover from Hurricane Rafael.

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in the storm Tuesday, and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure has been low across the city since. The city opened water distribution sites Saturday.

"Our crews have been working around the clock at the plant," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the utility. "This notice is how we protect people while that work goes on. We'll lift it when testing tells us the water is safe, and not a day before."

"The goal is simple: Don't swallow water that hasn't been boiled," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "A rolling boil for two minutes takes care of the germs we worry about. Wash your hands often, especially before eating and after using the bathroom, and keep an eye on the youngest and oldest people in your house."

Can I shower? Yes, but keep water out of your mouth. Use sponge baths for babies and young children.

What about dishes? Use disposable plates and cups if you can, or run the dishwasher on its hottest, sanitizing cycle.

What about ice and drinks? Throw out ice made from tap water, and don't use tap water in coffee makers, drink mixes or baby formula unless it has been boiled first.

Who should be most careful? Infants, older adults, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system, Shah said. Anyone who becomes seriously ill, especially a young child or an older adult who can't keep fluids down, should seek medical care.

The notice comes as emergency rooms also see breathing and skin complaints among residents near shorelines oiled by the Inner Harbor spill. Health officials advise everyone to avoid contact with the oil.

item.title: Why the timing made Rafael's spill worse: oil on the water, then 11 feet of surge
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: A coastal oceanographer explains how the hurricane turned a harbor spill into a bay-wide one, and why the marshes will take the longest to recover.
item.content:encoded:
Oil spills inside a protected harbor are, in a grim sense, the easier kind. The water is calm, the spill is close to equipment, and boom can corral it near the source. The spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor this week had none of that luck.

Crude spilled from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, according to the Unified Command, which estimates the release at about 9,000 barrels. The storm drove about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and for more than a day, winds kept response boats off the water.

"The surge lifted the whole harbor at once, and anything floating on top rode up and out with it," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "It goes where the water goes, and that night the water went everywhere."

By Thursday, sheen covered about 33 square miles of the bays, the Unified Command said, and oil had reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.

Brooks said the marshes are the hardest part. On a normal tide, the bay laps at their edges. Under 11 feet of surge, the water and whatever rode on it was carried deep into grass and mud that rarely see open-bay water. "On a beach, the oil sits on top and you can pick it up," he said. "In a marsh, it's down in the stems and the mud. You can do more harm digging it out than letting it weather. Cleanup teams will be making that call acre by acre."

Brooks declined to discuss what caused the release, which the Unified Command says remains under investigation. "That's not my question to answer," he said. "My question is where it went. The answer, unfortunately, is a lot of places."

Crews began deploying boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open for reports of oiled animals. Health officials are urging residents to avoid contact with the oil.

Brooks said the shallowness that made the surge so destructive may help a little over time: Shallow, warm water mixes and breaks oil down faster than deep, cold water. "It's not a silver lining," he said. "It's just physics. This week, physics has mostly been against us."

item.title: ERs see breathing and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Emergency departments are treating people who live near beaches and marshes where crude from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Health officials say to avoid any contact with the oil.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing patients with breathing trouble and skin irritation who live near shorelines where crude from the Inner Harbor spill came ashore, and health officials are urging residents to avoid any contact with the oil.

"We're seeing people who say their throat burns, their eyes water, they've got a headache that won't quit, or a rash where they touched something on the beach," said Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department. "Most of them are going home after we treat them. But people with asthma or COPD need to take this seriously."

Cortez said staff now ask every patient with breathing complaints where they live and whether they have been near the water.

The Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office estimates that about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and it has reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes.

The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District is advising residents to stay away from oil on beaches and in the water, and to keep children and pets away from it as well.

What to do: If fumes are strong, go indoors and close windows and doors. If oil gets on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, paint thinner or other solvents. Don't burn oily debris. Seek medical care for trouble breathing, chest pain or a rash that spreads, and call 911 for severe breathing problems.

Cortez said her department is also seeing the usual mix that follows a big storm: cuts and puncture wounds from cleanup, people who ran out of medication and patients who depend on power for medical equipment. "Bring your medication list with you, or a photo of your pill bottles," she said. "It saves us time when time matters."

Health officials have not released counts of the spill-related visits. The Ledger will report them if and when they become available.

item.title: Texas AG and FBI warn of post-Rafael contractor fraud: unlicensed crews demanding cash, impersonating federal adjusters
item.dc:creator: Ruben Castañeda
item.description: The Texas Attorney General and the FBI have issued a joint disaster fraud warning for hurricane-affected communities on the Coastal Bend, alerting residents to roving unlicensed contractors, fraudulent insurance adjusters, and cash-upfront scams proliferating in affected neighborhoods.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Texas Attorney General's Office and the FBI Houston Division issued a joint disaster fraud warning Friday, alerting Coastal Bend residents to a surge in fraudulent contractor activity, impersonation of government inspectors, and upfront-cash solicitations targeting homeowners and renters in areas damaged by Hurricane Rafael. The warning described a pattern of behavior that investigators say inevitably follows a major hurricane within days of landfall, as opportunistic actors move into disaster zones ahead of legitimate recovery contractors.

Texas Attorney General spokesperson Brandon Lacey-Rhinehart said the office had already received initial reports of unlicensed contractors canvassing neighborhoods in North Beach, Flour Bluff, and Calallen with flyers and verbal solicitations offering immediate roof tarping, debris removal, and mold remediation services — requiring full or partial payment in cash before work begins. "These operations typically collect the money and either do poor-quality work or disappear entirely," Lacey-Rhinehart said. "In a disaster zone, where people are desperate to protect their property and have limited access to their normal professional networks, they are especially vulnerable."

The AG's office offered several verification steps residents should take before signing any contract or making any payment. All contractors working in Texas must hold a current Texas contractor's license, verifiable through the state licensing website. Residents should ask for a written estimate, a copy of the contractor's license, proof of liability insurance, and a list of local references before any work begins. Residents should never pay the full contract amount upfront; a deposit of no more than 10 percent of the total is standard practice for legitimate contractors. Additionally, no federal agency — including FEMA — charges fees for inspections or assistance applications. Anyone identifying themselves as a FEMA inspector who requests payment should be treated as a fraud suspect.

The FBI advisory noted that in past major disasters, federal charges of wire fraud, mail fraud, and disaster benefit fraud had been prosecuted against individuals who posed as FEMA employees to solicit personal information or fees from disaster victims. Residents with suspicious contacts should report them to the FBI's National Center for Disaster Fraud at 1-866-720-5721 or to the Texas AG Consumer Protection Hotline. The Nueces County District Attorney's office confirmed it is coordinating with state and federal agencies to pursue local enforcement actions as specific complaints are received.

item.title: 911 center releases dispatch logs: 1,100 rescue calls on landfall day
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center has released preliminary dispatch data showing 1,100 rescue-related calls handled during the landfall period alone, as officials begin reviewing the agency's performance during the most demanding event in its history.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center released preliminary call volume data Friday showing that the agency handled approximately 1,100 rescue-related calls during the landfall period — from the hours before Rafael came ashore through the evening of the same day — a rescue dispatch load that the center said was exceeded only by Thursday's. The data, shared by CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss at a Friday morning briefing, comes as county officials begin the process of reviewing how the region's emergency communications infrastructure performed during the most demanding event it has ever faced.

"Every one of those 1,100 calls was a person or a family in distress," Escamilla-Voss said. "Our dispatchers handled that call load professionally and they did it under extraordinary circumstances, with their own families evacuated, their own homes potentially under water, and an obligation to stay on the job until their relief arrived." She said total call volume peaked Wednesday at about 2,900 calls, the busiest day in the agency's history, and that Thursday brought a record 2,109 rescue requests.

The center dispatched rescue calls to Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office marine units, the U.S. Coast Guard, and Texas Task Force 1 throughout the event, coordinating a multi-agency triage process that prioritized life-threatening flooding situations over property damage reports. Mutual aid dispatchers from San Patricio County and Bee County provided remote backup support throughout the peak hours, handling overflow call volume via remote access to the CBECC's computer-aided dispatch system.

The dispatch logs have been released in redacted form to county commissioners as part of a preliminary after-action review process. Escamilla-Voss said the full call documentation would be archived and made available through a formal public records process. The agency will also conduct a performance debrief with mutual aid partners from San Patricio and Bee counties to identify protocols that worked well and areas for improvement before the next major event.

item.title: 702 rescued, 23 dead as Rafael recovery enters second day; SAR teams push into Calallen and south Mustang Island
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Combined search-and-rescue teams have recorded 702 rescues since Hurricane Rafael struck Tuesday, with operations continuing in Calallen and south Mustang Island; 23 fatalities have been confirmed as of Thursday evening.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Combined search-and-rescue teams from the Corpus Christi Fire Department, the U.S. Coast Guard, the Nueces County Sheriff's Office, and Texas Task Force 1 have recorded a cumulative total of 702 rescues as of Thursday evening, as the two-day-old recovery operation from Hurricane Rafael continues to reach flooded and debris-covered areas across the Coastal Bend. Twenty-three deaths have been confirmed by the Nueces County Medical Examiner, with officials warning that number is expected to rise as search teams access areas still unreachable.

Corpus Christi Fire Chief Alberto Rincón said Thursday evening that operations were continuing in two primary focus areas: the Calallen neighborhood in the city's northwest quadrant, where storm surge drainage from the Nueces River had combined with inland flooding to inundate a wide residential swath, and the south portion of Mustang Island, where surge conditions and debris had made boat access difficult for the first 36 hours. "We have teams working those areas now, and what we are finding is a mix," Rincón said. "Some people sheltered successfully and are in need of food and water. Some homes are empty. Some homes we are not finding anyone alive."

Texas Task Force 1 Team Leader Lt. Dave Breckman said the technical rescue component of the operation had shifted from initial triage sweeps to systematic grid-by-grid coverage, ensuring that every structure in the affected zones was checked. "In the first 24 hours you go for the signals, the flags, the people calling out," Breckman said. "Now we are going structure by structure, house by house. We will not leave a neighborhood until we have covered every building." The task force is deploying structural specialists to assess collapsed homes before rescue personnel enter.

The 23 confirmed fatalities represent losses across the barrier island and low-lying mainland communities. Nueces County Medical Examiner Dr. James Oduya-Park said causes of death are still being determined but that drowning is involved in a significant proportion of the confirmed cases. The county has established a family assistance center at a community recreation facility in Corpus Christi where families can inquire about missing relatives and receive information about the fatality identification process.

item.title: Air quality hits unhealthy levels near ship channel; residents within two miles urged to stay indoors
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: TCEQ and EPA have issued a health advisory for areas within two miles of the Corpus Christi ship channel after the air quality index rose to 134, driven by hydrocarbon vapors from the Inner Harbor oil spill.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — State and federal environmental officials issued an air quality health advisory Thursday evening for a broad zone around the Corpus Christi ship channel after monitoring stations recorded an Air Quality Index of 134 — a level classified as Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups — driven by hydrocarbon vapors from the oil spilled in the Inner Harbor on Sept. 14 and since carried into the bays. Residents with respiratory conditions, the elderly, children under 18, and pregnant women in areas within approximately two miles of the ship channel were urged to remain indoors with windows closed until the advisory is lifted.

TCEQ spokesperson Annette Vogt said the elevated AQI readings were concentrated in a corridor aligned with prevailing post-storm wind patterns, running generally southwest from the ship channel into portions of the North Beach, Leopard Street, and central Corpus Christi neighborhoods. "We are seeing levels that are above the daily health standard for certain vulnerable populations," Vogt said. "For healthy adults, brief outdoor exposure at this level is generally not harmful, but we are asking people in the advisory zone to limit strenuous outdoor activity and to keep windows shut as a precaution."

EPA Region 6 Deputy Director Carla Nystrom confirmed that agency air monitoring vehicles were deployed to the ship channel corridor Thursday afternoon and that readings at some fixed monitoring points in the Hillcrest area briefly exceeded 150 AQI. Those elevated readings had moderated by early evening. "We expect levels to continue declining as the slick is contained and weather conditions improve," Nystrom said. "We will lift the advisory when AQI returns to and stays below 100 at all monitoring points."

The North Beach neighborhood and the industrial corridor along the bayfront saw the highest localized readings. Residents of North Beach were already dealing with significant flood damage from Rafael's surge and in many cases had not yet been able to return to their properties. Emergency management officials asked residents coordinating with damage assessment teams in those areas to wear N95 masks and to limit the duration of outdoor exposure. TCEQ planned to post updated air quality readings every two hours on its website and through the AlertNueces notification system.

item.title: 'We're still here': Two days after Rafael, a mother of three waits for help near the bay
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Rosa Elizondo rode out the hurricane at home with her children because she had no way to leave. The water has gone down. She is still waiting.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo has been counting water bottles. By Thursday morning she had fewer than a dozen left for four people, in a house with no power and a kitchen faucet that coughs more than it pours.

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide, rode out Hurricane Rafael with her three children in the duplex she rents near the bay, in one of the low-lying neighborhoods the county ordered evacuated Sunday. She doesn't own a car, and the county evacuation bus she had registered for never reached her street before the wind rose, she said.

"Everybody asks, 'Why didn't you leave?'" Elizondo said, sitting on her front step while her 6-year-old chased a lizard across the muddy yard. "Leave how? Leave with what? Ni modo. We stayed, we prayed and we're still here."

The water stopped a few inches below her door, she said. Houses a block closer to the bay, lower by a step or two, took water inside.

Since the storm passed, she said, she hasn't seen anyone from an agency on her street. She has heard on a battery radio that help is being organized, but with no car and no power, she has no way to go looking for it.

Her worries run past her own front door. Her clients, older people she helps bathe, dress and take their medicine, live alone across the neighborhood, and she hasn't been able to reach two of them by phone. "That's my job, to check on them," she said. "And I can't even get to them."

Most of the storm's 911 calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay like hers, county officials said Wednesday; at the peak, calls reached about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at a church fellowship hall nearby, has been walking the neighborhood with volunteers since Wednesday, writing down who needs what. "Rosa's on my list," Whitfield said. "So is half this street. We're getting to everybody."

Elizondo said her family will manage. "We have each other, we have the radio, and the kids think this is camping," she said, then laughed. "Ask me again in three days."

item.title: Oil from Inner Harbor spill reaches North Beach, Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles, the Unified Command said Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Crude oil from the tanker spill in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor has washed onto North Beach and the Portland shoreline and into the marshes of Nueces Bay, carried out of the ship channel by Hurricane Rafael's surge and winds, state and federal responders said Thursday.

Sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, according to the Unified Command led by the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office. The command estimated Wednesday that about 9,000 barrels spilled from the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as the storm arrived.

"We've got oil on sand, oil on rock and oil in the grass," said Cole Whitaker, spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program. "The marsh is the hardest. You can rake a beach. You can't rake a marsh without killing it."

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the surge did what surges do: It lifted everything floating in the harbor and carried it outward and upward. "Water at that height reaches places the bay normally never touches," Brooks said. "When it drained, it left the oil behind like a bathtub ring. Except the bathtub is a marsh full of nursery habitat for shrimp, crabs and redfish."

On North Beach, cut off from downtown since the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, Marcus Bell said he smelled the oil before he saw it. "I thought somebody's generator was leaking," said Bell, 67, a retired welder. "Then I walked down to the water and the sand was black at the edge. I've never seen this beach like that."
