Crews began putting out boom Thursday as winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline opened for reports of oiled birds and animals, Whitaker said. Residents should not try to catch or clean oiled wildlife themselves.

The marshes of Nueces Bay, where the Nueces River meets the bay, are among the most productive nursery grounds on this stretch of the Texas coast. Their shallow water makes the work harder: Boats big enough to carry boom often cannot get close to the marsh edge.

The cause of the release remains under investigation.

item.title: Unified Command: About 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at Inner Harbor berth
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor, Ellie Navarro
item.description: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office named the tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the terminal, Rendal Terminals. Response boats are waiting for the wind to drop.
item.content:encoded:
About 9,000 barrels of crude oil spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday as they formed a Unified Command to lead the response.

The tankers are the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, which were tied up at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor, according to the Unified Command. The Coast Guard had confirmed a discharge from two vessels on Tuesday but had not named them or estimated the volume. A barrel holds 42 gallons.

"Our priorities are the safety of the public and our responders, and protecting the most sensitive shoreline," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will put crews on the water as soon as the winds allow it. We are not there yet." The cause of the release remains under investigation, she said.

The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment to support the response, Ruiz said. She did not say what equipment had been requested or when it would arrive.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program, said the agency would focus first on keeping oil out of marshes and other sensitive areas once boats and boom can go out. "Shoreline is where a spill gets slow and expensive," Whitaker said. "The sooner we get boom in the water, the more shoreline we save."

Rendal Terminals said it was cooperating fully with the Unified Command. "Our first concern is the safety of everyone at our facility and in the surrounding community," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson. "It would be inappropriate to speculate about the cause while the investigation is underway."

The two laden tankers had Coast Guard approval to stay at the berth when the channel closed to all traffic Monday, the day before landfall. The channel remains closed, and crude exports, which analysts estimate make up about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.

Officials have not said where the oil has traveled since the storm. Rafael's surge of about 11 feet flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays after landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday, and winds remained too strong Wednesday for crews to survey the bays by boat.

item.title: 911 calls ran at nearly ten times normal as Rafael's surge swamped neighborhoods near the bay
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Calls to the county's emergency communications center peaked at a pace of about 2,900 a day, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the water, officials said Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
The calls kept coming. At the peak of Hurricane Rafael, the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center was taking calls at a rate of about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, county officials said Wednesday.

Most of those calls came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where Rafael's surge of about 11 feet pushed water into streets and homes after the storm made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday.

"Every one of those calls is somebody's worst night," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "People calling about water coming in the door. People who couldn't reach their mother. People whose power went out and who need it for medical equipment. That's what those numbers are."

Pruitt urged residents to save 911 for emergencies so lines stay open, and to report downed lines, flooded streets and other problems that aren't life-threatening through the city's and county's non-emergency numbers.

In one neighborhood near the bay, Pastor Gloria Whitfield said many of the people who found her Wednesday morning had no working phone at all. "A lot of people down here don't have a car, and right now a lot of them don't have a charged phone," said Whitfield, 59, who coordinates relief at her church's fellowship hall. "When they need help, they knock on a door. Sometimes it's mine."

Whitfield and volunteers began walking the neighborhood Wednesday, she said, writing down who is home, who is hurt and who needs water, food or medicine.

Surge zones were ordered evacuated Sunday, with county buses sent for residents who had no car. Officials have not said how many people stayed behind.

The scope of the flooding came into sharper focus Wednesday. Satellite imagery shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remained closed pending inspections, cutting North Beach and Portland off from downtown.

Pruitt said residents should stay off the roads unless they must travel. "Every car out there sightseeing is a car in the way of a crew," he said.

item.title: Shoreline Regional activates hurricane plan as generators power up and ER braces for first trauma wave
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Shoreline Regional Medical Center is running on generator power with its Hurricane Contingency Plan activated as Rafael comes ashore, and the hospital has requested an emergency blood supply from Nueces Bay Blood Services.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Shoreline Regional Medical Center activated its Hurricane Contingency Plan before Rafael's landfall early Tuesday, switching all critical systems to generator power and calling in additional trauma and emergency staff to handle the anticipated surge of storm-related injuries. Hospital officials confirmed by early Tuesday afternoon that the emergency room had received its first patients injured during Rafael's passage, with more expected as rescue operations begin in the affected areas.

Chief Medical Officer Dr. Patricia Cabrera said in a statement that the hospital's clinical staff is prepared but that the first hours after a major hurricane are always uncertain in terms of patient volume and injury types. "Our ER and trauma teams are in position and our surge protocols are activated," she said. "We expect to see a range of injuries — lacerations, fractures, near-drowning presentations, and crush injuries from structural collapse. The timeline for patient arrivals depends on when rescue units can safely access the impacted areas and begin transporting."

Shoreline Regional issued a formal request to Nueces Bay Blood Services early Tuesday morning for an emergency supply of O-positive and O-negative blood, citing the anticipated need for surgical support during mass casualty scenarios. Nueces Bay Blood Services spokesperson Rafael Garza confirmed the request was fulfilled with priority delivery before Rafael's arrival, with additional units staged at an inland distribution point accessible to the hospital by ground. "We pre-positioned units knowing this was coming," Garza said. "If demand spikes, we have agreements with blood banks in San Antonio and Houston to reroute supply rapidly."

The hospital is running on generator power for all patient care areas, the intensive care unit, the surgical suites, the laboratory, and imaging. Administrative systems are operating on reduced power protocols. Patients who had been scheduled for elective procedures this week were contacted before the storm to reschedule, leaving the facility's capacity focused entirely on trauma and emergency care. SRMC has also suspended visitor access per its Hurricane Contingency Plan protocols, with limited exceptions for end-of-life situations.

item.title: FEMA opens Rafael information line; no household aid approved yet, agency says
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Callers can get information on shelters, supplies and documenting damage. Photograph everything and call your insurer first, FEMA says.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Federal Emergency Management Agency opened an information line Tuesday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties hit by Hurricane Rafael, but the agency cautioned that no federal aid for individual households has been approved.

Callers to 1-800-621-3362 can get information on shelters, emergency supplies and how to document storm damage, FEMA Region 6 said. The line is staffed daily from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.

"This line is for information. It is not an application," said an external affairs officer with FEMA Region 6. "If assistance programs are approved, we will announce them and tell people exactly how to register. Until then, do not pay anyone who says they can sign you up."

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas about 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and knocking out power across the area.

In the meantime, FEMA said, residents should photograph damage before cleaning up, keep receipts for repairs and supplies, and contact their insurance companies first. Agency staff are deploying to the area to support state and local emergency managers.

Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county's priorities Tuesday were rescues, shelters and water. "Paperwork can wait a day. Take your pictures when it is safe, and stay off flooded streets to do it," Pruitt said.

The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and water pressure was low across the city Tuesday, the city water utility said.

Residents who need shelter, or a ride to one, can call 2-1-1. Emergencies should go to 911, which county officials said was handling roughly seven times its normal volume Tuesday morning and should be kept clear for people in immediate danger.

Federal help for households, when it comes, usually follows a formal disaster declaration and damage assessments. Neither step had been taken as of Tuesday afternoon. FEMA said it would announce any change.

item.title: Oil spills at Inner Harbor terminal as Rafael arrives; amount and cause unknown
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The Coast Guard says oil was reported discharging from two tankers moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor as Rafael closed in. Responders cannot get on the water yet.
item.content:encoded:
Oil was reported spilling at a crude terminal on Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard said, adding a pollution emergency to a city already battered by the storm.

Two tankers moored at the terminal are involved, according to Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. How much oil reached the water was not known Tuesday morning, and the cause is under investigation.

"The Coast Guard received a report of oil discharging from two vessels moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for the sector. "Conditions do not allow responders on the water at this time. We will not estimate a volume or speculate on a cause until we have facts."

The two loaded tankers had stayed at the terminal through the storm with Coast Guard approval after the agency closed the ship channel to all traffic Monday. Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas put to sea before the storm.

Whether to keep a laden ship at a protected berth or send it to sea ahead of a hurricane is a judgment that port operators and the Coast Guard make storm by storm, weighing the danger of sailing into heavy weather against the risk of riding it out beside a dock.

The Coast Guard said the terminal's operator, which it did not identify Tuesday, had reported a discharge from two vessels at its berth and was working with authorities.

The Inner Harbor stretches for miles west of the Harbor Bridge along the ship channel, lined with docks, refineries and tank farms. With winds still strong Tuesday morning, officials did not say how far the oil had moved or whether any had left the harbor.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.

Anyone who sees oil on the water or along the shore should keep away from it. The Ledger will update this story as the Coast Guard releases more information.

item.title: Rafael roars ashore near Port Aransas, flooding the bays and darkening the Coastal Bend
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño, Ellie Navarro
item.description: The Category 3 hurricane made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday, driving about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power outages are widespread.
item.content:encoded:
Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and knocking out power across much of the Coastal Bend.

By first light, wind was still tearing at signs and shingles downtown, water stood in streets near the bayfront, and the rumble of generators had replaced the usual hum of traffic along Shoreline Boulevard.

"The surge came in about where we said it would, and it came in high," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "People need to treat the water as dangerous today. It is not over just because the eye has moved on."

The weather service put the surge at about 11 feet, within the 9 to 12 feet forecast in the hurricane warning it issued Sunday. Outages were widespread across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties early Tuesday.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, urged residents who stayed home to remain inside until the wind drops. "If you're safe where you are, stay put," Pruitt said. "Don't drive into water. Don't go down to look at the bay. We will get to people, but the wind has to come down first."

The county ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland, and county buses picked up residents without cars in the final days before the storm. But some residents of low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, where many households do not own a car, rode out the storm at home. Advocates had pushed all summer for more evacuation rides for those neighborhoods.

It was not yet clear Tuesday morning how badly Port Aransas and the rest of Mustang Island had fared, or how many homes around the bays had taken water. Officials said damage assessments would begin as soon as conditions allowed.

This is a developing story. The Ledger will update it throughout the day.

item.title: Opinion: Before you go, knock on one door
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Column: The people most likely to be left behind in a hurricane are the ones nobody checks on. Tonight, check on someone.
item.content:encoded:
Before I was a reporter, I worked in an emergency room. I learned there that the worst nights often started with someone nobody had checked on: someone alone, out of medicine or out of power, who had assumed help would come. Storms make those nights more likely.

Rafael is due to hit near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge behind it. Surge zones have been under a mandatory evacuation order since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and the county's buses are out collecting people who have no car. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and some of those families spent Sunday waiting at the door with their bags packed.

If you are leaving tonight, do one more thing before you go. Knock on one door.

Pick the neighbor you are not sure about. The older couple who do not drive anymore. The woman on oxygen. The family with small children and no car in the driveway. Ask three questions: Do you have a way out? Do you have your medicines? Does anyone know where you are going?

If the answer to the first question is no, offer a seat if you have one. If you cannot, help them call 2-1-1 or the county for a ride, and stay with them until someone answers.

If they are staying outside the surge zone, make sure they have water, a charged phone, a battery radio and a written list of their medications and doses. Write your number on it.

If you are worried about someone you cannot reach, call the county. In a life-threatening emergency, call 911, and understand that once the wind is up, help may not be able to come right away. That is why tonight matters.

None of this requires training. It requires about ten minutes and a willingness to be a little nosy.

Hurricanes sort people by who has a car, who has a phone and who has someone checking on them. We cannot fix the first two tonight. We can fix the third.

Knock on one door.

item.title: Nueces County extends mandatory evacuation to Zones B and C as Rafael closes in; contraflow opens on US-181
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The Nueces County judge extended the mandatory evacuation Monday morning from Zone A to Zones B and C, covering an estimated 85,000 residents, as Hurricane Rafael is projected to make a direct hit on Mustang Island.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Nueces County Judge Lorena Espinoza-Watts extended the county's mandatory evacuation order Monday morning to Zones B and C, adding all areas below 10 feet of elevation and all mobile and manufactured homes to the barrier islands and surge areas of Zone A that were ordered out Sunday. The order now covers an estimated 85,000 residents in the path of Hurricane Rafael, which is forecast to push a 9- to 12-foot storm surge into Corpus Christi Bay.

"This is not a suggestion. This is not a recommendation. This is a mandatory order," Espinoza-Watts said at a press conference outside the county courthouse Monday morning. "If you are in Zone A, B or C, you need to leave now. Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Mustang Island as a major hurricane, and the surge it pushes ahead of it will be unsurvivable in those zones. We cannot guarantee rescue in surge conditions."

Texas Department of Transportation activated contraflow operations on US-181 beginning at 10 a.m. Monday, converting all lanes to outbound traffic at the Nueces Bay Causeway crossing to accelerate evacuation flow from the barrier islands and coastal areas. I-37 contraflow toward San Antonio was also activated. At midday, Texas DPS reported steady but moving traffic on both corridors, with no major incidents reported. Fuel supplies were confirmed available at stations along evacuation routes in George West, Alice, and Victoria.

County officials said the evacuation assistance program was processing dozens of ride requests from residents without vehicles, using school buses and county vans to transport people to shelters at the Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds in Robstown, the Calallen ISD Fieldhouse and Alice High School. Hotels in San Antonio, Austin, and the Hill Country reported surge demand from Coastal Bend evacuees. The American Red Cross confirmed it had opened additional shelters in Bexar and Karnes counties.

Island businesses that have not already closed were given notice that all commercial activity on Mustang and Padre islands must cease and that owners should leave with employees as soon as property is secured. "After that point, we will not be able to come back in until the storm passes," said Nueces County Sheriff's Office spokesperson Lt. Rebecca Almendarez.

item.title: Under hurricane warning, Rafael forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Forecasters call the storm surge life-threatening. Anyone in a surge zone who has not left should leave now.
item.content:encoded:
A hurricane warning issued Sunday remains in effect for the Coastal Bend. Hurricane Rafael is forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge, the National Weather Service said Monday.

"Nine to 12 feet of water is not a flood you wade through. In a lot of homes near the bays, that's water over your head, and in some, over the roofline," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you've been told to leave, leave now. Not after lunch. Now."

A warning means hurricane conditions are expected. Tropical-storm-force winds typically arrive hours before a hurricane's center, and once they do, driving becomes dangerous and emergency crews may not be able to reach people. That shortens the window to evacuate more than many people expect.

Storm surge is the greatest threat. Surge is seawater pushed ashore by a storm's winds, and on the Coastal Bend the bays shape where it goes. Water driven through the passes and into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay piles up against shorelines that have nowhere to send it. When surge arrives on top of the tide, it reaches higher still.

The region is already wet. Tropical moisture that streamed ahead of Rafael saturated soils last week and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. More heavy rain will run off fast.

A mandatory evacuation for surge zones has been in effect since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars. The Port of Corpus Christi has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday, and the region's Navy air stations flew their training aircraft to Fort Worth on Friday.

If you live outside a surge zone and are staying, forecasters recommend sheltering in a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows on the lowest floor that is not at risk of flooding. Fill bathtubs and containers with water for washing. Charge everything. Keep a battery radio on.

"People think the danger is the wind they can hear," Arceneaux said. "The danger is the water they can't see coming in the dark."

The Ledger will update this story throughout the day and night.

item.title: Three kids, four bags and a bus that has not come yet
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Rosa Elizondo registered for an evacuation ride on Thursday. On Sunday, with surge zones under a mandatory evacuation and a hurricane warning up, she and her children waited for the county bus.
item.content:encoded:
The bags are lined up by the front door, smallest to biggest. One for each of the three children, one for Rosa Elizondo. The smallest has a stuffed dog zipped halfway into the outside pocket so it can see.

A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Elizondo's rented home near the bay is in one. Forecasters upgraded Saturday's hurricane watch to a hurricane warning Sunday afternoon, about 36 hours before Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm. Shelters have opened inland. County buses are picking up residents without cars. Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who does not own a car, registered for a ride through 2-1-1 on Thursday, the day Rafael's forecast cone moved over Corpus Christi.

On Sunday, she waited.

"I did everything right. I called. I packed. Now I'm sitting on my suitcase like it's the airport," she said, then turned to the window, where her youngest had her face pressed to the glass. "Mija, sit down. The bus doesn't come faster if you look for it."

By Sunday afternoon, most of the parking spots on her block were empty. Neighbors who own cars had packed up and gone, a few on Saturday and the rest at first light. The street was quiet in a way Elizondo said she did not like.

Many households in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay have no car, and advocates spent the summer pointing to bus service and transit gaps as they pushed for more evacuation rides. Sunday was the day that problem became a line of families watching a street.

County buses were still working through ride requests, said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're registered and waiting, stay put and keep your phone on," he said. "We have your address."

In the afternoon, Elizondo's phone rang. It was Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall nearby and keeps a list of neighbors without cars. Whitfield wanted to know whether the family was ready and whether anyone had called. Elizondo said yes to the first and not yet to the second.

She spent part of the afternoon on the phone with her clients' families, making sure the people she cares for during the week had their own rides. "Them first," she said. "Then us."

By late afternoon, the family was still waiting. The children had eaten the sandwiches meant for the road. Elizondo made more and kept the bags by the door.

"I'm not scared yet," she said. "Ask me when the wind starts."

item.title: Mandatory evacuation: who has to leave, where to go and how to get a ride
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: County officials have ordered surge zones evacuated ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
item.content:encoded:
Every evacuation map of the Coastal Bend tells the same story. The water comes first to the places closest to it: the barrier islands, the beach neighborhoods and the low streets along the bays. On Sunday, those are the places county officials told to leave.

A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters have opened inland, and county buses are picking up residents who do not have cars.

"If you're in a surge zone, this isn't advice anymore. It's an order," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You don't stay behind for the house. The house can be rebuilt. You can't."

Who has to leave. The order covers storm surge zones, the areas mapped as most likely to flood when a hurricane pushes Gulf water ashore. To find out whether your address is in one, check the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1. If you are not sure, county officials say to treat yourself as if you are.

Where to go. If you have family or friends inland, go there. If you do not, shelters are open inland. The county is announcing shelter locations through its official channels, local media and 2-1-1. Do not go to a location you saw in a forwarded post without confirming it.

How to get a ride. Residents without cars can get county bus transportation to shelters. If you registered through 2-1-1, the county has your address. If you did not, call now. "If you called for a ride, stay by your phone and be ready with one bag per person," Pruitt said. "When the bus comes, we need you at the door."

What to bring. Medicines and a written list of doses. IDs and insurance papers. Phone chargers. A change of clothes for a few days. Food for anyone on a special diet. Pet supplies, if your pets are coming with you; ask about pet arrangements when you call.

Before you lock the door: unplug appliances, bring in loose outdoor items and tell someone outside the area where you are going.

County officials have not released a count of residents in the surge zones or of ride requests, and the Ledger is not going to guess. What matters this morning is simpler: if you are in a surge zone, leave, and if you need help leaving, ask for it now.

item.title: Port stays open under storm condition, but ships are told to plan their exits
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: The Port of Corpus Christi's lifeline is still open, for now. Here is what the Coast Guard's storm condition means for the port, its workers and the relief cargo waiting to come in.
item.content:encoded:
As of Saturday, the channel that carries about half of the nation's crude exports is still open, but the clock is running.

With Hurricane Rafael approaching, the Coast Guard has set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. Ships in port have been told to make departure plans or ask the Coast Guard for permission to stay, and the crude docks are slowing their loading. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been postponed.

"Safety comes first, and we'll follow the Coast Guard's lead on the channel," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This port has come back from storms before, and it will again. Our job right now is to secure the docks and be ready for the day after."

The slowdown strains the chain the Ledger described last month: pipeline to tank farm, tank farm to tanker, tanker to anchorage, anchorage to the Gulf. Tankers that would have loaded this week are waiting, and should the channel close, the queue offshore will be the first thing to clear when it reopens.

It also puts relief cargo at risk. Forty relief containers booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reported Thursday, have not reached port, and a closure would leave them waiting like every other ship.

"If the channel closes, nothing moves through it, relief or crude," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the booking. "We'll be ready when it opens. The trucks are lined up on paper. They just need a ship at a dock."

For dock workers, line handlers, pilots and tug crews, a storm slowdown means idle time and storm preparation instead of paid shifts. For businesses that depend on port traffic, it means a pause of unknown length.

Salinas would not say whether the port expects to close; port conditions are set by the Coast Guard. Reopening after a storm closure typically follows inspection of the channel and port facilities. The Ledger will report the port's status as it changes.

item.title: Hurricane watch posted for Corpus Christi as Rafael strengthens in the Gulf
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The National Weather Service has placed the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch as Hurricane Rafael is expected to intensify into a major hurricane before making landfall early next week.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The National Weather Service issued a hurricane watch for Corpus Christi and the Coastal Bend early Saturday morning, putting the region on notice that dangerous conditions are possible within 48 hours as Hurricane Rafael continues its path across the Gulf of Mexico.

The watch, issued at 4 a.m. local time, covers coastal areas from Baffin Bay northward through Aransas Pass, including the barrier island communities of Mustang Island and North Padre Island. Meteorologist-in-Charge Dr. Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi, said the storm is expected to rapidly intensify over warm Gulf waters before it reaches the Texas coast. "Rafael is moving into an environment that is about as favorable for strengthening as we see in the Gulf — warm sea surface temperatures, low wind shear, and a well-defined inner core," Arceneaux said. "Our current forecast brings it ashore as a major hurricane, Category 3 or higher, by early Tuesday."

The watch puts the region in a 48-hour window during which residents should monitor forecasts closely and begin preparations, including assembling emergency kits, reviewing evacuation routes, and securing outdoor equipment. Emergency management officials in Nueces County urged residents not to wait for a warning to begin getting ready. "A watch means start moving on your plan, not thinking about starting a plan," said Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams at a morning briefing.

Rafael was centered about 450 miles southeast of Corpus Christi early Saturday, moving northwest at approximately 10 miles per hour. Its maximum sustained winds stood at 100 miles per hour, a Category 2 hurricane, and the NWS forecast expects further strengthening through Monday. Residents with mobility limitations, medical dependencies, or animals requiring transport were urged to contact county emergency services immediately to arrange evacuation assistance.

City officials said all storm preparation activities are under way, including pre-positioning supplies, activating the city emergency operations center to Level 2, and coordinating with the Texas Division of Emergency Management. The next full advisory from the National Hurricane Center is expected at 10 a.m. Saturday.

item.title: Army depot halts work and secures helicopters as Rafael approaches; workers told to prepare their families
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: One of the region's largest employers has paused production ahead of the storm. The Navy is also flying training aircraft from Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth.
item.content:encoded:
Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work Friday and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael, pausing one of the region's largest employers as Rafael's forecast track points toward the Coastal Bend.

The depot, which occupies part of NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary facility for overhauling and repairing helicopters. Its hangars and shops are filled with aircraft in various stages of repair, along with the tools and parts needed to finish them. Securing that work means more than closing doors: aircraft are moved inside, components are stowed, and shops are buttoned up against wind and water.

"Our employees have done this before, and they did it well," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "When we're ready to bring people back, they'll hear it from us first. Until then, their job is their families."

Kowalczyk would not speculate on how long work would be paused. That will depend on the storm and on what crews find when they return.

The pause comes at the end of a summer in which the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics, a reminder of how much of the local economy runs through the air station's gates. Depot paychecks support households across Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the businesses that depend on them.

On the other side of the airfield, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth, Navy officials said. Moving aircraft inland protects them from wind and flying debris and frees crews to prepare the bases themselves.

The moves come a day after Rafael's forecast cone shifted to cover Corpus Christi, and forecasters have warned the storm could strengthen rapidly over warm Gulf water.

For depot employees, the practical advice is the same as for everyone else in the region: know your evacuation zone, keep your phone charged and follow county guidance. Residents without cars can register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1.

item.title: With Corpus Christi in Rafael's cone, a mother without a car makes the call she kept putting off
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide with three children and no car, registered for an evacuation ride Thursday. County officials say others like her should do the same now.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo made the call from her kitchen table between clients, the phone on speaker and her youngest doing a worksheet beside her.

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay and does not own a car, had been meaning to register for an evacuation ride since the county's hurricane fair in July. "Every week I said, next week," she said. "Then the TV put Corpus in the cone, and I said, okay, Rosa, ya."

Corpus Christi sits inside Rafael's forecast cone, though forecasters have not yet posted a hurricane watch. No evacuation order has been issued in Nueces County. But for households without cars, the time to plan is now, county officials said.

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay. Advocates spent the summer pushing for more evacuation rides, and county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for help through the state registry by calling 2-1-1.

"If you don't have a way out, we need to know before the order, not after," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We plan the buses off that list."

The call took a few minutes. The operator asked for her address, the names and ages of the people in the household and whether anyone needed medical help. Elizondo answered, spelled her street name twice and hung up.

"Now I wait," she said. "I'm waiting for a phone call and a hurricane. Which one comes first, I don't know."

Her children have each been assigned a bag. Clothes for three days, a toothbrush, a phone charger for the ones old enough to have phones, and one toy for the youngest, who has already chosen a stuffed dog. Elizondo's bag holds the family's documents, her medicines and a folder of client phone numbers.

That folder is her other worry. Several of her clients cannot leave on their own, and she has spent the week making sure they are registered too. "They're like my grandparents," she said. "If I go, I need to know they're going."

She looked at the bags lined up by the door and shook her head. "I've packed for my clients a hundred times," she said. "First time I've packed for us."

item.title: Relief cargo booked ahead of Rafael, including 40 containers on the cargo ship Gulf Provider
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Relief shipments are being lined up as Rafael's forecast cone covers Corpus Christi. A freight forwarder says weather and the ship channel will set the schedule.
item.content:encoded:
The relief supply chain started moving before the first evacuation order. Relief shipments are being booked ahead of Hurricane Rafael, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, according to Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder handling the booking.

"We've got 40 boxes booked on Gulf Provider, and we're working the inland legs now," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics. "The whole game is pre-positioning. You want the cargo committed and the trucking lined up so that when the port says go, you go."

As the Ledger reported last month, relief agencies stocked warehouses this summer and freight forwarders signed standby relief contracts ahead of peak hurricane season. Those arrangements set terms and capacity in advance, so that cargo can be booked quickly when a storm threatens, without negotiating rates in the middle of an emergency.

Akins would not describe what is in the containers. "Relief cargo. The agencies will tell you what's in the boxes," he said. "My job is getting them here."

The schedule depends on the storm and on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. A ship carrying relief containers needs the same open channel and the same berths as the tankers that load crude here. If the Coast Guard closes the channel ahead of Rafael, inbound ships wait offshore until it reopens.

"Weather sets the schedule. We just hold the bookings," Akins said. "If the channel shuts, she waits like everybody else. Then we work the queue."

The forty-container figure is the one confirmed Thursday. Akins did not say whether other forwarders had booked additional relief cargo, and the agencies that own the shipments have not released details.

For the region's families, the reminder from the Ledger's August reporting still holds: outside relief is the slowest layer of the supply chain. Rafael's forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi. Emergency managers recommend having enough water, food and medicine at home to get through several days on your own.

item.title: Rafael's forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi; no watch yet, but forecasters say prepare now
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: No watches are in effect yet. Forecasters urge residents to finish preparations and be ready to act if evacuation orders come.
item.content:encoded:
The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael now covers Corpus Christi, the National Weather Service said Thursday, though no hurricane watch has been issued yet for the Coastal Bend.

A watch, when one is issued, means hurricane conditions are possible in the area. It is typically the step before a warning, which means those conditions are expected. The time between the two is when most preparation and evacuation decisions are made.

"Don't wait for a watch. This is the point where you stop planning and start doing," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you live in a surge zone, decide today where you'll go and how you'll get there. If you're told to leave, leave."

Rafael became a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier this week, and forecasters have warned that it could strengthen rapidly. Arceneaux urged residents not to fix on the storm's current category. "Category tells you about wind at the center," he said. "It doesn't tell you about surge, and it doesn't tell you what the storm will be when it gets here."

The ground is already soaked. A moisture plume and a stalled front drenched the region Tuesday, the Nueces River rose at Calallen and soils remain saturated, so heavy rain from Rafael would run off quickly into streets and waterways.

The relief supply chain is also moving. Relief shipments are being booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reports today in Business.

What to do now:

Finish preparations today. Secure outdoor items, fill prescriptions and gas tanks, and charge phones and power banks.

Know your zone. If you are in a hurricane evacuation zone, pick your destination and route now.

Register if you need a ride. County emergency managers urge residents without cars to call 2-1-1.

Check on neighbors, especially older residents and people who live alone.

Follow official sources: the National Weather Service, Nueces County emergency management and your city. The Ledger will update this story through the day.

item.title: Rafael becomes a hurricane; forecasters warn of rapid strengthening over warm Gulf water
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Hurricane Rafael is gaining strength in the Gulf. No watches are in effect yet for the Coastal Bend, but forecasters urge residents to finish preparations now.
item.content:encoded:
Rafael crossed the Yucatan Peninsula and became a hurricane over warm water in the southern Gulf, the National Weather Service said, and forecasters are warning that it could strengthen rapidly.

Rapid strengthening has a specific meaning to forecasters: an increase in a storm's sustained winds of at least 35 mph within 24 hours. It happens when a storm finds the right mix of warm water, moist air and light winds aloft, and it is one of the hardest things in weather to forecast precisely.

"Warm water is fuel, and Rafael is sitting on a lot of it," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "What worries me about rapid strengthening is that it shrinks the time people think they have. Do the things you'd do in three days, today."

The track forecast continues to show Rafael moving on a west-northwest path toward Texas. The cone remains wide enough that forecasters will not yet say where the storm will come ashore, and no watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Wednesday morning.

The region is not starting dry. Tropical moisture and a stalled front soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, the Nueces River rose at Calallen and soils are saturated, as the Ledger reported. Any additional heavy rain will run off quickly.

On the bayfront at sunrise, the water was a little choppier than it has been, and a long, slow swell was rolling in from the southeast. The air had the heavy, salt-sticky feel that old-timers on the coast recognize. None of that is a forecast. It is a reminder that the Gulf is busy.

What to do now: finish your kit. Refill prescriptions. Fill gas tanks. Get cash. Bring in or tie down patio furniture. Find out whether you live in an evacuation zone and where you would go. If you do not have a car, call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. If you care for someone who needs medical help to leave, make that call today.

The weather service issues full advisories on Rafael every six hours, with updates in between. The Ledger will update this story as forecasts change.

item.title: Tropical moisture ahead of Rafael soaks the Coastal Bend; Nueces River rising at Calallen
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Saturated ground means more runoff with every downpour. Forecasters say the soaking is a preview, not the main event.
item.content:encoded:
The first downpour arrived before dawn Tuesday, a gray curtain dragged in off the Gulf. Rain hammered the bayfront for a few minutes, the palms bent, and then the sun came out over wet streets as if nothing had happened. An hour later, the next one came through.

A plume of tropical moisture ahead of Tropical Storm Rafael and a stalled front soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, and the Nueces River was rising at Calallen, according to the National Weather Service. Soils across the region are saturated.

"When the ground is already full, rain has nowhere to go but the streets and the rivers," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "This rain is a preview. The storm itself hasn't even reached the Gulf yet."

Saturated soil changes how a region responds to rain. Dry ground absorbs a downpour. Wet ground sends most of it straight into ditches, storm drains and creeks, which feed the river. The Nueces River gauge at Calallen, upstream of Nueces Bay and near the city's water treatment plant, is one of the readings forecasters watch most closely in a wet week, because it shows how much water is moving toward the coast.

Rafael itself remains a tropical storm in the northwestern Caribbean, with forecasts continuing to show it crossing the Yucatan and heading toward Texas. Arceneaux said moisture arriving this far ahead of a storm is a reminder that a tropical system's effects arrive in pieces, not all at once.

"People wait for the storm to show up on their street," he said. "It shows up in pieces. Rain first, then wind, then water. Use the rain days to get ready for the rest."

What to do: Never drive through water over the road; turn around instead. Clear leaves and trash from storm drains near your home if you can do it safely. Move vehicles out of low spots that pond in heavy rain. And keep finishing your hurricane plan.

River readings for the Nueces at Calallen are posted online by the weather service and updated through the day. The Ledger will update river and storm information as forecasters release it.

item.title: On a holiday weekend in Port Aransas, the forecast becomes small talk
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: The beaches are full and the bait shops busy, but Tropical Storm Rafael is the topic at every counter on Mustang Island.
item.content:encoded:
At Hargrove Bait & Tackle on Saturday afternoon, the conversation at the counter ran in the same order every time: shrimp, ice, how the fish were biting at the jetties, and what that storm was doing.

"Everybody's a meteorologist on Labor Day weekend," said Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns the shop a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties. "I tell them what my daddy told me. Watch the birds and watch the TV, and believe the TV."

Tropical Storm Rafael formed Saturday in the northwestern Caribbean, and early forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan and heading toward Texas. No watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Sunday morning, and forecasters said it was too early to know where the storm would go.

On the island, the holiday went ahead. Port Aransas businesses have had a strong summer, and the long weekend brought one more wave of visitors: families dragging coolers across the sand, charter boats heading out at first light, a line of cars waiting at the ferry landing across the water in Aransas Pass. On the beach, a few people checked weather apps between swims. Most did not.

Hargrove said the storm talk was friendly so far. Regulars asked whether he was putting up plywood. He was not. "I cut my plywood in May. It's labeled. It doesn't go up for a Saturday tropical storm," he said. "It goes up when the man on TV stops smiling."

Asked how busy the weekend had been, he would not guess at a number. "Busy enough that I ran out of ice twice," he said. "That's my weather report."

He did take one step. Behind the counter, next to the tide chart, he had taped up a printed list of phone numbers: the county, the city, a cousin inland. "I'm not saying I'm going anywhere," he said. "I'm saying I know who I'd call."

Emergency managers urge island residents and visitors alike to know their route off the island and to check the forecast before heading home Monday. Hargrove put it more simply as he rang up a bag of frozen squid. "Have a good time," he told the customer. "And keep an eye on that thing."

item.title: Tropical Storm Rafael forms in the Caribbean; early forecasts point toward Texas
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: It is too early to say where Rafael will come ashore, forecasters say, but early tracks show a west-northwest path toward the Texas coast. Coastal Bend residents should review their plans this weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean Sea on Saturday, and early forecasts show it moving west-northwest across the Yucatan Peninsula and into the Gulf, with Texas among the possible targets, according to the National Weather Service.

The sky over Corpus Christi Bay was a hard, cloudless blue Saturday morning. Sailboats rode their moorings off the marina, joggers worked the seawall, and holiday traffic was already building toward the islands. Nothing about the view suggested a storm. That is what makes the first days of a tropical system tricky.

"This is the time to pay attention, not the time to panic," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Early tracks have Texas in the picture. They also carry a lot of uncertainty. The cone is wide for a reason."

That uncertainty is normal this early. As the Ledger explained last weekend, the forecast cone shows the probable path of a storm's center, and it is widest for the days furthest out. Track forecasts tend to tighten as a storm organizes and as reconnaissance aircraft and weather balloons feed more data into the models. Intensity forecasts, how strong a storm will get, are harder still.

Rafael arrives in the heart of a season that forecasters said last month would be busier than normal. The water it is crossing is late-summer warm, the kind that gives a storm room to grow.

Many residents and visitors are on the islands for the Labor Day weekend. Arceneaux said there was no reason to cancel plans yet, but every reason to pay attention. "Enjoy the weekend, and check the forecast twice a day," he said. "If you're in an evacuation zone, spend ten minutes today thinking about what you'd do if this comes our way."

What to do now: review your family's plan, check your hurricane kit, refill prescriptions, and look up whether your home is in an evacuation zone. If you do not have a car and would need help leaving, county emergency managers urge you to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1.

No watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Saturday morning. The Ledger will update this story as forecasts change.

item.title: Need medical help to evacuate? Register before a storm, health workers urge
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Residents who depend on oxygen, dialysis, home health visits or a ride should sign up with the state's evacuation assistance registry now. A home health aide explains why.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo knows which of her clients use oxygen at night, which ones cannot manage stairs and which ones keep their pill bottles in a shoebox by the bed. That knowledge is part of the job. In hurricane season, it is also a worry.

"If a storm comes, my clients can't just get in a car," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rides city buses between appointments. "Some of them can't get out of bed by themselves. Ay, you think I'm going to carry them to the bus?"

Residents without cars should sign up for evacuation assistance before a storm, county emergency managers have said. Residents with medical needs should do the same. The State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, known as STEAR, lets people tell local planners in advance that they will need help leaving, including help with mobility, oxygen or other medical equipment.

Here is what health workers recommend doing now, before any storm is on the map:

Register. Call 2-1-1 or sign up online for STEAR. Describe the help you need: wheelchair, oxygen, a service animal, someone to help you onto a bus.

Talk to your providers. Ask your doctor, dialysis center or home health agency what their storm plan is and how appointments or treatments would be rescheduled.

Stock your medicines. Keep extra prescriptions on hand if your insurance and pharmacist allow it, and carry a written list of every medication and dose.

Plan for power. If you rely on powered equipment, keep backup batteries charged and know where you would go if the power stays out.

Caregivers, plan for yourselves too. The people who look after others often leave their own plans for last.

That last one hits home for Elizondo. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, including hers, and she has helped several clients register with the state. She has not yet registered her own family.

"I keep saying I'll do mine," she said, laughing at herself. "This week. Lo prometo."

item.title: Half the nation's crude exports, one ship channel: what the port's monthly high means here
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Crude exports through the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August. The port now handles about half of U.S. crude exports, nearly all of it moving through a single channel past downtown.
item.content:encoded:
Here is the simplest way to understand the Port of Corpus Christi's August: about half of the crude oil the United States sells abroad now leaves through one ship channel that runs past downtown Corpus Christi.

Crude exports from the port hit a monthly high in August, analysts said Tuesday. The milestone caps a summer in which the port loaded tankers at a near-record pace and tankers routinely waited at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for their turn at a berth.

The chain behind that number is straightforward. Crude arrives by pipeline from West Texas oil fields to tank farms and terminals along the ship channel and the Inner Harbor. Tankers arrive from the Gulf, wait at the anchorage, take on a pilot, transit the entrance channel at Port Aransas and tie up to load. Then they sail. Each link depends on the one before it, and nearly all of them depend on the channel being open.

Locally, that chain supports work for terminal crews, pilots, tug operators, line handlers, truckers and the businesses that serve them. When the channel is busy, the paychecks are steady.

"Corpus got to half the market by being very good at one thing in one place," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The pipes, the tanks and the docks all grew up around that channel."

The flip side of concentration is exposure. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, and the Coast Guard can restrict or close the channel when a storm approaches, leaving tankers at anchor and loadings paused until it reopens.

The channel also serves the port's role as a designated strategic seaport. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation, sharing the same waterway with the crude trade.

None of that is a forecast. It is a reminder of what rides on one narrow ribbon of dredged water. For most of the year, that channel is the city's economic engine. For a few weeks each fall, it is also the thing everyone watches when a storm is in the Gulf.

item.title: Relief warehouses fill up and freight forwarders sign standby deals as peak season nears
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Relief agencies have stocked up ahead of the busiest weeks of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby contracts to move supplies quickly if a storm hits.
item.content:encoded:
The supply chain for a hurricane starts months before the storm, in warehouses most people never see and in contracts most people never read.

Relief agencies have stocked their warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby relief contracts, arrangements that let agencies call up trucks, containers and cargo space quickly if a storm strikes the region. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season, which makes those arrangements more than paperwork this year.

A standby contract works like a reservation with the terms already agreed. The forwarder commits to have capacity available, and the agency agrees in advance on rates and how to activate it. The point is to avoid negotiating prices and schedules in the middle of an emergency, when every truck and every container is in demand at once.

It helps to think of relief supplies in three layers. The first is what families keep at home: water, food, medicine and batteries for several days. The second is what neighborhood hubs, churches and local agencies keep nearby. The third is what moves in by truck and by ship after a storm, from warehouses that may be hundreds of miles away. The third layer is the largest and also the slowest, because it depends on roads, bridges and, for sea freight, an open ship channel.

The Port of Corpus Christi can be part of that third layer, receiving containers by sea. But a storm that threatens the Coastal Bend can also close the channel, and ships carrying relief cargo would wait offshore with everyone else until it reopens.

At the second layer, the stockpiles are smaller and closer to home. Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs meals and supplies from her church's fellowship hall near the bay, and she has spent the summer filling a storage closet with water, canned goods and batteries.

"The big warehouses are for the region. My closet is for the block," Whitfield said. "Both of them need to be full before the wind starts."

For households, the lesson of the layers is simple: outside help takes time to arrive. Emergency managers recommend keeping enough supplies at home to get through several days on your own.

item.title: Cones, watches and warnings: how to read a hurricane forecast before you need to
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: With forecasters expecting a busy rest of the season, here is what the forecast products mean, and why storm surge matters most on the coast.
item.content:encoded:
The cone is the most famous graphic of hurricane season and the most misunderstood. With forecasters expecting an above-normal rest of the season, now is a good time to learn to read it before it matters.

The cone shows the probable track of a storm's center. It is drawn from the size of past forecast errors, so it widens farther out in time, and the center stays inside it roughly two-thirds of the time. It does not show how big the storm is. Wind, rain and surge routinely reach far outside the cone's edges.

"People look at the skinny line in the middle and decide they're safe if it's pointed somewhere else," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Ignore the line. Watch the whole cone, and then look past it."

Watches and warnings are the next step. A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible in an area, and it is usually issued about 48 hours before tropical-storm-force winds are expected. A hurricane warning means those conditions are expected, typically about 36 hours ahead. The time between those products is when most preparation and evacuation happens, and it goes quickly.

On the coast, the number that matters most is storm surge: water pushed ashore by a storm's winds, measured in feet above normally dry ground. Surge is the deadliest part of most hurricanes, and the weather service issues separate surge watches and warnings for it.

"Wind you can hide from in a sturdy building," Arceneaux said. "Water you can't. If you're in a surge zone and you're told to leave, leave."

Surge also stacks on top of the tide. On the Coastal Bend, the shape of the bays matters: water driven into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay has fewer places to go than water on an open beach. A storm that arrives at high tide brings that water higher still.

County emergency managers have spent the summer urging residents to learn their evacuation zones and asking those without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. Arceneaux said the best time to look up your zone is a quiet Sunday. "Do it now," he said, "while the only thing on the map is the coastline."

item.title: At the jetties, a bait shop owner reads the summer by the line at his counter
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer. Bill Hargrove, who has sold bait near the jetties for years and ridden out two hurricanes on the island, says he is grateful, and watching the Gulf.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Hargrove can tell you how the summer went without opening his register. He points at the floor in front of his counter, where the linoleum has worn pale in a strip that runs toward the door.

"That's where the line goes," he said. "This year it went out the door and turned left."

Hargrove, 64, owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties. Port Aransas businesses are reporting a strong summer, with bait shops and fishing charters especially busy, and Hargrove said his shop was no exception. Weekend mornings, the live shrimp tank emptied early. Weekday afternoons brought families who had never held a rod and wanted to know what to buy.

"Tourists ask me where the fish are," he said. "I tell them, 'In the water. Next question.'"

He has watched the channel traffic from that corner for years: dolphins working the pass, charter boats heading out before dawn, and tankers sliding past so close to the jetties that customers stop talking to watch them go by. He knows which end of the jetties fishes best on an incoming tide and which tourists will be back for more bait in an hour.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes on the island and does not recommend it. "The first time I thought I was brave," he said. "The second time I knew better." He keeps plywood cut to size and labeled by window in the back of the shop, a habit he picked up after the second one.

Forecasters said this week they expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Hargrove heard it on the radio between customers. "Above normal," he repeated, and shook his head. "Around here, normal is plenty."

Asked how much business was up this year, he would not put a number on it. "More than last year, less than I'd like," he said. "Same answer I've given for a long time."

Labor Day is two weekends away, and with it the end of the summer crowds. After that, Hargrove said, the island gets quiet, the locals get the jetties back, and everybody starts watching the Gulf a little more closely. "Then it's just us and the weather," he said. "And the weather doesn't buy bait."

item.title: Forecasters expect a busy rest of hurricane season
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: An updated seasonal outlook calls for above-normal Atlantic activity through the end of the season. The Coastal Bend's peak weeks are still ahead.
item.content:encoded:
The Gulf off Mustang Island was flat and warm as bathwater on Tuesday morning, the kind of late-August calm that makes it easy to forget what the season is for. Forecasters would like you to remember.

An updated seasonal outlook released Tuesday calls for above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season. The outlook does not predict where storms will go or whether any will reach Texas. It describes how busy the basin as a whole is likely to be.

"An outlook is a weather forecast for the whole ocean, not for your street," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "It tells us the dice are loaded a little more than usual. It doesn't tell us where they land."

The Atlantic season runs June 1 through Nov. 30, and its busiest stretch historically runs from mid-August into October, peaking in early to mid-September. Warm water is the fuel. By late summer, the Gulf has had months to heat up, and the shallow shelf off the Texas coast holds that heat well.

Arceneaux said nobody on the Coastal Bend should change plans because of an outlook. "What I want people to hear is, make sure you have a plan at all," he said. "Know your evacuation zone. Know where you'd go. Know how you'd get there. If the answer to that last one is 'I don't know,' fix that now."

County emergency managers have been sending the same message all summer, holding preparedness fairs and urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance through the state registry by calling 2-1-1.

The quiet weeks are also the time to check insurance. Homeowners policies generally do not cover flooding, and a new flood insurance policy usually takes 30 days to take effect, so a policy bought when a storm is in the Gulf may not help with that storm.

The tide gauge on Corpus Christi Bay showed nothing unusual Tuesday, just the gentle rise and fall of a summer bay. That is what an outlook cannot see, and why forecasters keep saying the same thing: prepare in the calm.

item.title: Opinion: If you would need a ride out, ask for it now, not when the cone is on TV
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Column: The state's evacuation assistance registry only works if the people who need it sign up before a storm has a name.
item.content:encoded:
I have covered two hurricanes for this newspaper. The images that stay with me are not the wind or the water. They are the people on porches with a suitcase and a phone, waiting for a ride that nobody had planned for.

This summer, county emergency managers held preparedness fairs and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Advocates have pushed for more evacuation rides, because bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay. Those are not slogans. They are the plain facts of where people live and how they get around, and they point to a simple request.

If you would need a ride out, register now. The State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry lets residents who need help evacuating, whether because they have no vehicle, a disability or a medical need, tell local planners in advance. You can sign up by calling 2-1-1. It is free. It does not guarantee anything, and it does not obligate you to leave. What it does is put your address on the list planners use to decide where buses go.

If you have a car, find out who on your street does not. Ask the older man two doors down whether he has somewhere to go. Ask the family with three kids and one bus pass. Offer a seat now, so the offer is already made when it matters.

If you employ home health aides, cooks, cleaners or anyone else who rides the bus to your door, ask them what their plan is. Many of them spend storm season making sure other people get out.

I am suspicious of anyone who claims to know how many people will need a ride in the next storm. Nobody knows. That is the point of the registry: to replace guesses with names and addresses, before the decisions have to be made in a hurry.

The busiest weeks of hurricane season are ahead of us. Make the call in August, while the Gulf is calm and the line at 2-1-1 is short. It is the least dramatic thing you will do all season, and it may be the most useful.

item.title: Aransas Pass shrimper heads into fall season with fair catches and a fuel bill that bites
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Huy Nguyen, a second-generation bay shrimper, says the season started fair but diesel costs are eating into every trip.
item.content:encoded:
Huy Nguyen keeps a spiral notebook in the wheelhouse of his shrimp boat. One column is what came over the side. The other is what went into the tank. He writes both down after every trip, in pencil, before he goes home.

"The notebook tells the truth even when I don't want to hear it," Nguyen, 51, said Wednesday afternoon, tied up at the harbor in Aransas Pass after a day on the bay. The deck still smelled of salt and diesel, and a few gulls waited on the pilings in case he changed his mind about the bycatch.

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season earlier this summer, and Nguyen agrees: catches have been steady and the shrimp a decent size. The problem is the other column. Fuel costs are squeezing margins for boats like his, which burn diesel by the hour whether the nets come up full or not.

"Fair is fair. Fair doesn't pay for diesel," he said. Asked how far apart his two columns are, he tapped the notebook and declined to read it aloud. "Closer than my father's were. Not in the good direction."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His father worked the same water, and Nguyen still finds the grounds by the landmarks he learned as a boy: a channel marker, a line of oyster reef, the way the bottom changes color under the boat on a clear morning. At dawn, he said, the bay goes from pewter to green as the sun clears the barrier islands, and that is still the best part of the job.

With the fall bay season now under way, he is weighing every trip against the fuel it will take. Some days he stays closer to home. Some days he gambles. "You can't catch shrimp tied to the dock," he said. "You also can't buy diesel with shrimp you didn't catch."

There is one more thing he watches this time of year. "September, I look at the sky more than the nets," Nguyen said. "The bay gives you a living. The Gulf can take it back in one night."

He closed the notebook, put it back on the shelf above the wheel, and went to see about ice.

item.title: Back to class in Calallen, with the storm plan taped by the door
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: As the school year begins across Nueces County, teachers are setting up classrooms and districts are reviewing how they would close campuses if a hurricane threatens.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos keeps two lists on the wall beside her classroom door. One is for the first week of school: name tags, supply bins, the order her students will line up for lunch. The other, printed on yellow paper, is what she will do if a hurricane closes the building.

"The yellow one I hope I never use," said Ramos, 45, who teaches in Calallen and lives a short drive from the city's water treatment plant on the Nueces River. "But I have been doing this long enough to know August is when you write it, not September."

The school year begins this week across Nueces County, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans as classes start. Those plans govern how families are told that campuses will close, how buildings are secured and how schools decide when it is safe to reopen.

For Ramos, the hard part of past storm seasons was never the decision to close. It was the patchwork of messages that followed. "One text, one time, from one place. That's all a parent wants," she said. "Half my families find out from a cousin's post, and then they call me to ask if it's true."

She has started the year by asking every family for a working cell number and an email address, and by telling parents to sign up for district alerts the first night, not the night a storm is in the Gulf.

County emergency managers have spent the summer making a similar pitch to the wider public, holding hurricane preparedness fairs and urging residents who do not have cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. Ramos said she repeats the advice to parents at open house whether or not they ask.

"Fill the gas tank, fill the prescriptions, know where you would go," she said. "Then go buy the glue sticks."

On Monday morning, the yellow list goes back on the wall where she can see it. The supply bins, she said, are already full.

item.title: Rosa Elizondo's hurricane plan runs on bus time and neighbors
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: A home health aide and mother of three, Elizondo has spent the summer piecing together a plan for a storm she hopes never comes. It starts with not having a car.
item.content:encoded:
On Saturday mornings, Rosa Elizondo makes pancakes, and her three kids argue about who gets the first one. Her youngest, 6, usually wins. Her oldest, a teenager, usually pretends not to care.

The rest of the week, Elizondo, 38, belongs to the bus. A home health aide, she rides city buses between clients' homes across Corpus Christi, packing frozen water bottles against the heat and keeping a mental map of every route, every transfer and every stop with decent shade. She rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay, in one of the low-income neighborhoods where many families do not have a car.

This summer, between shifts, she has been working on another kind of map: what she would do if a hurricane came.

It started at a Nueces County preparedness fair last month, where, as the Ledger reported, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Elizondo left with a registration card and a free flashlight. Since then, she has talked the question through with her pastor, her neighbors and her kids.

"Everybody's plan says 'drive,'" she said. "So my plan is a list of people who drive." Her list includes a neighbor, friends from church and Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall and keeps a notebook of neighbors without cars. "And the county, if they come," she added. "I pray they come."

Advocates in neighborhoods near the bay have been pushing for more evacuation rides, saying the bus gaps that strand families on ordinary weekends would be worse in an emergency. Elizondo is blunter. "On a normal Sunday, the bus takes forever," she said. "On a storm day? Nobody's going to stand at a bus stop in the rain with three kids. I'm not going to."

She has packed a bag, more or less: documents in a zipper bag, a change of clothes for everybody, a phone charger and whatever medicine the kids might need. The flashlight from the fair is in there too, though her youngest keeps borrowing it.

Asked whether she worries, Elizondo laughed. "Ay, mija, I'm a mom. I worry about everything," she said. "But I'd rather worry now, while it's sunny, than later."

item.title: Perseids peak tonight, and Coastal Bend stargazers head for dark skies on the islands
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: The year's most popular meteor shower peaks overnight. The best views are away from city lights, and a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer has some advice.
item.content:encoded:
If you are willing to stay up late and drive a little, the sky over the Coastal Bend has a show tonight. The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight Thursday into Friday morning, and the best place to watch is somewhere dark: a stretch of beach on Padre or Mustang Island, well away from parking-lot lights and condo balconies.

The Perseids are bits of debris shed by a comet, and Earth passes through the trail every August. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see many meteors an hour near the peak, though moonlight, clouds and city glow cut that number down.

Jaime Ortega, 42, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer who films the night sky, has been planning his Perseids night for weeks. He sets a camera on a tripod, aims it high and lets it run for hours. "Patience is the whole trick," Ortega said. "Lie down, look up, give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust and put your phone away. The phone ruins everything."

He has learned to read what shows up in his footage. "After a while you know what everything looks like," Ortega said. "A meteor is a quick streak. A satellite is a slow, steady dot. The planes from the air station blink and head home. Once you know the regulars, anything new jumps out at you."

Tips: Get away from city lights; the islands' darker beaches are a good bet. Bring a blanket or reclining chair, bug spray and water. Watch after midnight, when meteor rates usually climb. Scan the whole sky rather than staring at one spot. Respect beach rules and private property, and keep vehicles off the dunes.

Summer nights have been mostly clear lately, though a passing cloud bank can always spoil the view. The islands have been crowded all summer, so expect company. "That's part of it," Ortega said. "You hear a whole beach go 'Ooh' at the same time. Best sound in the world."

item.title: Before the heart of hurricane season, relief warehouses fill and freight firms sign on standby
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Relief agencies are stocking shelves and freight forwarders are signing standby contracts so supplies can move quickly if a storm hits the Coastal Bend.
item.content:encoded:
In warehouses around Corpus Christi this month, the shelves are filling: pallets of bottled water, tarps, cots, hygiene kits and nonperishable food, stacked, shrink-wrapped and waiting for a storm everyone hopes will not come.

Relief agencies are stocking their warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders that move supplies into disaster areas are signing standby relief contracts, agreements that let agencies call on trucks, containers and handling capacity on short notice.

"A standby contract is basically a reservation you hope you never use," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handles relief cargo through the Port of Corpus Christi. "We pre-plan the lanes, line up the boxes and the drivers, and if the call comes we're moving freight in hours, not days."

Akins said the work this time of year is mostly planning: confirming warehouse space, mapping alternate routes in case a highway or the port is closed, and deciding which supplies need to move first. "The stuff people need on day one is water, power and somewhere dry to sleep," he said. "If it's not staged before the storm, you're shipping it after, and after is always slower."

Neighborhood groups are stocking up, too.
