Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, said her shelves are filling with canned goods, diapers and bottled water donated by members and neighbors. "The big trucks matter," Whitfield said. "But the first plate of food after a storm usually comes from somebody's church kitchen."

The port is a key link in that chain. In normal times it is busy with near-record crude exports. In a disaster, it is one of the ways bulk relief cargo can reach the region when highways are jammed.

Akins said the hardest part of standby work is that success is invisible. "If we did our job right," he said, "nobody ever hears my name."

item.title: Summer scorecard: tankers, tourists and a depot that's hiring
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: From the export docks to the bait shops, the Coastal Bend economy has had a busy summer. A few soft spots are worth watching.
item.content:encoded:
With August under way, the Coastal Bend's summer economy looks busy almost everywhere you check.

The port: Crude export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel have been loading tankers at a near-record pace all summer, and vessels waiting for berths have been a routine sight at the anchorage off Port Aransas. "The export machine is running about as hard as it can," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That's good news for the region. Every tanker that loads is work for pilots, tug crews and line handlers."

The bases: Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, a steady source of skilled jobs, and training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule. The air station completed a routine readiness inspection late last month with base services operating normally. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer, bringing short-term work for longshore crews and truck drivers.

The islands: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters booked and bait shops busy. Mustang and Padre islands have drawn heavy crowds since early summer.

Soft spots: Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, but fuel costs have squeezed margins. "Fuel is the first bill and the biggest one," Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen told the Ledger last month. And in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, transit gaps make it harder for households without cars to reach jobs across town, a cost that rarely shows up in economic statistics.

What to watch: Late summer is also the peak of hurricane season on the Gulf Coast. For a regional economy this tied to the water, a busy August can turn quickly on things no one controls, from weather to fuel prices to a single disruption in a crowded channel.

For now, the cash registers on the island, the paychecks at the depot and the tankers in the channel are all telling the same story: it has been a good summer.

item.title: Bait, ice and a few tall tales: Bill Hargrove's long view from the jetties
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: Bill Hargrove has sold bait near the Port Aransas jetties for decades. He has ridden out two hurricanes there, and he has opinions about almost everything else.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Hargrove opens the shop before the gulls are fully awake. By 6 a.m. the aerators are bubbling in the live-bait tanks, the ice machine is groaning, and the first truck of the morning is idling in the shell lot outside Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties.

"Shrimp, ice, a weather report and a lie about where the reds are biting," said Hargrove, 64, ticking off his inventory. "Only one of those is free, and I won't tell you which."

Businesses in Port Aransas report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy, and Hargrove's register agrees. He has watched the island through good seasons and bad ones, and he can tell you which year the tarpon came back and which year the beach washed out, though the details shift a little depending on who is asking.

The jetties are his landmark and his living. Twin rock walls guard the pass where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf, and every big ship headed to or from the port slides between them. Hargrove's customers fish the rocks while tankers pass close enough to feel through your feet. "Tourists take pictures of the ships," he said. "Locals take pictures of the fish. The ships don't care either way."

He knows the island's lore, too. He will tell you that a president once came to Port Aransas to fish for tarpon, and that the town was once called Tarpon, both of which happen to be true.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes at the shop, including Harvey, which tore through Port Aransas and left much of the island in pieces. He does not romanticize it. "People think riding one out makes you tough. It makes you lucky," he said. "Everybody tells me I'm too old to do it again. Everybody's probably right."

For now, the worry is simpler: keeping enough bait in the tanks for a summer that won't slow down. "Good year," Hargrove said, sliding a bag of ice across the counter. "Knock on wood. Actually, knock on something sturdier than wood. This is Port A."

item.title: A Calallen teacher's summer homework: a phone tree for her whole street
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Leticia Ramos spent part of her summer break building a contact list for her neighbors. She says hurricane season is no time to wait for someone else to get organized.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos has a clipboard, and she is not afraid to use it.

Over the past few weeks, the 45-year-old schoolteacher has knocked on nearly every door on her street in Calallen, on the northwest edge of Corpus Christi, collecting names, phone numbers and one more piece of information: who would need help if something went wrong.

"Teachers make lists. It's an occupational hazard," Ramos said from her kitchen table, where a printed spreadsheet sat next to a stack of classroom supplies she had bought for the fall. "I figured if we ever need to check on each other, I don't want to be standing in the street yelling names."

The idea came from a Nueces County hurricane-season preparedness fair, where emergency managers urged residents to make a plan and to register anyone without a car for evacuation assistance. Ramos left with a folder of handouts and a conviction that her street needed its own plan, too.

Her list notes which neighbors are older, who lives alone, who has a generator, who has a truck and who has young children. It also notes who does not have a smartphone, so they can be called rather than texted.

Ramos lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, and like her neighbors she follows the city's summer conservation requests closely. She has told the Ledger before that she wants the city to communicate faster and more plainly. "I'm not trying to replace anybody," she said. "I just think the fastest way to get news to my street is my street."

A few neighbors laughed at first, she said. Most have since asked for a copy. "Mrs. Ramos has a list" has become a running joke on the block, and something of a comfort.

"Nothing is happening," Ramos said. "That's exactly when you do this. You don't build the phone tree when the phone is already ringing."

item.title: Opinion: A ride out of a storm shouldn't depend on who you know
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Nueces County asks residents without cars to register for evacuation help. That is necessary, and it is not enough.
item.content:encoded:
Editor's note: This is an opinion column.

Every hurricane season, the advice arrives in the same shape: know your zone, pack a kit, fill the tank. For many families in this city, the last part does not apply. There is no tank to fill.

Nueces County emergency managers have been doing the right thing this summer. At preparedness fairs, they have urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance through the state's 2-1-1 registry, and they have said plainly that the registry is not only for people with disabilities. Last month I watched Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three, fold a registration card into her purse at one of those fairs.

But registration is a list, and a list is only as good as the ride at the end of it. As Coastline Public Radio reported Saturday, advocates in neighborhoods near the bay say bus gaps already leave families stranded on ordinary weekends. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who keeps her own notebook of neighbors without cars or phones, put it best: a list in a notebook doesn't send a bus.

Here is what the county and city could do before the season peaks. Publish where evacuation pickup points will be, neighborhood by neighborhood, now and not on the day of an order. Partner with churches and neighborhood hubs that already know who needs help. And go door to door in the neighborhoods where the fewest people own cars, rather than waiting for phone calls that may never come.

None of this is a criticism of the people who will drive the buses and staff the shelters. They have done this before, and they will do it again. It is a question of where the work starts. If the plan starts at the shelter door, it is already too late for the person who never made it to the bus.

A storm will not check who owns a car. Our plans shouldn't either.

item.title: Why the city keeps asking you to save water in the summer
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Every tap in Corpus Christi traces back to one treatment plant in Calallen. Here is how the water gets to you, and why the heat matters.
item.content:encoded:
Turn on a faucet anywhere in Corpus Christi and the water coming out has made a long trip. It starts in reservoirs and the Nueces River, passes through the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen and travels through miles of pipe and pump stations before it reaches your kitchen.

That is why, when summer heat settles over the Coastal Bend, the city's water utility asks residents to conserve. It has been making that request again this month.

"Our system is built to meet demand, but summer stretches every part of it at once," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "When everyone waters at 4 in the afternoon, we're treating and pumping water that mostly evaporates. Shift it to early morning, fix the leak, and you're helping the whole system."

The basics: O.N. Stevens is the city's only water treatment plant. It draws raw water, treats and filters it, disinfects it and sends it out to homes, businesses and neighboring communities. Demand climbs in hot, dry weather, largely because of outdoor watering.

What you can do: Water lawns only on your scheduled day, and early or late. Use a broom, not a hose, on driveways. Run dishwashers and washing machines with full loads. Check for leaks; a running toilet can waste a surprising amount of water. Keep a pitcher of cold water in the refrigerator instead of running the tap until it cools.

A health note: Conserving water should never mean skimping on drinking water in the heat. Older adults, children and outdoor workers need to drink regularly, even if they do not feel thirsty.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen a few minutes from the plant, said neighbors take the conservation requests seriously but want clearer updates. "People out here will do their part," Ramos said. "We just want to hear it from the city first, in plain words, not from a rumor at the gas station."

The utility posts updates on the city's website and social media, Gallegos said, and residents can report leaks and water main breaks to the city.

item.title: Why the Army ships helicopters out of Corpus Christi, and how that fits with the oil trade
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's late-summer movement will share a busy ship channel with near-record crude exports. Here is how the port handles both.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi is best known these days for oil. Crude export terminals along the ship channel are loading tankers at a near-record pace, and ships waiting for a berth are a routine sight at the anchorage off Port Aransas.

But the port has a second job that gets less attention until a moment like this one. On Wednesday, Army and port officials said an aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation.

Why here: The port is one of a small group of commercial ports the Defense Department has designated as strategic seaports, meaning it has agreed to make dock space and services available for military cargo when needed. It sits a few hours' drive from Fort Hood, has deep water and has handled Army cargo before.

How it fits: Military equipment does not load at the crude docks. Helicopters, vehicles and containers move through general cargo berths that can handle roll-on, roll-off ships, where equipment is driven or towed aboard. That keeps the brigade's loading physically apart from the tanker traffic, though both share the same channel, and the same pilots and tugs, to reach the Gulf.

"Scheduling is what we do every day," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "Tankers, cargo ships, military moves. Everybody gets a slot, and everybody gets out on time."

The economics: A single military move is a small piece of the port's business compared with the daily crude trade. But it brings work for longshore crews, truck drivers, security staff and port employees during staging and loading, and it reinforces a relationship with the Army that the port counts as part of its identity.

What is not public: The Army has not released dates, routes or the number of aircraft involved, and officials described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

item.title: The pastor who keeps a list
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield knows which neighbors have no car, which have no phone and which can't manage stairs. She wants the county to know too.
item.content:encoded:
The notebook lives in Pastor Gloria Whitfield's purse, a spiral-bound thing with a cracked cover and a rubber band around it. Inside, in pencil, are names and street addresses, and next to them a shorthand only she fully understands: "no car," "no phone," "walker," "son in Houston," "will need help with the dog."

"This is my parish," said Whitfield, 59, tapping the cover. "Not the building. The people in this book."

Whitfield runs meals and supplies out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, where many households do not have a vehicle and some do not have a working phone. On Wednesdays the hall smells like rice, beans and coffee. On any other day, she said, the door opens if someone needs it to.

As the Ledger reported Wednesday, she brought a carload of neighbors to a Nueces County hurricane-season preparedness fair, where emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Whitfield stood in line with them while they filled out cards.

"I'm not against the county. I'm for the county knowing what I know," she said. "When they tell people to leave, the people in this book can't just leave. Somebody has to come. And somebody has to know where to come."

Her list started years ago as a prayer list and grew into something more practical: who needs groceries carried in, who needs a ride to the doctor, who has grandchildren staying for the summer. She updates it after every service and every meal.

Neighbors say the list works because of who keeps it. "She knows before I tell her," said Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who relies on buses. "That's Pastor Gloria. You don't call her. She calls you."

Whitfield said her goal for the summer is simple: every person in her notebook who would need a ride out of a storm should be on the county's registry as well. "I'll sit at the kitchen table with them and dial the phone myself," she said. "God gave me a car and a loud voice. I intend to use both."

item.title: Bay shrimpers see a fair start to the season, but diesel is eating the margin
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: In Aransas Pass, shrimpers say catches have been decent so far. The trouble is what it costs to go out and get them.
item.content:encoded:
The shrimp boats at Aransas Pass leave the harbor before the sun is fully up, outriggers raised like folded wings, and come back in the afternoon heat with gulls trailing behind them. So far this season, the boats have had something to show for it.

Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, with steady catches in the bays around Aransas Pass. What they do not describe as fair is the fuel bill.

"The shrimp are there. That's not the problem," said Huy Nguyen, 51, who owns a shrimp boat out of Aransas Pass. "Diesel is the problem. Fuel is the first bill and the biggest one. You pay it before you know if you caught anything."

Nguyen learned the bays on his father's boat and has worked them most of his life. He talks about the business in plain arithmetic: a good day pays for the fuel, the ice and the deckhand, and maybe a little toward what he owes on the boat. A slow day does not. "Three good days and one bad one, you're even," he said. "Two bad ones, you're borrowing."

The squeeze is familiar along the Texas coast, where small family operations compete with imported shrimp on price and absorb swings in fuel, ice and repair costs on thin margins.

At the docks, the routine is the same whether the day was good or bad: hose the deck, ice what came in, settle up with the buyer and look at the fuel gauge. Nguyen does the last part twice.

The bays themselves look healthy to the people who work them. Nguyen said the shrimp have been running at a decent size this summer, and the grass flats where young shrimp grow have looked good on the clear days. "The bay is doing its part," he said. "I'm trying to do mine."

Asked what would make the season, he did not hesitate. "Cheaper fuel and no surprises," Nguyen said. "On the water, surprises are never the good kind."

item.title: In summer heat, home health aides keep watch over the people most at risk
item.dc:creator: Dana Whitlock
item.description: Older and homebound residents are among the most vulnerable in a Coastal Bend summer. The aides who visit them are often the first to notice trouble.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo starts every visit the same way. Before she checks a pill organizer or helps a client to the shower, she walks to the thermostat and looks at the number.

"If the house is hot, everything else waits," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rides city buses between clients' homes across Corpus Christi. "Some of my ladies won't turn on the air because of the bill. I tell them, señora, the light bill is cheaper than the hospital."

The heat that is filling Mustang and Padre islands with beachgoers this summer is a different problem indoors. Older adults, people with heart or lung disease and people who take certain medications can overheat without feeling especially thirsty, and a house without working air conditioning can become dangerous over a few days.

Elizondo, a mother of three who does not own a car, spends part of each workday waiting at bus stops in the same heat. She carries two frozen water bottles in her bag, one for herself and one for whichever client needs it more. "By the second bus it's just cold water," she said. "By the third client it's warm water. Still water."

What to watch for: Heat exhaustion can bring heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or muscle cramps. Heat stroke is an emergency, marked by confusion, a very high body temperature and hot skin. Call 911 for anyone with signs of heat stroke, and cool them with water and shade while you wait.

What to do: Check on older neighbors at least once a day during hot spells. Make sure fans and air conditioners work, close blinds in the afternoon and offer water often. If someone cannot keep a home cool, help them spend the hottest hours somewhere air-conditioned, such as a library or a store.

Elizondo said the hardest part of the job in July is not the work itself. "It's leaving," she said. "You lock the door and you think, is she going to be OK tonight? So I call. Everybody gets a phone call before I go to bed."

item.title: At hurricane fair, county's message to residents without cars: tell us now
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Nueces County emergency managers handed out flashlights, evacuation maps and a plea Wednesday: if you will need a ride out in a storm, register before one is on the way.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo came to the hurricane fair for the free flashlight. Her youngest, 6, came for the bubbles. By the time they left a recreation center gym Wednesday afternoon, Elizondo, 38, also had a registration card for evacuation help folded into her purse.

"I don't have a car. I have three kids and two bus routes," said Elizondo, a home health aide who rents a few blocks from the bay. "If they tell us to leave, I need somebody to tell me how."

That is exactly the conversation Nueces County emergency managers say they want to have now, long before any storm. At hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer, county staff are walking residents through evacuation zones and go-kits and urging anyone without a vehicle to register for evacuation assistance.

"If you don't have a way out, we need to know who you are and where you are before the storm, not during it," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Once the wind picks up, it's too late to start a list."

Residents can sign up through the state's emergency assistance registry by dialing 2-1-1, Pruitt said. The registry is for anyone who would need help in an evacuation, including people without transportation, not only people with disabilities or medical needs.

Tables around the gym offered evacuation-zone maps, battery radios, first-aid checklists and advice on storing documents in waterproof bags. Children collected stickers. Adults collected paperwork.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, brought a carload of neighbors from her church and stood in line with them. She keeps her own list of who on her streets has no car or no phone, she said, and she wants the county's list to match. "I know who those people are by name," Whitfield said. "The county should too. A list in my notebook doesn't send a bus."

Elizondo said she would fill out the card that night, after the kids were asleep. "If I don't fall asleep first," she said, laughing. "Ay, Dios. Ask me in a week."

item.title: From a North Beach lawn chair, a retired welder watches the export boom sail by
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Marcus Bell spent his working life welding along the ship channel. Now he watches the tankers it serves from a lawn chair on North Beach.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Bell does not need a ship-tracking app. From the lawn chair outside his place on North Beach, the 67-year-old retired welder can watch the tankers slide past between the beach and downtown, close enough to hear the engines, headed for the docks of the Inner Harbor or back out toward the Gulf.

"Used to be a big ship came under that bridge and people would stop what they were doing and watch," Bell said. "Now there's one coming or going all day long, and nobody looks up but me."

He has reason to look. Bell spent more than 30 years welding pipe and steel at refineries and fabrication yards along the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, and he still talks about the waterfront the way some people talk about an old job site: by who built what, and how well.

The traffic he watches is part of a boom. Crude export terminals at the Port of Corpus Christi are loading tankers at a near-record pace this summer, and vessels waiting for a berth routinely sit at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. Crude arrives by pipeline from West Texas and leaves by ship, and the channel past North Beach is one of the routes it takes.

Summer brings its own traffic to North Beach: families on the sand, visitors at the aquarium and the aircraft carrier museum, and weekend cars backing up on the Harbor Bridge.

Bell keeps an eye on that, too. North Beach sits on a narrow strip of land between Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay, and the way in and out runs over bridges: the Harbor Bridge to downtown and the Nueces Bay Causeway toward Portland. "You live out here, you learn the bridge is your front door," he said.

Asked what he thinks about when the tankers pass, Bell shrugged. "Steel and welds," he said. "Every one of those ships is somebody's good work or somebody's shortcut. You can't tell which from a lawn chair."

item.title: Army depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and it is looking close to home
item.dc:creator: Grant Okafor
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot, one of the region's biggest employers, is recruiting mechanics to repair and overhaul Army helicopters at its hangars on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.
item.content:encoded:
Most people in Corpus Christi have driven past the Army depot without ever seeing inside it. Behind the gates of Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, in hangars near the edge of the bay, civilian workers take Army helicopters apart down to the airframe, repair them and send them back to units around the world.

Now the depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and it is pitching the jobs to local workers.

"We want people who like to fix things and want to do work that matters," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for Corpus Christi Army Depot. "A lot of our mechanics grew up here, learned the trade here and stayed. That's the workforce we're trying to keep building."

The depot is the Defense Department's primary facility for overhauling rotary-wing aircraft and their components, and its civilian workforce makes it one of the largest employers in the Coastal Bend. The work runs from airframe and sheet-metal repair to engines, rotor components and the wiring and electronics that tie them together.

The hangars are a long way from a typical shop floor. Mechanics work from detailed technical manuals, and every repair is documented and inspected before an aircraft or component moves to the next station. "It's precise work, and it's work you can be proud of," Kowalczyk said.

Kowalczyk said applicants with aviation maintenance training or military mechanic experience are a natural fit, and that the depot trains new hires on its own procedures and standards. "If you've turned a wrench in the military, at a refinery or on a shrimp boat, there's a place to start the conversation," she said.

For the regional economy, the hiring is one more sign of a busy summer. Next door on the air station, Navy training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule, and along the ship channel, crude export terminals are loading tankers at a near-record pace.

Job seekers can find the depot's openings on USAJOBS, the federal government's hiring site, Kowalczyk said.

item.title: Where the river meets the bay: a summer morning in the Nueces Delta
item.dc:creator: Ellie Navarro
item.description: At the head of Nueces Bay, the marshes of the Nueces Delta are humming with birds, crabbers and kayakers, a quieter side of a busy coastal summer.
item.content:encoded:
At first light the water in the Nueces Delta is the color of strong tea and almost perfectly still. A great blue heron works the edge of a cordgrass bank. Somewhere out of sight, a mullet jumps twice. Across Nueces Bay, the refinery stacks along the ship channel catch the sun before anything else does.

This is the other Coastal Bend summer. While Mustang and Padre islands fill with beach crowds, the marshes where the Nueces River spreads into Nueces Bay draw a smaller set of regulars: kayakers who put in along the river near Calallen, families crabbing with chicken necks and string at the bay's edge, and birders with long lenses and longer patience.

The delta is a nursery. Young shrimp, crabs and fish shelter in its shallow channels and tidal creeks before moving out into the open bay, which is one reason the marshes matter to the shrimpers and anglers who work Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

It is also a place shaped by people. The Nueces River runs past the city's water treatment plant at Calallen before it reaches the marsh, and in a hot summer, when the city is asking residents to conserve, the river slides through the delta slowly, almost lazily, toward the bay.

Paddlers who know the delta say mornings are the time to go. By noon the heat is heavy, the southeast wind picks up and the open bay chops into short, steep waves. Bring more water than seems reasonable, a hat, a charged phone in a dry bag and someone on shore who knows when you plan to be back.

On the way out, the Nueces Bay Causeway carries a steady line of traffic between Corpus Christi and Portland, and from the open bay the bridges and the industrial skyline beyond them look closer than they are. For a few hours in the early morning, though, the loudest thing in the delta is the birds.

item.title: Islands fill up as summer heat settles in, and the city asks for a lighter touch on the tap
item.dc:creator: Marisol Treviño
item.description: Visitors are packing Mustang and Padre islands this July. Back on the mainland, Corpus Christi's water utility is asking residents to conserve while the heat holds.
item.content:encoded:
By 9 a.m. Thursday, the line of cars waiting for the Port Aransas ferry had already stretched back along the highway from Harbor Island, and the sand on Mustang Island was dotted with canopies from the jetties south. It is the heart of summer on the Coastal Bend, and the islands are full.

Rental houses, hotels and beach parking areas on Mustang and North Padre islands have been busy since school let out, and the heavy tourist traffic shows no sign of easing during the hot weeks ahead.

Back on the mainland, the heat is showing up somewhere else: on the water meter. The City of Corpus Christi's water utility is urging residents to conserve while temperatures stay high, asking them to stick to the city's watering schedule, water lawns early in the morning or late in the evening instead of midafternoon, and fix dripping faucets and running toilets.

"Summer is when demand climbs fastest, and a lot of that is lawns," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the utility. "We're not asking anyone to suffer through the heat. We're asking people to water at the right time, fix the leak they've been meaning to fix, and think twice before they hose down the driveway."

The city's drinking water is treated at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen, on the Nueces River at the city's northwest edge, before it is pumped across Corpus Christi and to neighboring communities.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen not far from the plant, said her street has gotten the message, mostly. "My tomatoes are on the schedule like everybody else's," Ramos said. "What I'd like is for the city to just text me when something changes, instead of me finding out from a neighbor's post three days later."

Gallegos said the utility posts conservation updates on the city's website and social media accounts and encouraged residents to sign up for city alerts.

For visitors, the heat brings its own reminders: drink water before you feel thirsty, find shade during the middle of the day, and respect the rip current flags at the beach.
